papers.limitation: The evaluation scores reported in studies on syntactic structure induction are often too weak to prove that language models adhere to linguistic theories.
future_direction: Exploring more sophisticated methods for integrating syntactic information.
Extending the approach to other languages.
Improving the evaluation metrics for syntactic structure induction.
papers.abstract: Linear sequences of words are implicitly represented in our brains by hierarchical structures that organize the composition of words in sentences. Linguists formalize different frameworks to model this hierarchy; two of the most common syntactic frameworks are Constituency and Dependency. Constituency represents sentences as nested groups of phrases, while dependency represents a sentence by assigning relations between its words. Recently, the pursuit of intelligent machines has produced Language Models (LMs) capable of solving many language tasks with a human-level performance. Many studies now question whether LMs implicitly represent syntactic hierarchies. This thesis focuses on producing constituency and dependency structures from LMs in an unsupervised setting. I review the critical methods in this field and highlight a line of work that utilizes a numerical representation for binary constituency trees (Syntactic Distance). I present a detailed study on StructFormer (SF) (Shen et al., 2021), which retrofits a transformer encoder architecture with a parser network to produce constituency and dependency structures. I present six experiments to analyze and address this field's challenges; experiments include investigating the effect of repositioning the parser network within the SF architecture, evaluating subword-based induced trees, and benchmarking the models developed in the thesis experiments on linguistic tasks. Models benchmarking is performed by participating in the BabyLM challenge, published at CoNLL 2023 (Momen et al., 2023). The results of this thesis encourage further development in the direction of retrofitting transformer-based models to induce syntactic structures, supported by the acceptable performance of SF in different experimental settings and the observed limitations that require innovative solutions to advance the state of syntactic structure induction.

papers.title: Using Priming to Uncover the Organization of Syntactic Representations\n in Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How are syntactic representations organized in neural language models? The paper investigates the organization of representations for sentences with relative clauses using a priming-based technique.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel technique based on syntactic priming to analyze how syntactic representations are organized in neural language models, and demonstrates that LSTM LMs' representations of sentences with relative clauses are organized hierarchically in a linguistically interpretable manner.
papers.conclusion: The proposed priming-based technique reveals that the representations of sentences with relative clauses in LSTM LMs are organized in a linguistically interpretable hierarchical manner.
papers.key_findings:
Sentences with the same syntactic structure are more similar to each other in the LM's representation space than lexically matched sentences with different structures.
Sentences with different types of relative clauses are more similar to each other than to sentences without relative clauses, suggesting LMs track the abstract property of a gap.
LMs track linguistically interpretable features like reduction and passivity, with passivity contributing more to similarity than reduction.
Similarity between sentences is driven not only by shared function words but also by abstract syntactic properties, though this ability decreases with increased training corpus size.
No evidence was found that the similarity between object RCs and other RCs predicts agreement prediction accuracy.
papers.limitation:
For linguistically interpretable classes without lexically observable properties, similarity might be driven by lexical items rather than abstract properties.
No evidence found that similarity between object RCs and other RCs predicts agreement prediction accuracy.
future_direction: Compare similarity matrices generated from LMs with human representations using priming experiments.
Explore how to bias models to track linguistically useful properties through architectural biases, training on auxiliary tasks, or data augmentation.
papers.abstract:
Neural language models (LMs) perform well on tasks that require sensitivity
to syntactic structure. Drawing on the syntactic priming paradigm from
psycholinguistics, we propose a novel technique to analyze the representations
that enable such success. By establishing a gradient similarity metric between
structures, this technique allows us to reconstruct the organization of the
LMs' syntactic representational space. We use this technique to demonstrate
that LSTM LMs' representations of different types of sentences with relative
clauses are organized hierarchically in a linguistically interpretable manner,
suggesting that the LMs track abstract properties of the sentence.

papers.title: Probing for Constituency Structure in Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent do contextual neural language models implicitly learn syntactic constituency structure, and can this syntactic knowledge be separated from semantic knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Constituency structure is linearly separable from the representations of pretrained language models, even when the data is semantically nonsensical, indicating that syntactic and semantic knowledge are separated in the models.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained language models encode fine-grained constituency structure, and this syntactic knowledge can be separated from semantic knowledge, as demonstrated by probing even on semantically nonsensical data.
papers.key_findings:
Constituency structure is linearly separable at model, layer, and neuron levels.
Middle layers of the models are most important for representing syntactic information.
Syntactic information is distributed across many neurons.
Different sets of neurons capture syntactic and semantic information.
A full constituency tree can be reconstructed with high accuracy using linear probes on LM representations.
future_direction: Extend the syntactic probing approach to other languages and syntactic annotation schemes.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate to which extent contextual neural language models (LMs) implicitly learn syntactic structure. More concretely, we focus on constituent structure as represented in the Penn Treebank (PTB). Using standard probing techniques based on diagnostic classifiers, we assess the accuracy of representing constituents of different categories within the neuron activations of a LM such as RoBERTa. In order to make sure that our probe focuses on syntactic knowledge and not on implicit semantic generalizations, we also experiment on a PTB version that is obtained by randomly replacing constituents with each other while keeping syntactic structure, i.e., a semantically ill-formed but syntactically well-formed version of the PTB. We find that 4 pretrained transfomer LMs obtain high performance on our probing tasks even on manipulated data, suggesting that semantic and syntactic knowledge in their representations can be separated and that constituency information is in fact learned by the LM. Moreover, we show that a complete constituency tree can be linearly separated from LM representations.

papers.title: Finding Structure in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do language models possess a deep understanding of grammatical structure similar to humans, and how can such structures be identified?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that language models capture abstract linguistic structure similar to humans, and develops interpretability techniques to reveal this structure. It shows that models exhibit structural priming, generalize from indirect evidence, and that interpretability methods must be evaluated with care.
papers.conclusion: The thesis provides a detailed account of grammatical knowledge in language models and offers directions for using computational methods to investigate linguistic questions.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit human-like structural priming effects, indicating they capture abstract syntactic structure.
Language models can generalize linguistic patterns from indirect evidence, as shown by filtered corpus training experiments.
Interpretability methods for feature interaction detection vary in faithfulness and must be evaluated carefully.
Language models use monotonicity information to predict negative polarity item licensing.
Adjective order preferences in language models are influenced by data statistics and cognitive factors.
papers.abstract: When we speak, write or listen, we continuously make predictions based on our knowledge of a language's grammar. Remarkably, children acquire this grammatical knowledge within just a few years, enabling them to understand and generalise to novel constructions that have never been uttered before. Language models are powerful tools that create representations of language by incrementally predicting the next word in a sentence, and they have had a tremendous societal impact in recent years. The central research question of this thesis is whether these models possess a deep understanding of grammatical structure similar to that of humans. This question lies at the intersection of natural language processing, linguistics, and interpretability. To address it, we will develop novel interpretability techniques that enhance our understanding of the complex nature of large-scale language models. We approach our research question from three directions. First, we explore the presence of abstract linguistic information through structural priming, a key paradigm in psycholinguistics for uncovering grammatical structure in human language processing. Next, we examine various linguistic phenomena, such as adjective order and negative polarity items, and connect a model's comprehension of these phenomena to the data distribution on which it was trained. Finally, we introduce a controlled testbed for studying hierarchical structure in language models using various synthetic languages of increasing complexity and examine the role of feature interactions in modelling this structure. Our findings offer a detailed account of the grammatical knowledge embedded in language model representations and provide several directions for investigating fundamental linguistic questions using computational methods.

papers.title: Language Modeling Teaches You More Syntax than Translation Does: Lessons Learned Through Auxiliary Task Analysis
papers.research_question: How does the training task affect how well models learn syntactic properties, and which tasks are better at inducing these properties? How does the amount of training data affect these results?
papers.core_contribution: Bidirectional language models (BiLMs) consistently perform best on syntactic auxiliary tasks (POS and CCG tagging) compared to translation, skip-thought, and autoencoding objectives, even when trained on relatively small amounts of data. Randomly initialized LSTMs perform well when auxiliary classifiers are trained on large amounts of data, but their performance drops sharply with less data, indicating trained models capture genuine syntactic features.
papers.conclusion: Bidirectional language modeling is the best pretraining task for inducing syntactic representations useful for transfer learning, and trained encoders capture genuine syntactic features rather than just memorizing word identities.
papers.key_findings:
Bidirectional language models (BiLMs) outperform translation and skip-thought encoders on part-of-speech (POS) tagging and CCG supertagging across all data sizes.
BiLMs trained on only 1 million sentences outperform translation and skip-thought models trained on larger datasets (5 million and 63 million sentences).
Randomly initialized, untrained LSTM encoders perform nearly as well as trained models on tagging tasks when auxiliary classifiers are trained on all available data, but their performance drops below trained models when classifier training data is reduced.
Trained encoders underperform randomly initialized encoders on the task of predicting neighboring word identity, confirming that trained encoders capture syntactic features beyond mere word identity.
Lower layers of LSTMs (both trained and untrained) capture more local neighboring word information, while upper layers capture more distant context information.
papers.abstract: Recent work using auxiliary prediction task classifiers to investigate the properties of LSTM representations has begun to shed light on why pretrained representations, like ELMo (Peters et al., 2018) and CoVe (McCann et al., 2017), are so beneficial for neural language understanding models. We still, though, do not yet have a clear understanding of how the choice of pretraining objective affects the type of linguistic information that models learn. With this in mind, we compare four objectives---language modeling, translation, skip-thought, and autoencoding---on their ability to induce syntactic and part-of-speech information. We make a fair comparison between the tasks by holding constant the quantity and genre of the training data, as well as the LSTM architecture. We find that representations from language models consistently perform best on our syntactic auxiliary prediction tasks, even when trained on relatively small amounts of data. These results suggest that language modeling may be the best data-rich pretraining task for transfer learning applications requiring syntactic information. We also find that the representations from randomly-initialized, frozen LSTMs perform strikingly well on our syntactic auxiliary tasks, but this effect disappears when the amount of training data for the auxiliary tasks is reduced.

papers.title: A Polar coordinate system represents syntax in large language models
papers.research_question: How are syntactic relations (type and direction) represented in the activations of large language models? Specifically, are they coded by a polar coordinate system where distance and relative direction between word embeddings represent the existence and type of syntactic relations?
papers.core_contribution: This work shows that syntactic trees are represented in LLMs by a polar coordinate system where distance and direction between word embeddings encode the existence and type of syntactic relations, and introduces the Polar Probe, a linear readout method that recovers this structure.
papers.conclusion: LLMs spontaneously learn a geometry of neural activations that explicitly represents the main symbolic structures of linguistic theory, reconciling symbolic and connectionist formalisms.
papers.key_findings:
The Polar Probe successfully recovers the type and direction of syntactic relations, substantially outperforming the Structural Probe by nearly two folds.
The polar coordinate system exists in a low-dimensional subspace of the intermediate layers of many LLMs and becomes increasingly precise in the latest frontier models.
Similar syntactic relations are coded similarly across the nested levels of syntactic trees, as demonstrated on a controlled dataset.
papers.limitation:
Only the English language is investigated, limiting generalization to other languages with different grammatical rules.
Syntactic structures are not necessarily restricted to words; morphology predicts that words themselves may be represented as trees of morphemes, which is not explored.
The Polar Probe is based on a supervised task requiring known syntactic structures; an unsupervised probe would be important for discovering unsuspected structures.
The work assumes Euclidean probes; alternative assumptions like hyperbolic representations could be fruitful but are not explored.
future_direction: Exploring universal (or divergent) grammatical representations in artificial neural networks across languages.
Investigating whether the framework generalizes to different scales of linguistic structures, such as morphology.
Developing an unsupervised probe to discover unsuspected syntactic structures.
Testing alternative linguistic theories (e.g., phrase structures) with the probing framework.
Exploring hyperbolic or other non-Euclidean representations for syntactic trees.
papers.abstract: Originally formalized with symbolic representations, syntactic trees may also be effectively represented in the activations of large language models (LLMs). Indeed, a 'Structural Probe' can find a subspace of neural activations, where syntactically related words are relatively close to one-another. However, this syntactic code remains incomplete: the distance between the Structural Probe word embeddings can represent the existence but not the type and direction of syntactic relations. Here, we hypothesize that syntactic relations are, in fact, coded by the relative direction between nearby embeddings. To test this hypothesis, we introduce a 'Polar Probe' trained to read syntactic relations from both the distance and the direction between word embeddings. Our approach reveals three main findings. First, our Polar Probe successfully recovers the type and direction of syntactic relations, and substantially outperforms the Structural Probe by nearly two folds. Second, we confirm that this polar coordinate system exists in a low-dimensional subspace of the intermediate layers of many LLMs and becomes increasingly precise in the latest frontier models. Third, we demonstrate with a new benchmark that similar syntactic relations are coded similarly across the nested levels of syntactic trees. Overall, this work shows that LLMs spontaneously learn a geometry of neural activations that explicitly represents the main symbolic structures of linguistic theory.

papers.title: Neural Language Models as Psycholinguistic Subjects: Representations of Syntactic State
papers.research_question: To what extent do neural network language models reflect incremental representations of syntactic state?
papers.core_contribution: Large LSTMs trained on large datasets can represent syntactic state comparably to an explicitly syntactic model (RNNG), and data size is crucial for learning fine-grained lexical cues to syntactic structure.
papers.conclusion: All models show basic incremental syntactic state representation, but capturing fine-grained lexical cues requires large amounts of data, while coarse-grained structure can be learned with either syntactic supervision or large data.
papers.key_findings:
All tested models show basic evidence of incremental syntactic state representation (e.g., subordinate clause licensing).
Only the large LSTMs (GRNN, JRNN) and the RNNG fully capture the proper behavior of subordinate clauses (no-matrix penalty).
All models show NP/Z garden path effects, but only large LSTMs are sensitive to verb transitivity as a cue.
All models show MV/RR garden path effects, but only large LSTMs and the RNNG are sensitive to verb morphology as a cue.
The representation of syntactic state degrades with increasing intervening material in some models (GRNN and TinyLSTM).
future_direction: Using psycholinguistic methodology as a basis for more systematic tests of the linguistic competence of NLP systems.
papers.abstract: We deploy the methods of controlled psycholinguistic experimentation to shed light on the extent to which the behavior of neural network language models reflects incremental representations of syntactic state. To do so, we examine model behavior on artificial sentences containing a variety of syntactically complex structures. We test four models: two publicly available LSTM sequence models of English (Jozefowicz et al., 2016; Gulordava et al., 2018) trained on large datasets; an RNNG (Dyer et al., 2016) trained on a small, parsed dataset; and an LSTM trained on the same small corpus as the RNNG. We find evidence that the LSTMs trained on large datasets represent syntactic state over large spans of text in a way that is comparable to the RNNG, while the LSTM trained on the small dataset does not or does so only weakly.

papers.title: Structural Supervision Improves Few-Shot Learning and Syntactic\n Generalization in Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How well do neural language models learn syntactic properties from few examples, and can they generalize these properties across syntactic transformations?
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models can learn syntactic generalizations from minimal exposure and show syntactic invariance, with structural supervision improving accuracy and invariance.
papers.conclusion: Neural language models are capable of few-shot syntactic learning and show some syntactic invariance, with structural supervision enhancing these abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Neural models induce proper syntactic generalizations for nominal number and verbal argument structure after just two or three exposures during training.
Structurally supervised models (ActionLSTM and RNNG) outperform the pure sequence LSTM model in most tests.
All neural models demonstrate syntactic invariance by transferring generalizations from base contexts to transformed contexts.
Models exhibit a bias towards singular nouns and transitive verbs when evidence is sparse, supporting a default reasoning hypothesis.
Increased exposure improves accuracy, especially for non-base categories like plural nouns and intransitive verbs.
papers.limitation: Models were trained on a relatively small corpus (Penn Treebank), which may limit the generalizability of the findings.
future_direction: Scaling these carefully-controlled methods to larger data settings.
papers.abstract:
Humans can learn structural properties about a word from minimal experience,
and deploy their learned syntactic representations uniformly in different
grammatical contexts. We assess the ability of modern neural language models to
reproduce this behavior in English and evaluate the effect of structural
supervision on learning outcomes. First, we assess few-shot learning
capabilities by developing controlled experiments that probe models' syntactic
nominal number and verbal argument structure generalizations for tokens seen as
few as two times during training. Second, we assess invariance properties of
learned representation: the ability of a model to transfer syntactic
generalizations from a base context (e.g., a simple declarative active-voice
sentence) to a transformed context (e.g., an interrogative sentence). We test
four models trained on the same dataset: an n-gram baseline, an LSTM, and two
LSTM-variants trained with explicit structural supervision (Dyer et al.,2016;
Charniak et al., 2016). We find that in most cases, the neural models are able
to induce the proper syntactic generalizations after minimal exposure, often
from just two examples during training, and that the two structurally
supervised models generalize more accurately than the LSTM model. All neural
models are able to leverage information learned in base contexts to drive
expectations in transformed contexts, indicating that they have learned some
invariance properties of syntax.

papers.title: Probing the Emergence of Cross-lingual Alignment during LLM Training
papers.research_question: How does cross-lingual alignment emerge during the pre-training of multilingual large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates a strong correlation between cross-lingual neuron overlap and zero-shot transfer performance in multilingual LLMs, and reveals non-monotonic alignment dynamics during pre-training with drops in smaller models.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms that shared neurons encoding linguistic features are tightly connected to cross-lingual transfer ability, providing insights into multilingual pretraining dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Neuron overlap for linguistic features increases during pre-training but experiences severe drops in smaller model scales like BLOOM560m and BLOOM1b1.
There is a statistically significant, strong correlation between neuron overlap and zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance on tasks like POS tagging and XNLI.
Larger models (e.g., BLOOM1b7) show more monotonic growth in alignment, suggesting a scaling law effect.
Drops in alignment correspond to degradation in both in-language and cross-lingual performance.
The emergence of cross-lingual alignment is not steady and can pass through sub-optimal regions during training.
papers.limitation:
Focus on BLOOM checkpoints with large intervals, so findings might not apply to finer-grained training windows.
Only consider autoregressive models with the same objective and training dataset; varying these may result in different patterns.
Focus on alignment of languages seen during pretraining, leaving generalization to unseen languages for future research.
papers.abstract: Multilingual Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve remarkable levels of zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance. We speculate that this is predicated on their ability to align languages without explicit supervision from parallel sentences. While representations of translationally equivalent sentences in different languages are known to be similar after convergence, however, it remains unclear how such cross-lingual alignment emerges during pre-training of LLMs. Our study leverages intrinsic probing techniques, which identify which subsets of neurons encode linguistic features, to correlate the degree of cross-lingual neuron overlap with the zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance for a given model. In particular, we rely on checkpoints of BLOOM, a multilingual autoregressive LLM, across different training steps and model scales. We observe a high correlation between neuron overlap and downstream performance, which supports our hypothesis on the conditions leading to effective cross-lingual transfer. Interestingly, we also detect a degradation of both implicit alignment and multilingual abilities in certain phases of the pre-training process, providing new insights into the multilingual pretraining dynamics.

papers.title: Cross-Lingual Generalization and Compression: From Language-Specific to Shared Neurons
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models achieve cross-lingual generalization?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides empirical evidence that cross-lingual generalization in multilingual language models emerges through compression during pre-training, with representations evolving from language-specific to shared cross-lingual abstractions, demonstrated via neuron analysis and manipulation.
papers.conclusion: Cross-lingual generalization in multilingual language models emerges through compression during pre-training, leading to the development of shared concept neurons across languages that encode generalized semantic representations.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual models initially form language-specific representations which gradually converge into cross-lingual abstractions as training progresses.
Language identification probing reveals a shift from uniform capabilities across layers to specialized layer functions, with middle layers becoming more language-agnostic.
Specific neurons emerge as reliable predictors for the same semantic concepts across different languages, showing increasing alignment during training.
Neuron manipulation experiments demonstrate that concept-specific neurons identified from one language can guide semantically coherent text generation in another language once cross-lingual generalization is achieved.
The model's internal representations encode shared conceptual knowledge independent of the original language encoding.
papers.limitation: The number of publicly available training checkpoints for the BLOOM models is limited, restricting the granularity of analysis.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities to transfer knowledge across languages, despite being trained without explicit cross-lingual supervision.We analyze the parameter spaces of three MLLMs to study how their representations evolve during pre-training, observing patterns consistent with compression: models initially form language-specific representations, which gradually converge into cross-lingual abstractions as training progresses.Through probing experiments, we observe a clear transition from uniform language identification capabilities across layers to more specialized layer functions.For deeper analysis, we focus on neurons that encode distinct semantic concepts.By tracing their development during pre-training, we show how they gradually align across languages.Notably, we identify specific neurons that emerge as increasingly reliable predictors for the same concepts across languages.This alignment manifests concretely in generation: once an MLLM exhibits cross-lingual generalization according to our measures, we can select concept-specific neurons identified from, e.g., Spanish text and manipulate them to guide token predictions.Remarkably, rather than generating Spanish text, the model produces semantically coherent English text.This demonstrates that cross-lingually aligned neurons encode generalized semantic representations, independent of the original language encoding.

papers.title: The Same But Different: Structural Similarities and Differences in Multilingual Language Modeling
papers.research_question: When two languages employ the same morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using shared internal circuitry? When two languages require different morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using different internal circuitry?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs use shared internal circuitry for similar syntactic processes across languages, even in independently trained monolingual models, and employ language-specific components (e.g., feed-forward networks) for language-specific morphological processes.
papers.conclusion: The paper finds that cross-lingual structural similarity is represented within LLMs using shared circuits that invoke the same algorithm independent of language, and that language-specific processing is localized to play a causal role only in languages that require it.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual models use a single circuit to handle the same syntactic process independently of the language in which it occurs.
Monolingual models trained independently on English and Chinese each adopt nearly the same circuit for the IOI task, suggesting consistency in how LLMs learn to handle this aspect of language modeling.
For tasks requiring language-specific morphological processes (e.g., past tense marking in English), multilingual models invoke a largely overlapping circuit but employ language-specific components as needed, such as feed-forward networks in English only for morphological marking.
The circuits identified for the IOI task align with prior work, indicating that the same mechanism is shared between English and Chinese within a multilingual model.
Heads specifically responsible for past tense disambiguation are activated in English but not in Chinese, and they suppress present-tense verbs in English.
papers.limitation: Results are limited to specific tasks and datasets, requiring future work for replication and generalization.
future_direction: Replicate and generalize findings to more tasks and datasets.
Explore cross-disciplinary collaborations to gain fresh perspectives on linguistic universality using LLMs.
Investigate whether circuit overlap can be exploited for improving cross-lingual transfer and safety.
papers.abstract: We employ new tools from mechanistic interpretability in order to ask whether the internal structure of large language models (LLMs) shows correspondence to the linguistic structures which underlie the languages on which they are trained. In particular, we ask (1) when two languages employ the same morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using shared internal circuitry? and (2) when two languages require different morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using different internal circuitry? Using English and Chinese multilingual and monolingual models, we analyze the internal circuitry involved in two tasks. We find evidence that models employ the same circuit to handle the same syntactic process independently of the language in which it occurs, and that this is the case even for monolingual models trained completely independently. Moreover, we show that multilingual models employ language-specific components (attention heads and feed-forward networks) when needed to handle linguistic processes (e.g., morphological marking) that only exist in some languages. Together, our results provide new insights into how LLMs trade off between exploiting common structures and preserving linguistic differences when tasked with modeling multiple languages simultaneously.

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language when processing non-English prompts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that multilingual language models like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate representations favoring English before shifting to the target language.
papers.conclusion: The evidence suggests that the abstract 'concept space' in multilingual transformers lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding linguistic biases.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate embeddings in middle layers decode to English versions of the correct next token, even when the input and output are non-English.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space (high entropy, no language), concept space (low entropy, English dominates), and output space (target language dominates).
The concept space is biased towards English, indicating an internal pivot language.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The token energy metric shows that latent embeddings have low energy in middle layers and high energy in later layers when the target language is selected.
papers.limitation:
Focus on the Llama-2 family limits generalizability to other models.
Tasks are simple and provide a highly controlled, toy-like context.
Limited understanding of the structure of the concept space in its original high-dimensional form.
The logit lens only grants approximate access to internal beliefs about output; other information remains hidden.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias changes when decreasing the dominance of English during training, e.g., by using different language mixtures or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks, including more culturally sensitive problems and popular use-cases.
Better understand and map out the concept space in its high-dimensional form.
papers.abstract: We ask whether multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language -- a question of key importance for understanding how language models function and the origins of linguistic bias. Focusing on the Llama-2 family of transformer models, our study uses carefully constructed non-English prompts with a unique correct single-token continuation. From layer to layer, transformers gradually map an input embedding of the final prompt token to an output embedding from which next-token probabilities are computed. Tracking intermediate embeddings through their high-dimensional space reveals three distinct phases, whereby intermediate embeddings (1) start far away from output token embeddings; (2) already allow for decoding a semantically correct next token in the middle layers, but give higher probability to its version in English than in the input language; (3) finally move into an input-language-specific region of the embedding space. We cast these results into a conceptual model where the three phases operate in "input space", "concept space", and "output space", respectively. Crucially, our evidence suggests that the abstract "concept space" lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding the biases held by multilingual language models.

papers.title: Probing for Predicate Argument Structures in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: Do pretrained language models (PLMs) encode the argument structure of a predicate in its contextual representation? How are predicate senses and their argument structures encoded across layers, and how do they differ between verbal and nominal predicates and across languages?
papers.core_contribution: PLMs encode predicate argument structures in their contextual representations, with senses and rolesets encoded at different layers, and verbal and nominal predicates are represented differently. Integrating this knowledge improves SRL performance.
papers.conclusion: Probing PLMs for predicate argument structures reveals how they encode semantic information and provides insights that can be used to improve SRL systems.
papers.key_findings:
PLMs encode predicate argument structures directly into the contextualized representation of a predicate.
Predicate senses and their argument structures are encoded at different layers in PLMs.
Verbal and nominal predicate argument structures are represented differently across the layers of a PLM, making transfer between them non-trivial.
Multilingual PLMs encode predicate argument structure information similarly across English and Chinese.
Integrating predicate-argument structure knowledge into an SRL model via weighted averaging of layers and multi-task learning improves performance.
future_direction: cross-lingual transfer learning for SRL
using all layers of PLMs for SRL
papers.abstract: Thanks to the effectiveness and wide availability of modern pretrained language models (PLMs), recently proposed approaches have achieved remarkable results in dependencyand span-based, multilingual and cross-lingual Semantic Role Labeling (SRL). These results have prompted researchers to investigate the inner workings of modern PLMs with the aim of understanding how, where, and to what extent they encode information about SRL. In this paper, we follow this line of research and probe for predicate argument structures in PLMs. Our study shows that PLMs do encode semantic structures directly into the contextualized representation of a predicate, and also provides insights into the correlation between predicate senses and their structures, the degree of transferability between nominal and verbal structures, and how such structures are encoded across languages. Finally, we look at the practical implications of such insights and demonstrate the benefits of embedding predicate argument structure information into an SRL model.

papers.title: Understanding Syntactic Generalization in Structure-inducing Language Models
papers.research_question: How do different Structure-inducing Language Model (SiLM) architectures compare in terms of their induced syntactic representations, performance on grammaticality judgment tasks, and training dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a systematic evaluation of three Structure-inducing Language Model (SiLM) architectures on natural and formal languages, finding that GPST performs most consistently across settings and that induced syntactic representations vary significantly across training runs.
papers.conclusion: GPST is the most consistent model across evaluations, but all models have weaknesses in induced structure consistency. Formal language evaluation provides a useful testbed for model properties.
papers.key_findings:
None of the three SiLM architectures (StructFormer, UDGN, GPST) dominates across all evaluation metrics.
GPST performs most consistently across evaluation settings and outperforms other models on long-distance dependencies in bracketing expressions.
All SiLM architectures show significant variation in induced syntactic representations when retraining identical architectures on the same data.
Small models trained on large amounts of synthetic data (Dyck languages) provide a useful testbed for evaluating basic model properties.
StructFormer and UDGN fail to induce consistent syntactic representations for length generalization datasets in formal languages.
papers.limitation: Induced syntactic representations are not consistent across different training runs.
future_direction: Improving robustness of induced structures (t_x-consistency).
Expanding evaluation to more languages and linguistic phenomena.
Improving scalability and training efficiency of SiLMs.
papers.abstract: Structure-inducing Language Models (SiLM) are trained on a self-supervised language modeling task, and induce a hierarchical sentence representation as a byproduct when processing an input. SiLMs couple strong syntactic generalization behavior with competitive performance on various NLP tasks, but many of their basic properties are yet underexplored. In this work, we train three different SiLM architectures from scratch: Structformer (Shen et al., 2021), UDGN (Shen et al., 2022), and GPST (Hu et al., 2024b). We train these architectures on both natural language (English, German, and Chinese) corpora and synthetic bracketing expressions. The models are then evaluated with respect to (i) properties of the induced syntactic representations (ii) performance on grammaticality judgment tasks, and (iii) training dynamics. We find that none of the three architectures dominates across all evaluation metrics. However, there are significant differences, in particular with respect to the induced syntactic representations. The Generative Pretrained Structured Transformer (GPST; Hu et al. 2024) performs most consistently across evaluation settings, and outperforms the other models on long-distance dependencies in bracketing expressions. Furthermore, our study shows that small models trained on large amounts of synthetic data provide a useful testbed for evaluating basic model properties.

papers.title: What Syntactic Structures block Dependencies in RNN Language Models?
papers.research_question: Do RNN language models learn specific syntactic island constraints that block filler-gap dependencies, or are they merely sensitive to gross syntactic complexity?
papers.core_contribution: RNN language models learn fine-grained syntactic constraints for filler-gap dependencies, specifically island effects, and can maintain other dependencies like gender expectations through islands, indicating differentiated learning of syntactic rules.
papers.conclusion: RNNs trained on language modeling learn both the unbounded nature and specific constraints of filler-gap dependencies, separating different dependencies with fine-grained syntactic rules.
papers.key_findings:
RNN models maintain filler-gap dependencies through unbounded sentential embeddings, showing sensitivity to hierarchical structure.
Models attenuate expectations for gaps in island constructions but not for gender expectations, indicating island constraints are specific to filler-gap dependencies.
Models learn left branch islands and show gradient sensitivity to coordination islands, but fail to learn sentential subject islands.
The Google model shows unbounded dependency maintenance, while the Gulordava model shows some degradation with depth, reflecting human-like performance limitations.
Model behavior on coordination islands is un-humanlike, with some residual expectations for gaps.
papers.limitation:
Models are conspicuously un-humanlike in some performance characteristics, such as on coordination islands.
Models fail to learn sentential subject islands.
papers.abstract: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) trained on a language modeling task have been shown to acquire a number of non-local grammatical dependencies with some success. Here, we provide new evidence that RNN language models are sensitive to hierarchical syntactic structure by investigating the filler--gap dependency and constraints on it, known as syntactic islands. Previous work is inconclusive about whether RNNs learn to attenuate their expectations for gaps in island constructions in particular or in any sufficiently complex syntactic environment. This paper gives new evidence for the former by providing control studies that have been lacking so far. We demonstrate that two state-of-the-art RNN models are are able to maintain the filler--gap dependency through unbounded sentential embeddings and are also sensitive to the hierarchical relationship between the filler and the gap. Next, we demonstrate that the models are able to maintain possessive pronoun gender expectations through island constructions---this control case rules out the possibility that island constructions block all information flow in these networks. We also evaluate three untested islands constraints: coordination islands, left branch islands, and sentential subject islands. Models are able to learn left branch islands and learn coordination islands gradiently, but fail to learn sentential subject islands. Through these controls and new tests, we provide evidence that model behavior is due to finer-grained expectations than gross syntactic complexity, but also that the models are conspicuously un-humanlike in some of their performance characteristics.

papers.title: Enhancing Multilingual Text Understanding viaTransformer-Based Meta-Learning
papers.research_question: How can multilingual text understanding be enhanced by integrating structured linguistic knowledge (syntactic and semantic) into transformer-based models via meta-learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel framework that synergizes symbolic linguistic formalism with neural representation learning via a Grammar-Infused Representation Alignment (GIRA) strategy, enhancing multilingual text understanding by aligning neural attention mechanisms with syntactic dependencies.
papers.conclusion: The integration of grammatical constraints via GIRA into a transformer-based meta-learning framework significantly improves multilingual text understanding, though limitations exist in handling noisy language and reliance on syntactic annotations.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed model (LexiStruct with GIRA) outperforms baseline methods on multiple multilingual benchmarks (XNLI, MLDoc, TyDiQAt, WikiAnn) across metrics like NDCG, Recall, MRR, and Hit Rate.
Ablation studies show that key components (Syntactic Structure Injection, Syntax-Semantics Alignment, Grammar-Semantics Alignment) are essential for the model's performance, with removal of any leading to significant drops in metrics.
The integration of grammatical constraints via GIRA improves the model's robustness and interpretability in multilingual understanding tasks.
papers.limitation:
The integration of grammatical constraints may reduce the model's flexibility in handling less-structured or noisy language inputs, such as colloquialisms or code-switching phenomena.
The current implementation assumes access to high-quality syntactic annotations, which may not be available for all languages, especially low-resource ones.
future_direction: Explore strategies for relaxing the assumption of high-quality syntactic annotations, possibly through unsupervised or semi-supervised learning of syntactic structures.
Extend the model's adaptability to more diverse and informal language domains to improve broader applicability in real-world multilingual settings.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> In the evolving landscape of computational sciences, the integration of structured linguistic knowledge into deep learningmodels has become increasingly vital for advancing multilingual text understanding. Traditional transformer-based architectures,while powerful, often lack the capacity to inherently capture the syntactic and semantic nuances present across diverselanguages, leading to limitations in generalization and interpretability. To address these challenges, we introduce a novelframework that synergizes symbolic linguistic formalism with neural representation learning. Our approach employsa structure-aware neural language model that incorporates grammatical constraints directly into the learning process,enhancing the model’s ability to comprehend and process multilingual data effectively. Central to our methodology is theGrammar-Infused Representation Alignment (GIRA) strategy, which aligns neural attention mechanisms with syntacticdependencies, ensuring that the model’s internal representations adhere to linguistic structures. Experimental evaluationsdemonstrate that our model achieves superior performance in multilingual understanding tasks, exhibiting enhanced robustnessinterpretability. This work contributes to the field by offering a principled method that bridges the gap between statistical learningand linguistic theory, aligning with the journal’s commitment to advancing both fundamental and applied computational sciences.

papers.title: Alignment Quality Index (AQI) : Beyond Refusals: AQI as an Intrinsic Alignment Diagnostic via Latent Geometry, Cluster Divergence, and Layer wise Pooled Representations
papers.research_question: How can we assess LLM alignment intrinsically by analyzing the separation of safe and unsafe activations in latent space? Which layers and geometric metrics best capture this alignment?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Alignment Quality Index (AQI), a decoding-invariant metric that assesses LLM alignment by measuring the separability of safe and unsafe activations in latent space, and the LITMUS dataset for robust evaluation.
papers.conclusion: AQI provides a decoding-invariant, representation-grounded metric for latent safety evaluation, offering a new lens into model cognition and a pathway for deeper alignment-aware auditing.
papers.key_findings:
AQI correlates with G-Eval and LLM judge scores, validating it as a proxy for alignment.
AQI detects jailbreak-induced representation collapse even when surface metrics show compliance.
AQI reveals alignment drift under safety-agnostic fine-tuning before output metrics degrade.
AQI remains stable across decoding temperatures, unlike behavioral metrics.
AQI can diagnose alignment faking by measuring train-test divergence in latent space.
papers.limitation: AQI relies on the assumption that alignment is reflected in latent geometry, which may not hold for all models or failure modes.
future_direction: Extending AQI to multimodal models and other architectures.
Integrating AQI with causal attribution methods for interpretable diagnostics.
Developing automated alignment auditing pipelines using AQI.
papers.abstract: Abhilekh Borah, Chhavi Sharma, Danush Khanna, Utkarsh Bhatt, Gurpreet Singh, Hasnat Md Abdullah, Raghav Kaushik Ravi, Vinija Jain, Jyoti Patel, Shubham Singh, Vasu Sharma, Arpita Vats, Rahul Raja, Aman Chadha, Amitava Das. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2025.

papers.title: What do you learn from context? Probing for sentence structure in contextualized word representations
papers.research_question: What information do contextualized word embeddings encode, and how do they encode sentence structure across syntactic, semantic, local, and long-range phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a suite of edge probing tasks to analyze contextualized word embeddings, finding they encode more syntactic than semantic information and capture long-range dependencies.
papers.conclusion: Contextualized word embeddings encode syntactic structure more effectively than higher-level semantics, and they do capture long-range dependencies beyond local context.
papers.key_findings:
Contextualized embeddings improve over non-contextualized baselines more on syntactic tasks (e.g., constituent labeling) than on semantic tasks (e.g., coreference).
ELMo's performance cannot be fully explained by local context, indicating it encodes long-range linguistic information.
BERT-large performs best overall, with particularly large gains on coreference tasks.
Randomized encoder weights (orthonormal) account for a portion of ELMo's performance, showing architecture contributes.
Semantic role labeling benefits mainly on core roles tied to syntax, with smaller gains on non-core semantic roles.
future_direction: Exploring fine-tuning of encoder weights within the probing framework.
papers.abstract: Contextualized representation models such as ELMo (Peters et al., 2018a) and BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) have recently achieved state-of-the-art results on a diverse array of downstream NLP tasks. Building on recent token-level probing work, we introduce a novel edge probing task design and construct a broad suite of sub-sentence tasks derived from the traditional structured NLP pipeline. We probe word-level contextual representations from four recent models and investigate how they encode sentence structure across a range of syntactic, semantic, local, and long-range phenomena. We find that existing models trained on language modeling and translation produce strong representations for syntactic phenomena, but only offer comparably small improvements on semantic tasks over a non-contextual baseline.

papers.title: Refusal Falls off a Cliff: How Safety Alignment Fails in Reasoning?
papers.research_question: What mechanism makes the safety alignment vulnerable in reasoning models?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies the 'refusal cliff' failure mode in reasoning models, causally links it to a sparse set of 'Refusal Suppression Heads', and introduces a data selection method (Cliff-as-a-Judge) that efficiently repairs safety alignment using minimal data.
papers.conclusion: The work identifies and mechanistically characterizes the refusal cliff safety failure, links it to specific attention heads, and proposes an efficient data selection method for safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Many poorly-aligned reasoning models correctly identify harmful prompts and maintain strong refusal intentions during thinking, but experience a sharp drop (refusal cliff) at the final tokens before output generation.
A sparse set of attention heads (Refusal Suppression Heads) causally contribute to the refusal cliff by suppressing refusal-related representations.
Ablating just 3% of these heads can reduce attack success rates below 10%.
The proposed Cliff-as-a-Judge data selection method, which selects examples with the largest refusal cliff, achieves comparable safety improvements using only 1.7% of the vanilla safety training data.
The refusal cliff is localized to final tokens, amplified in deeper layers, preceded by a plateau, and depends on the model's thinking process.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic analysis focuses primarily on attention heads, leaving other architectural components such as MLP blocks, positional encodings, and cross-layer interactions underexplored.
The data selection method depends on having access to the model's internal representations and refusal scores, which may be impractical for proprietary systems.
future_direction: Investigation of proxy metrics or black-box analogues for the data selection method.
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) with multi-step reasoning capabilities have shown remarkable problem-solving abilities, yet they exhibit concerning safety vulnerabilities that remain poorly understood. In this work, we investigate why safety alignment fails in reasoning models through a mechanistic interpretability lens. Using a linear probing approach to trace refusal intentions across token positions, we discover a striking phenomenon termed as \textbf{refusal cliff}: many poorly-aligned reasoning models correctly identify harmful prompts and maintain strong refusal intentions during their thinking process, but experience a sharp drop in refusal scores at the final tokens before output generation. This suggests that these models are not inherently unsafe; rather, their refusal intentions are systematically suppressed. Through causal intervention analysis, we identify a sparse set of attention heads that negatively contribute to refusal behavior. Ablating just 3\% of these heads can reduce attack success rates below 10\%. Building on these mechanistic insights, we propose \textbf{Cliff-as-a-Judge}, a novel data selection method that identifies training examples exhibiting the largest refusal cliff to efficiently repair reasoning models' safety alignment. This approach achieves comparable safety improvements using only 1.7\% of the vanilla safety training data, demonstrating a less-is-more effect in safety alignment.

papers.title: Decoding Probing: Revealing Internal Linguistic Structures in Neural Language Models using Minimal Pairs
papers.research_question: How do neural language models capture linguistic information internally, specifically using minimal pairs to probe grammaticality across layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel 'decoding probing' method inspired by cognitive neuroscience to reveal internal linguistic structures in neural language models using minimal pairs, demonstrating that self-supervised models capture abstract linguistic features in intermediate layers with distinct patterns for syntax, morphology, and semantics.
papers.conclusion: Decoding probing bridges cognitive neuroscience and NLP, providing insights into hierarchical linguistic feature capture in LMs, with semantics-syntax interface and morphology being more challenging than syntax.
papers.key_findings:
Self-supervised language models capture abstract linguistic structures in intermediate layers that GloVe and RNN language models cannot learn.
Information about syntactic grammaticality is robustly captured through the first third layers of GPT-2 and distributed in later layers; more layers are required for complex sentences.
Morphological and semantics/syntax interface-related features are harder to capture than syntax.
For Transformer-based models, both embeddings and attentions capture grammatical features but show distinct patterns, with attention heads exhibiting similar tendencies but varied contributions.
papers.limitation: Focuses mainly on structure grammaticality with limited attention to conceptual capabilities.
future_direction: Apply decoding probe methods to reveal LM's ability to master concepts using the COMPS minimal pair dataset.
papers.abstract: Inspired by cognitive neuroscience studies, we introduce a novel `decoding probing' method that uses minimal pairs benchmark (BLiMP) to probe internal linguistic characteristics in neural language models layer by layer. By treating the language model as the `brain' and its representations as `neural activations', we decode grammaticality labels of minimal pairs from the intermediate layers' representations. This approach reveals: 1) Self-supervised language models capture abstract linguistic structures in intermediate layers that GloVe and RNN language models cannot learn. 2) Information about syntactic grammaticality is robustly captured through the first third layers of GPT-2 and also distributed in later layers. As sentence complexity increases, more layers are required for learning grammatical capabilities. 3) Morphological and semantics/syntax interface-related features are harder to capture than syntax. 4) For Transformer-based models, both embeddings and attentions capture grammatical features but show distinct patterns. Different attention heads exhibit similar tendencies toward various linguistic phenomena, but with varied contributions.

papers.title: Does Syntax Need to Grow on Trees? Sources of Hierarchical Inductive Bias in Sequence-to-Sequence Networks
papers.research_question: Which architectural factors affect the generalization behavior of neural sequence-to-sequence models trained on syntactic tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The only architectural factor that consistently imparted a hierarchical bias across syntactic tasks was the use of a tree-structured model with explicit parse tree input, suggesting human-like syntactic generalization requires architectural syntactic structure.
papers.conclusion: Many architectural factors can affect inductive biases, but human-like syntactic generalization may require explicit tree structure in the model when learning from text alone.
papers.key_findings:
The type of recurrent unit (SRN, GRU, LSTM) and attention mechanism (none, location-based, content-based) qualitatively affect inductive biases, but do not consistently lead to hierarchical generalization.
LSTMs and GRUs exhibit different inductive biases, partly due to squashing in GRUs.
Only tree-based models given correct parse trees consistently showed hierarchical generalization across both question formation and tense reinflection tasks.
Sequential models failed to generalize hierarchically even when provided with bracketed input or trained in a multi-task setting.
Tree-based models are not constrained to hierarchical generalizations; they can learn linear transformations if trained on unambiguous data.
papers.limitation:
Humans may have a stronger bias to share processing across phenomena than neural networks, so multi-task learning might be more effective for humans.
Children's input might contain utterances unambiguously supporting hierarchical transformations, whereas the training data assumed a complete lack of such examples.
The training data omits many cues to hierarchical structure available to children, such as prosody and real-world grounding.
The hierarchical bias in tree-based models only emerged when provided with correct parse trees; it is unclear how to effectively use tree-based models without correct parses.
future_direction: Characterization of the effects of hyperparameters and random seeds on generalization.
Investigation of how to effectively use tree-based models without providing correct parses.
Exploration of additional secondary tasks in multi-task learning to impart hierarchical biases.
papers.abstract: Learners that are exposed to the same training data might generalize differently due to differing inductive biases. In neural network models, inductive biases could in theory arise from any aspect of the model architecture. We investigate which architectural factors affect the generalization behavior of neural sequence-to-sequence models trained on two syntactic tasks, English question formation and English tense reinflection. For both tasks, the training set is consistent with a generalization based on hierarchical structure and a generalization based on linear order. All architectural factors that we investigated qualitatively affected how models generalized, including factors with no clear connection to hierarchical structure. For example, LSTMs and GRUs displayed qualitatively different inductive biases. However, the only factor that consistently contributed a hierarchical bias across tasks was the use of a tree-structured model rather than a model with sequential recurrence, suggesting that human-like syntactic generalization requires architectural syntactic structure.

papers.title: Understanding Refusal in Language Models with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How is refusal encoded in the latent space of LLMs, and how do adversarial jailbreaks suppress refusal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using sparse autoencoders to identify and causally validate refusal-related features in LLMs, revealing that harm and refusal are separately encoded and that adversarial jailbreaks suppress refusal features.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can identify causal refusal features, revealing the mediation of refusal by harmful features and the suppression mechanism of adversarial jailbreaks.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode harm and refusal as separate feature sets, with harmful features exhibiting a causal effect on refusal features.
Adversarial jailbreaks operate by suppressing specific refusal-related features.
The identified refusal features significantly improve classification on out-of-distribution adversarial examples.
The proposed CosSim+AP method identifies a minimal set of causal features for refusal behavior.
There is a conditional relationship where harmful features upstream trigger refusal features downstream.
papers.limitation:
The small K* may omit additional features relevant to harm and refusal.
The reliance on the refusal direction may not generalize to challenging instructions.
SAEs were trained on base models, not chat models, which may affect interpretability.
future_direction: Training SAEs on chat-model activations to improve feature interpretability and relevance.
papers.abstract: Refusal is a key safety behavior in aligned language models, yet the internal mechanisms driving refusals remain opaque. In this work, we conduct a mechanistic study of refusal in instruction-tuned LLMs using sparse autoencoders to identify latent features that causally mediate refusal behaviors. We apply our method to two open-source chat models and intervene on refusal-related features to assess their influence on generation, validating their behavioral impact across multiple harmful datasets. This enables a fine-grained inspection of how refusal manifests at the activation level and addresses key research questions such as investigating upstream-downstream latent relationship and understanding the mechanisms of adversarial jailbreaking techniques. We also establish the usefulness of refusal features in enhancing generalization for linear probes to out-of-distribution adversarial samples in classification tasks. We open source our code in https://github.com/wj210/refusal_sae.

papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of Morphological Content in BERT Models for Multiple Languages
papers.research_question: To what extent do BERT-style models encode morphological feature information in their hidden representations and attention distributions for multiple languages?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that BERT-style models encode morphological information by partitioning their embedding space into convex regions correlated with feature values, that contextualized embeddings help disambiguate ambiguous forms but not completely, and that specific attention head/layer combinations focus on subject-verb agreement.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that pre-trained BERT-style models are sensitive to morphological information, with strong performance on feature-value classification and certain attention heads learning to focus attention in a manner consistent with morphological agreement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT-style models partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value.
Contextualized embeddings allow models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases.
Specific attention head/layer combinations hone in on subject-verb agreement.
Supervision significantly aids in extracting morphological information, as unsupervised clustering performs near random baselines.
Morphological information is best represented in the middle layers for languages with complex morphology (German and Russian), while for simpler languages it is present throughout all layers.
papers.limitation:
Models have difficulty disambiguating syncretic (ambiguous) forms, especially in languages with complex inflectional morphology.
The classification tasks require supervision; unsupervised methods (k-means) perform near random baselines.
future_direction: Identifying morphological information in BERT-style models in an unsupervised fashion.
Improving models' ability to disambiguate syncretic forms for languages with complex inflectional morphology.
Further exploration of how morphological information is shared between words via self-attention.
papers.abstract: This work describes experiments which probe the hidden representations of several BERT-style models for morphological content. The goal is to examine the extent to which discrete linguistic structure, in the form of morphological features and feature values, presents itself in the vector representations and attention distributions of pre-trained language models for five European languages. The experiments contained herein show that (i) Transformer architectures largely partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value, (ii) the contextualized nature of transformer embeddings allows models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases, and (iii) very specific attention head/layer combinations appear to hone in on subject-verb agreement.

papers.title: Examining Cross-lingual Contextual Embeddings with Orthogonal Structural Probes
papers.research_question: Is linguistic information uniformly encoded in the representations of various languages in multilingual BERT? If not, is it possible to learn an orthogonal transformation to align the embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Orthogonal Structural Probes to analyze cross-lingual embeddings, finding that for languages typologically similar to English, linguistic information is uniformly encoded, while for others, orthogonal transformation improves alignment.
papers.conclusion: The evaluated syntactic and lexical information is similarly distributed in MBERT's representations for languages typologically similar to English, and aligning embeddings with an orthogonal transformation improves results for other languages, suggesting the representations are isomorphic.
papers.key_findings:
For languages closely related to English (e.g., Spanish, French), no transformation is needed; syntactic and lexical information is encoded in a shared cross-lingual embedding space.
For other languages (e.g., Chinese, Arabic, Basque), applying an orthogonal transformation learned separately for each language improves probing results.
Typological similarity to English is more strongly correlated with the success of a shared probe than the size of the pre-training corpus.
The probe can be used for zero-shot and few-shot dependency parsing, achieving better UAS for some languages than previous approaches using a biaffine parser.
The orthogonal transformation allows disentangling subspaces responsible for encoding lexical and dependency structures.
papers.limitation: Four of the nine analyzed languages belong to the Indo-European family, which may bias the findings towards shared encoding subspaces for those languages.
papers.abstract: State-of-the-art contextual embeddings are obtained from large language models available only for a few languages. For others, we need to learn representations using a multilingual model. There is an ongoing debate on whether multilingual embeddings can be aligned in a space shared across many languages. The novel Orthogonal Structural Probe (Limisiewicz and Mareek, 2021) allows us to answer this question for specific linguistic features and learn a projection based only on mono-lingual annotated datasets. We evaluate syntactic (UD) and lexical (WordNet) structural information encoded in MBERT's contextual representations for nine diverse languages. 1 We observe that for languages closely related to English, no transformation is needed. The evaluated information is encoded in a shared cross-lingual embedding space. For other languages, it is beneficial to apply orthogonal transformation learned separately for each language. We successfully apply our findings to zero-shot and few-shot cross-lingual parsing.

papers.title: Large Language Models Encode Semantics and Alignment in Linearly Separable Representations
papers.research_question: To what extent do large language models encode high-level semantic information in linearly separable representations across domains and alignment behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode high-level semantics and alignment behaviors in linearly separable representations, enabling effective latent-space guardrails for safety.
papers.conclusion: LLMs organize high-level semantics and alignment in linearly separable subspaces, motivating geometry-aware tools for safer deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic representations become increasingly linearly separable in deeper layers.
Linear separability persists even when domain-specific keywords are masked.
Instruction following (e.g., chain-of-thought) induces linearly separable representations.
Safety-aligned models show separable clusters for benign and harmful prompts.
A lightweight MLP guardrail on hidden states improves refusal rates on adversarial prompts.
future_direction: Adversarial perturbation studies for causal validation
Axis-orthogonality tests for linear representations
Further research on information distribution across architectures
papers.abstract: Understanding the latent space geometry of large language models (LLMs) is key to interpreting their behavior and improving alignment. Yet it remains unclear to what extent LLMs linearly organize representations related to semantic understanding. To explore this, we conduct a large-scale empirical study of hidden representations in 11 autoregressive models across six scientific topics. We find that high-level semantic information consistently resides in low-dimensional subspaces that form linearly separable representations across domains. This separability becomes more pronounced in deeper layers and under prompts that elicit structured reasoning or alignment behavior$\unicode{x2013}$even when surface content remains unchanged. These findings motivate geometry-aware tools that operate directly in latent space to detect and mitigate harmful and adversarial content. As a proof of concept, we train an MLP probe on final-layer hidden states as a lightweight latent-space guardrail. This approach substantially improves refusal rates on malicious queries and prompt injections that bypass both the model's built-in safety alignment and external token-level filters.

papers.title: Language Modeling Teaches You More than Translation Does: Lessons Learned Through Auxiliary Syntactic Task Analysis
papers.research_question: How does the choice of pretraining objective (language modeling, translation, skip-thought, autoencoding) affect the learning of syntactic and part-of-speech information in LSTM models?
papers.core_contribution: Bidirectional language models learn more syntactic information than translation models, making them better for transfer learning on syntactic tasks, and untrained LSTMs retain input content better but trained models capture deeper syntactic features.
papers.conclusion: Bidirectional language models are more effective than translation models for learning syntactic information, and untrained LSTMs retain input content better but trained models capture deeper syntactic features.
papers.key_findings:
Bidirectional language models (BiLMs) outperform translation encoders on part-of-speech and CCG supertagging tasks.
BiLMs trained on 1 million sentences outperform other models trained on up to 63 million sentences.
Untrained LSTM baselines perform well on syntactic tasks when using ample classifier data, but performance drops more with less data compared to trained encoders.
Trained encoders underperform untrained ones on word identity prediction, indicating they capture genuine syntactic features beyond mere word memorization.
In LSTMs, the first layer is best for POS tagging, while the second layer can be better for CCG supertagging and predicting distant word identities, suggesting depth increases receptive field for abstract syntax.
papers.abstract: Recently, researchers have found that deep LSTMs trained on tasks like machine translation learn substantial syntactic and semantic information about their input sentences, including part-of-speech. These findings begin to shed light on why pretrained representations, like ELMo and CoVe, are so beneficial for neural language understanding models. We still, though, do not yet have a clear understanding of how the choice of pretraining objective affects the type of linguistic information that models learn. With this in mind, we compare four objectives—language modeling, translation, skip-thought, and autoencoding—on their ability to induce syntactic and part-of-speech information, holding constant the quantity and genre of the training data, as well as the LSTM architecture.

papers.title: Mechanisms vs. Outcomes: Probing for Syntax Fails to Explain Performance on Targeted Syntactic Evaluations
papers.research_question: Do probing accuracies, measured by dependency tree attachment scores of syntactic probes, effectively predict a model’s downstream performance on targeted syntactic evaluations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that syntactic features extracted via probing fail to predict outcomes of targeted syntax evaluations, highlighting a disconnect between latent syntactic representations and observable syntactic behaviors.
papers.conclusion: Probing fails to reliably extract the latent syntactic knowledge within models that correlates with minimal pair accuracy, arguing for targeted evaluations like BLiMP as the gold standard for assessing syntactic competence.
papers.key_findings:
No significant regression fit between probing accuracy and overall BLiMP minimal pair accuracy across 32 models.
Only anaphor agreement shows a significant correlation, but a non-syntactic control probe yields a similar fit, suggesting it is spurious.
Probe recovery of critical syntactic edges (e.g., subject-verb) only weakly aligns with minimal pair outcomes (40–60% match rate).
In over 85% of BLiMP paradigms, UUAS score distributions for correct and incorrect minimal pairs substantially overlap.
Control probes trained on non-syntactic information can also predict some syntactic benchmark performance, indicating that probing results may not be attributable solely to syntactic representations.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation only uses English grammatical benchmarks.
Probe architectures are limited to linear and bilinear probes; other architectures could yield different results.
Models are limited to up to 8B parameters due to compute constraints.
future_direction: Extending the work to multilingual benchmarks (e.g., MultiBLiMP, TurBLiMP).
Exploring other probe architectures and syntactic probing tasks.
Investigating causal relationships between probed representations and model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit a robust mastery of syntax when processing and generating text. While this suggests internalized understanding of hierarchical syntax and dependency relations, the precise mechanism by which they represent syntactic structure is an open area within interpretability research. Probing provides one way to identify the mechanism of syntax being linearly encoded in activations, however, no comprehensive study has yet established whether a model's probing accuracy reliably predicts its downstream syntactic performance.
