Adopting a "mechanisms vs. outcomes" framework, we evaluate 32 open-weight transformer models and find that syntactic features extracted via probing fail to predict outcomes of targeted syntax evaluations across English linguistic phenomena. Our results highlight a substantial disconnect between latent syntactic representations found via probing and observable syntactic behaviors in downstream tasks.

papers.title: Does syntax need to grow on trees? Sources of hierarchical inductive\n bias in sequence-to-sequence networks
papers.research_question: Which architectural factors affect the generalization behavior of neural sequence-to-sequence models trained on two syntactic tasks, English question formation and English tense reinflection?
papers.core_contribution: Only tree-structured models given correct parse trees consistently displayed a hierarchical bias across syntactic tasks, suggesting that human-like syntactic generalization requires architectural syntactic structure.
papers.conclusion: Many architectural factors can affect inductive biases, but a consistent hierarchical bias across syntactic tasks only emerges in models with explicit tree structure and correct parse information, suggesting that human-like syntactic generalization may require such structure when learning from text alone.
papers.key_findings:
The type of recurrent unit and attention qualitatively affect inductive biases, with interactions between them.
LSTMs and GRUs have different inductive biases, partly due to squashing in GRUs.
Only tree-based models with correct parse trees consistently generalized hierarchically across both question formation and tense reinflection.
Sequential models failed to generalize hierarchically even when given bracketed input or in multi-task learning settings.
Tree-based models are not constrained to hierarchical generalizations and can learn linear transformations if trained on unambiguous data.
papers.limitation:
The training data omits many cues available to children, such as prosody and real-world grounding, which may affect generalization.
Multi-task learning had limited effect in imparting hierarchical bias, suggesting that neural networks may not readily transfer knowledge across tasks.
future_direction: Investigating how to effectively use tree-based models without providing correct parses.
Characterizing the effects of hyperparameters and random seeds on generalization.
papers.abstract:
Learners that are exposed to the same training data might generalize
differently due to differing inductive biases. In neural network models,
inductive biases could in theory arise from any aspect of the model
architecture. We investigate which architectural factors affect the
generalization behavior of neural sequence-to-sequence models trained on two
syntactic tasks, English question formation and English tense reinflection. For
both tasks, the training set is consistent with a generalization based on
hierarchical structure and a generalization based on linear order. All
architectural factors that we investigated qualitatively affected how models
generalized, including factors with no clear connection to hierarchical
structure. For example, LSTMs and GRUs displayed qualitatively different
inductive biases. However, the only factor that consistently contributed a
hierarchical bias across tasks was the use of a tree-structured model rather
than a model with sequential recurrence, suggesting that human-like syntactic
generalization requires architectural syntactic structure.

papers.title: Echoes of BERT: Do Modern Language Models Rediscover the Classical NLP Pipeline?
papers.research_question: How do modern language models encode linguistic structure, and do they rediscover the classical NLP pipeline observed in earlier models like BERT?
papers.core_contribution: Modern language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline, with lexical information concentrated in early layers and becoming nonlinear, while inflectional morphology remains linearly accessible across layers and languages.
papers.conclusion: Modern transformer language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline and exhibit robust representational regularities for lexical and inflectional information across architectures, sizes, and languages.
papers.key_findings:
Modern LMs consistently organize linguistic information hierarchically: early layers process syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entities, later layers capture discourse.
Lexical identity (lemma) information is most accessible in early layers and becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network.
Inflectional morphology remains highly linearly accessible across all layers and across six typologically diverse languages.
These representational patterns emerge early during pretraining and are robust across model architectures, sizes, and training regimes.
Inflectional features occupy compact, linearly accessible subspaces in the residual stream, enabling effective steering interventions.
papers.limitation:
Representation extraction for decoder-only models uses the final subword token, which may not be optimal for all architectures.
The study does not explicitly examine cases where different grammatical functions share the same surface form (e.g., infinitive and non-past verb forms).
Classifiers only detect correlations in hidden activations, not causal mechanisms.
Steering experiments measure changes in classifier performance rather than downstream model outputs.
future_direction: Develop better extraction methods for word representations from decoder-only models.
Examine how models separate form from function across languages in cases of surface-form ambiguity.
Design more complex experiments to evaluate steering effects on actual model generation.
papers.abstract: Large transformer-based language models dominate modern NLP, yet our understanding of how they encode linguistic information relies primarily on studies of early models like BERT and GPT-2. Building on classic BERTology work, we analyze 25 models spanning from classical architectures (BERT, DeBERTa, GPT-2) to modern large language models (Pythia, OLMo-2, Gemma-2, Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1), probing layer-by-layer representations across eight linguistic tasks in English. Consistent with earlier findings, we find that hierarchical organization persists in modern models: early layers capture syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entity-level information, and later layers encode discourse phenomena. We dive deeper, conducting an in-depth multilingual analysis of two specific linguistic properties - lexical identity and inflectional morphology - that help disentangle form from meaning. We find that lexical information concentrates linearly in early layers but becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network, while inflectional information remains linearly accessible throughout all layers. Additional analyses of attention mechanisms, steering vectors, and pretraining checkpoints reveal where this information resides within layers, how it can be functionally manipulated, and how representations evolve during pretraining. Taken together, our findings suggest that, even with substantial advances in LLM technologies, transformer models learn to organize linguistic information in similar ways, regardless of model architecture, size, or training regime, indicating that these properties are important for next token prediction. Our code is available at https://github.com/ml5885/model_internal_sleuthing

papers.title: Revisiting Robustness for LLM Safety Alignment via Selective Geometry Control
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether robustness failures in LLM safety alignment can be addressed by data-centric methods alone, and proposes a geometry-aware optimization framework to improve robustness under domain shift and noisy supervision.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ShaPO, a geometry-aware preference optimization framework that selectively stabilizes safety-critical parameter directions to improve robustness under domain shift and noisy supervision.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that optimization geometry is a complementary axis for robust LLM safety alignment, and ShaPO effectively improves robustness by selectively stabilizing safety-critical parameter directions.
papers.key_findings:
ShaPO consistently improves safety robustness over popular preference optimization methods across diverse safety benchmarks and noisy preference settings.
ShaPO composes cleanly with data-robust objectives, yielding additional gains.
Selective geometry control avoids over-regularization and improves cross-domain robustness compared to uniform control.
Token-level and reward-level ShaPO both improve robustness, with reward-level ShaPO offering additional stability under noisy supervision.
Perturbing a small fraction of safety-critical neurons accounts for most of the worst-case alignment loss, justifying selective control.
papers.limitation:
ShaPO introduces additional computational overhead due to geometry-aware optimization.
Identification of alignment-critical directions is based on approximate signals (linear probe).
future_direction: Improving the efficiency and scalability of geometry-aware optimization for larger-scale models.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment of large language models remains brittle under domain shift and noisy preference supervision. Most existing robust alignment methods focus on uncertainty in alignment data, while overlooking optimization-induced fragility in preference-based objectives. In this work, we revisit robustness for LLM safety alignment from an optimization geometry perspective, and argue that robustness failures cannot be addressed by data-centric methods alone. We propose ShaPO, a geometry-aware preference optimization framework that enforces worst-case alignment objectives via selective geometry control over alignment-critical parameter subspace. By avoiding uniform geometry constraints, ShaPO mitigates the over-regularization that can harm robustness under distribution shift. We instantiate ShaPO at two levels: token-level ShaPO stabilizes likelihood-based surrogate optimization, while reward-level ShaPO enforces reward-consistent optimization under noisy supervision. Across diverse safety benchmarks and noisy preference settings, ShaPO consistently improves safety robustness over popular preference optimization methods. Moreover, ShaPO composes cleanly with data-robust objectives, yielding additional gains and empirically supporting the proposed optimization-geometry perspective.

papers.title: Probing Pretrained Language Models for Lexical Semantics
papers.research_question: How can lexical semantic knowledge be extracted from pretrained language models, how is this knowledge distributed across layers, and how do the extracted representations compare to traditional static word embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a systematic study of how to extract type-level lexical semantic knowledge from pretrained language models, showing that monolingual models store rich lexical information primarily in lower layers and that extracted vectors can outperform traditional word embeddings on several monolingual tasks.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained language models store a wealth of type-level lexical knowledge, and effectively uncovering this knowledge depends on careful configuration of extraction strategies, with universal best practices including using monolingual LMs, encoding words with multiple contexts, excluding special tokens, and averaging over lower layers.
papers.key_findings:
Lexical semantic knowledge is concentrated in the lower Transformer layers of pretrained language models.
Averaging representations across multiple layers yields better performance than using a single layer.
Monolingual language models contain more lexical information for a target language than massively multilingual models like mBERT.
Extracted 'BERT-based' static word embeddings outperform fastText on monolingual tasks (e.g., lexical similarity, analogy, relation prediction) but not on cross-lingual tasks (BLI, CLIR).
Translation pairs obtain similar representations in independently trained monolingual LMs, indicating approximate isomorphism between the monolingual spaces.
papers.limitation: The comparison with fastText word embeddings is not strictly apples-to-apples because the models were trained on different corpora (Wikipedia dumps for fastText vs. the corpora used for pretraining the LMs).
future_direction: Investigating how domains of external corpora affect the extraction of word representations and how to sample representative contexts.
Extending the study to more languages, more lexical semantic probes, and other larger underlying language models.
Developing more sophisticated lexical representation extraction methods, such as layer weighting or attention, and lightweight methods to enrich lexical content in multilingual LMs.
papers.abstract: The success of large pretrained language models (LMs) such as BERT and RoBERTa has sparked interest in probing their representations, in order to unveil what types of knowledge they implicitly capture. While prior research focused on morphosyntactic, semantic, and world knowledge, it remains unclear to which extent LMs also derive lexical type-level knowledge from words in context. In this work, we present a systematic empirical analysis across six typologically diverse languages and five different lexical tasks, addressing the following questions: 1) How do different lexical knowledge extraction strategies (monolingual versus multilingual source LM, out-ofcontext versus in-context encoding, inclusion of special tokens, and layer-wise averaging) impact performance? How consistent are the observed effects across tasks and languages? 2) Is lexical knowledge stored in few parameters, or is it scattered throughout the network? 3) How do these representations fare against traditional static word vectors in lexical tasks? 4) Does the lexical information emerging from independently trained monolingual LMs display latent similarities? Our main results indicate patterns and best practices that hold universally, but also point to prominent variations across languages and tasks. Moreover, we validate the claim that lower Transformer layers carry more type-level lexical knowledge, but also show that this knowledge is distributed across multiple layers.

papers.title: Understanding and Rectifying Safety Perception Distortion in VLMs
papers.research_question: What causes the degradation of safety alignment in vision-language models (VLMs) when integrating the vision modality, and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that multimodal inputs cause a 'safety perception distortion' in VLMs by inducing an activation shift towards a safer direction, and proposes ShiftDC, a training-free method to disentangle and calibrate this shift to restore safety alignment without harming utility.
papers.conclusion: The safety perception distortion caused by the visual modality is a key factor in VLM safety degradation, and the proposed ShiftDC method effectively mitigates this issue without additional training, restoring safety alignment while preserving model utility.
papers.key_findings:
VLMs struggle to differentiate between safe and unsafe vision-language inputs, while their text-only LLM backbones can do so effectively.
Visual modality induces an activation shift that causes VLMs to misperceive unsafe instructions as safer.
The magnitude of the safety-relevant component of the activation shift correlates positively with the attack success rate (ASR).
The proposed ShiftDC method significantly reduces ASR on safety benchmarks without compromising visual reasoning utility.
ShiftDC restores the linear separability of safe and unsafe activations in VLMs, correcting the safety perception distortion.
papers.abstract: Recent studies reveal that vision-language models (VLMs) become more susceptible to harmful requests and jailbreak attacks after integrating the vision modality, exhibiting greater vulnerability than their text-only LLM backbones. To uncover the root cause of this phenomenon, we conduct an in-depth analysis and identify a key issue: multimodal inputs introduce an modality-induced activation shift toward a "safer" direction compared to their text-only counterparts, leading VLMs to systematically overestimate the safety of harmful inputs. We refer to this issue as safety perception distortion. To mitigate such distortion, we propose Activation Shift Disentanglement and Calibration (ShiftDC), a training-free method that decomposes and calibrates the modality-induced activation shift to reduce the impact of modality on safety. By isolating and removing the safety-relevant component, ShiftDC restores the inherent safety alignment of the LLM backbone while preserving the vision-language capabilities of VLMs. Empirical results demonstrate that ShiftDC significantly enhances alignment performance on safety benchmarks without impairing model utility.

papers.title: Syntax-guided Neural Module Distillation to Probe Compositionality in Sentence Embeddings
papers.research_question: Does syntax serve as a strong causal model for the compositional ability of sentence embedding models? What is the geometry of semantic composition guided by syntax?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SynNaMoN, a syntax-guided neural module net, to distill and probe sentence embedding models, finding that syntax explains compositional ability and that much syntax-guided composition is linear.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that syntax serves as a causal model for compositional ability in sentence embeddings, with composition largely linear and modules capturing semantic generalizations.
papers.key_findings:
GTR-T5 models are more compositional than MP-Net and BERT based on distillability to SynNaMoN.
Model size does not significantly affect distillability to syntax-guided composition.
Much of the syntax-guided composition in sentence embeddings is linear, as Linear SynNaMoN performs well.
Non-linearities in transformers may primarily handle non-compositional phrases rather than syntax-guided composition.
SynNaMoN modules learn composition functions that align with semantic intuition, as shown in determiner-noun analysis.
papers.limitation:
Computational constraints leading to out-of-memory errors with long sentences and limited hyperparameter tuning.
Potential influence of the chosen linguistic formalism (Penn Treebank) on probing results.
future_direction: Explore alignment with other compositionality metrics.
Investigate non-compositional semantics not captured by SynNaMoNs.
Study SynNaMoNs with different linguistic formalisms and other use cases beyond probing.
papers.abstract: Past work probing compositionality in sentence embedding models faces issues determining the causal impact of implicit syntax representations. Given a sentence, we construct a neural module net based on its syntax parse and train it end-to-end to approximate the sentence's embedding generated by a transformer model. The distillability of a transformer to a Syntactic NeurAl Module Net (SynNaMoN) then captures whether syntax is a strong causal model of its compositional ability. Furthermore, we address questions about the geometry of semantic composition by specifying individual SynNaMoN modules' internal architecture & linearity. We find differences in the distillability of various sentence embedding models that broadly correlate with their performance, but observe that distillability doesn't considerably vary by model size. We also present preliminary evidence that much syntax-guided composition in sentence embedding models is linear, and that non-linearities may serve primarily to handle non-compositional phrases.

papers.title: How Distributed are Distributed Representations? An Observation on the Locality of Syntactic Information in Verb Agreement Tasks
papers.research_question: Where is syntactic information localized in transformer representations for French object-past participle agreement tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Syntactic information is encoded locally in transformer representations in a way consistent with French grammar, as shown through probing and causal analysis.
papers.conclusion: Transformers process French object-past participle agreement in a linguistically-motivated manner, and this work is a step towards understanding inner representations.
papers.key_findings:
Syntactic information is encoded locally within context tokens and not distributed globally across the sentence.
Masking linguistically relevant tokens (antecedent and relative pronoun) degrades prediction performance, indicating a causal link.
Number information is encoded in a small number of dimensions but redundantly across the representation.
Probing accuracy is high in context tokens and drops in prefix and suffix, showing localized encoding.
Transformers rely on tokens consistent with French grammar for agreement prediction.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a specific linguistic phenomenon (object-past participle agreement) in French and could be extended to other languages and phenomena.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other linguistic phenomena and languages.
papers.abstract: This work addresses the question of the localization of syntactic information encoded in the transformers representations. We tackle this question from two perspectives, considering the object-past participle agreement in French, by identifying, first, in which part of the sentence and, second, in which part of the representation syntactic information is encoded. The results of our experiments using probing, causal analysis and feature selection method, show that syntactic information is encoded locally in a way consistent with the French grammar.

papers.title: What does it mean to be language-agnostic? Probing multilingual sentence encoders for typological properties
papers.research_question: How do multilingual sentence encoders capture typological properties of languages, and how does this vary with different pretraining strategies?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual sentence encoders capture typological properties, but the encoding differs based on pretraining objectives: models with cross-lingual objectives (LASER, XLM) lose typological information in higher layers and create a shared interlingual space, while models with monolingual objectives (M-BERT, XLM-R) retain typological information in all layers and partition the space into language-specific subspaces.
papers.conclusion: There is a trade-off between universality and language-specific information in multilingual encoders, and pretraining objectives influence how typological information is encoded.
papers.key_findings:
All encoders capture some typological properties (word order, pronouns, negation).
M-BERT and XLM-R outperform LASER and XLM on lexical and morphological properties.
Typological information is localizable in lower layers of LASER and XLM, but spread across all layers in M-BERT and XLM-R.
Cross-lingual training leads to more language-agnostic representations but at the cost of losing language-specific typological information in higher layers.
XLM generalizes to languages unseen during pretraining, capturing their typological properties.
papers.abstract: Multilingual sentence encoders have seen much success in cross-lingual model transfer for downstream NLP tasks. Yet, we know relatively little about the properties of individual languages or the general patterns of linguistic variation that they encode. We propose methods for probing sentence representations from state-of-the-art multilingual encoders (LASER, M-BERT, XLM and XLM-R) with respect to a range of typological properties pertaining to lexical, morphological and syntactic structure. In addition, we investigate how this information is distributed across all layers of the models. Our results show interesting differences in encoding linguistic variation associated with different pretraining strategies.

papers.title: Encodings of Source Syntax: Similarities in NMT Representations Across\n Target Languages
papers.research_question: Does the target language affect the syntactic information encoded in NMT encoder representations? How do NMT encoders compare to other models in learning syntax?
papers.core_contribution: NMT encoders learn similar source syntactic information regardless of target language, relying on explicit morphosyntactic cues, and they outperform directly-trained RNNs on constituent label prediction tasks.
papers.conclusion: NMT encoder representations encode similar source syntax across target languages, and RNN-based models are limited in the types of syntax they can learn due to their reliance on explicit cues and architectural constraints.
papers.key_findings:
NMT encoders learn syntactic information above baseline for parent, grandparent, and great-grandparent labels, but perform poorly on POS tags.
Syntactic information encoded by NMT encoders is highly similar across non-English target languages, with high correlation in individual label F1 scores.
NMT encoders rely on explicit morphosyntactic cues like infinitives and negation, and struggle with sentences containing null features such as null copulas or appositives.
NMT encoder representations outperform directly-trained RNNs on parent, grandparent, and great-grandparent constituent label prediction tasks.
The PCFG parser encodes different syntactic information than RNN-based models and performs well on sentences where RNNs perform poorly, suggesting RNNs are constrained in syntax learning.
papers.limitation: RNN architectures are constrained in the types of syntax they can learn due to their reliance on explicit morphosyntactic cues and inability to re-evaluate past inputs upon reading disambiguating words.
future_direction: Study whether bidirectional or Transformer architectures are less reliant on explicit morphosyntactic cues for syntactic encoding.
papers.abstract:
We train neural machine translation (NMT) models from English to six target
languages, using NMT encoder representations to predict ancestor constituent
labels of source language words. We find that NMT encoders learn similar source
syntax regardless of NMT target language, relying on explicit morphosyntactic
cues to extract syntactic features from source sentences. Furthermore, the NMT
encoders outperform RNNs trained directly on several of the constituent label
prediction tasks, suggesting that NMT encoder representations can be used
effectively for natural language tasks involving syntax. However, both the NMT
encoders and the directly-trained RNNs learn substantially different syntactic
information from a probabilistic context-free grammar (PCFG) parser. Despite
lower overall accuracy scores, the PCFG often performs well on sentences for
which the RNN-based models perform poorly, suggesting that RNN architectures
are constrained in the types of syntax they can learn.

papers.title: Extracting Syntactic Trees from Transformer Encoder Self-Attentions
papers.research_question: How to extract syntactic tree structures from Transformer encoder self-attention energies and analyze their characteristics with respect to established syntactic theories.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces methods to aggregate self-attention distributions and extract constituency and undirected syntactic trees from Transformer encoders, showing similarities to standard syntactic annotations.
papers.conclusion: Preliminary results demonstrate that syntactic trees can be extracted from Transformer encoder self-attentions, with structures resembling established syntactic theories.
papers.key_findings:
Constituency trees extracted from self-attentions often well recognize clauses, noun phrases, and verb phrases.
Undirected trees constructed from coattention scores bear similarities to dependency trees, with content words as heads and function words as leaves.
The encoder may concentrate the representation of whole phrases onto single tokens, such as content words.
papers.limitation:
Attention mechanisms on deeper layers operate on previous-layer neurons with mixed information from multiple tokens, which may affect tree extraction.
No sensible way was found to define coattention scores asymmetrically for directed dependency trees.
future_direction: Analyze how the trees evolve through layers.
Employ unsupervised or supervised selection of 'more syntactic' heads.
Perform experiments on more language pairs.
papers.abstract: This is a work in progress about extracting the sentence tree structures from the encoder’s self-attention weights, when translating into another language using the Transformer neural network architecture. We visualize the structures and discuss their characteristics with respect to the existing syntactic theories and annotations.

papers.title: The Blessing and Curse of Dimensionality in Safety Alignment
papers.research_question: What is the role of dimensionality in the linear representation of concepts (like safety) in LLMs, and how can we defend against jailbreaking attacks that exploit these linear structures?
papers.core_contribution: High-dimensional representations in LLMs make them vulnerable to linear jailbreaking attacks; the paper proposes dimensionality reduction methods (FJLT and Bottleneck) to defend against such attacks while preserving safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: High dimensionality is both a blessing (for representing complex concepts) and a curse (for vulnerability to jailbreaking); the proposed dimensionality reduction methods mitigate the curse while preserving alignment.
papers.key_findings:
High-dimensional representations in LLMs lead to linear separability of concepts like safety, which can be exploited for jailbreaking.
Linear probes show that linear separability of concepts emerges in models with sufficiently high hidden dimensions.
The proposed FJLT and Bottleneck methods significantly reduce susceptibility to ActAdd and Ablation jailbreaks.
The Bottleneck method preserves utility on various benchmarks better than FJLT.
Theoretical analysis links the effectiveness of linear jailbreaks to the Rademacher complexity of the linear hypothesis class, which grows with dimension.
papers.limitation:
FJLT model performs poorly on datasets dissimilar to the fine-tuning data.
The methods are primarily effective against linear attacks and may not generalize to non-linear attacks.
The Bottleneck method requires model-specific anchor datasets.
papers.abstract: The focus on safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) has increased significantly due to their widespread adoption across different domains. The scale of LLMs play a contributing role in their success, and the growth in parameter count follows larger hidden dimensions. In this paper, we hypothesize that while the increase in dimensions has been a key advantage, it may lead to emergent problems as well. These problems emerge as the linear structures in the activation space can be exploited, in the form of activation engineering, to circumvent its safety alignment. Through detailed visualizations of linear subspaces associated with different concepts, such as safety, across various model scales, we show that the curse of high-dimensional representations uniquely impacts LLMs. Further substantiating our claim, we demonstrate that projecting the representations of the model onto a lower dimensional subspace can preserve sufficient information for alignment while avoiding those linear structures. Empirical results confirm that such dimensional reduction significantly reduces susceptibility to jailbreaking through representation engineering. Building on our empirical validations, we provide theoretical insights into these linear jailbreaking methods relative to a model's hidden dimensions. Broadly speaking, our work posits that the high dimensions of a model's internal representations can be both a blessing and a curse in safety alignment.

papers.title: Differentiated Directional Intervention A Framework for Evading LLM Safety Alignment
papers.research_question: What is the granular mechanism of LLM safety alignment, and how can it be exploited for jailbreaking?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a bi-direction model of LLM safety, deconstructing refusal into harm detection and refusal execution directions, and introduces DBDI, a white-box framework that precisely neutralizes safety alignment by intervening on these directions.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that LLM safety is a composite of distinct, targetable directions, and DBDI provides a precise method for analyzing and controlling LLM behavior, paving the way for more robust defenses.
papers.key_findings:
DBDI achieves high attack success rates, up to 97.88% on models like Llama-2.
Safety alignment can be decomposed into two distinct directions: harm detection and refusal execution.
Sequential intervention on both directions is crucial for effectiveness.
The method is computationally efficient and data-efficient, requiring few calibration samples.
DBDI outperforms existing jailbreaking methods such as Directional Ablation and TwinBreak.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment instills in Large Language Models (LLMs) a critical capacity to refuse malicious requests. Prior works have modeled this refusal mechanism as a single linear direction in the activation space. We posit that this is an oversimplification that conflates two functionally distinct neural processes: the detection of harm and the execution of a refusal. In this work, we deconstruct this single representation into a Harm Detection Direction and a Refusal Execution Direction. Leveraging this fine-grained model, we introduce Differentiated Bi-Directional Intervention (DBDI), a new white-box framework that precisely neutralizes the safety alignment at critical layer. DBDI applies adaptive projection nullification to the refusal execution direction while suppressing the harm detection direction via direct steering. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DBDI outperforms prominent jailbreaking methods, achieving up to a 97.88\% attack success rate on models such as Llama-2. By providing a more granular and mechanistic framework, our work offers a new direction for the in-depth understanding of LLM safety alignment.

papers.title: When Does Syntax Mediate Neural Language Model Performance? Evidence from Dropout Probes
papers.research_question: When do language models use syntactic information causally? How can we design probes to avoid false negatives due to redundant encodings of syntax?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces dropout probes, a new neural probing architecture that encourages probes to use all relevant representations of syntax in model embeddings, enabling better causal analysis and performance improvement via syntactic information injection.
papers.conclusion: Dropout probes are effective for causal analysis of language models and can be used to improve model performance by injecting syntactic information, but further work is needed to extend the approach.
papers.key_findings:
Models encode syntactic information redundantly in their embeddings.
Dropout probes reveal causal use of syntactic representations in QA models where prior methods did not.
Injecting syntactic information at test time can improve QA model performance on syntactically challenging tasks.
NLI models do not show causal use of syntax even with dropout probes.
Dropout probes can boost model performance without retraining.
papers.limitation:
Systematic evaluation of models for many layers, multiple probes, and many counterfactuals is computationally challenging.
The transparency benefits require access to the internals of the pretrained model.
The technique is limited to diagnosis of existing models and does not train models to respond appropriately to interventions.
future_direction: Studying pretrained models beyond those considered in this work.
Further research into redundancy in embeddings.
More investigation into inserting symbolic knowledge into neural representations.
New methods for training models to respond appropriately to interventions.
papers.abstract: Recent causal probing literature reveals when language models and syntactic probes use similar representations. Such techniques may yield "false negative" causality results: models may use representations of syntax, but probes may have learned to use redundant encodings of the same syntactic information. We demonstrate that models do encode syntactic information redundantly and introduce a new probe design that guides probes to consider all syntactic information present in embeddings. Using these probes, we find evidence for the use of syntax in models where prior methods did not, allowing us to boost model performance by injecting syntactic information into representations.

papers.title: Open Sesame: Getting inside BERT’s Linguistic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes positional information in lower layers and switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. The paper also introduces a 'confusion score' to quantify intrusion effects in BERT's self-attention mechanism.
papers.conclusion: BERT composes increasingly abstract hierarchical representations of linguistic structure using self-attention, but does not show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure found in human processing.
papers.key_findings:
Diagnostic classifiers show BERT's lower layers encode positional information well, while higher layers encode hierarchical information.
The proposed confusion score reveals BERT's attention is sensitive to syntactic structure and grammatical features (number, gender) in subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora.
BERT's attention is not perfectly syntactic; it sometimes attends to grammatically inaccessible or mismatched distractors.
Confusion scores decrease with layer depth, and there is an increase in confusion at layer 4, coinciding with the degradation of positional information.
BERT's performance on possessive constructions in the subject noun task is poor, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
papers.limitation:
BERT performed poorly on possessive constructions in the subject noun task, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
BERT's attention is only incompletely modulated by structural and featural properties, and attention is sometimes spread across grammatically irrelevant elements.
future_direction: Investigate or visualize layer-on-layer changes in BERT’s structural and positional information, particularly between layers 3 and 4.
Retrieve the increasingly hierarchical representations of BERT across layers via the self-attention mechanism.
papers.abstract: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information? Recent work has shown that contextual representations like BERT perform well on tasks that require sensitivity to linguistic structure. We present here two studies which aim to provide a better understanding of the nature of BERT's representations. The first of these focuses on the identification of structurally-defined elements using diagnostic classifiers, while the second explores BERT's representation of subject-verb agreement and anaphor-antecedent dependencies through a quantitative assessment of self-attention vectors. In both cases, we find that BERT encodes positional information about word tokens well on its lower layers, but switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. We conclude then that BERT's representations do indeed model linguistically relevant aspects of hierarchical structure, though they do not appear to show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure that is found in human processing of reflexive anaphora.

papers.title: Detoxifying Large Language Models via Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: Can knowledge editing techniques be used to detoxify Large Language Models (LLMs) by precisely modifying toxic regions?
papers.core_contribution: This paper constructs a comprehensive benchmark SafeEdit for detoxification evaluation and proposes a knowledge editing method DINM that can detoxify LLMs efficiently with a single instance by locating and editing toxic regions.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge editing, particularly the proposed DINM method, is a promising approach for detoxifying LLMs efficiently with good generalization, providing insights into underlying mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge editing exhibits potential ability to detoxify LLMs with limited impact on general performance.
DINM demonstrates stronger detoxifying performance with better generalization, significantly increasing detoxification success rates.
Toxic regions location plays a significant role in detoxification.
DINM attempts to erase toxic regions of LLM, while DPO and SFT bypass toxic regions.
Editing one instance can generalize to various unsafe categories, indicating shared toxic regions.
papers.limitation:
DINM may compromise general abilities, with observed declines in knowledge question answering and repetitive text generation.
There is significant performance variance when using different instances for editing, indicating sensitivity to the editing instance.
future_direction: Developing improved detoxifying approaches based on insights from internal mechanisms.
Further exploration of knowledge editing for safety and underlying knowledge mechanisms of LLMs.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates using knowledge editing techniques to detoxify Large Language Models (LLMs). We construct a benchmark, SafeEdit, which covers nine unsafe categories with various powerful attack prompts and equips comprehensive metrics for systematic evaluation. We conduct experiments with several knowledge editing approaches, indicating that knowledge editing has the potential to detoxify LLMs with a limited impact on general performance efficiently. Then, we propose a simple yet effective baseline, dubbed Detoxifying with Intraoperative Neural Monitoring (DINM), to diminish the toxicity of LLMs within a few tuning steps via only one instance. We further provide an in-depth analysis of the internal mechanism for various detoxifying approaches, demonstrating that previous methods like SFT and DPO may merely suppress the activations of toxic parameters, while DINM mitigates the toxicity of the toxic parameters to a certain extent, making permanent adjustments. We hope that these insights could shed light on future work of developing detoxifying approaches and the underlying knowledge mechanisms of LLMs. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/zjunlp/EasyEdit.

papers.title: Generalizations across filler-gap dependencies in neural language models
papers.research_question: Does a neural language model learn a shared representation for filler-gap dependencies across different constructions, or does it rely on superficial properties of the input?
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models do not generalize across filler-gap dependencies via a shared representation; they rely on superficial properties of the input and piecemeal learning, indicating a need for linguistic inductive biases.
papers.conclusion: NLMs do not generalize from a shared representation to learn filler-gap dependencies; instead, they rely heavily on input that closely aligns with individual constructions, highlighting the importance of specific linguistic inductive biases for language acquisition.
papers.key_findings:
The pretrained RNN shows knowledge of filler-gap dependencies in Wh-movement, clefting, and tough-movement, but not in topicalization.
Augmenting training with clefting examples improves island constraints in clefting and Wh-movement, but not in tough-movement, and fails to generalize to topicalization.
Augmenting with topicalization examples does not lead to full learning of the dependency; the model learns to expect a gap given a filler but not the reverse.
NLMs do not generalize from a shared representation across filler-gap dependencies; they rely on piecemeal learning and input frequency.
The models often fail to capture island constraints fully, especially filled gap effects, and sometimes show reverse patterns relative to grammaticality.
papers.limitation:
Used an RNN architecture rather than a transformer, which may affect generalization capabilities.
Training data is less noisy than child-directed speech, which may not fully simulate language acquisition.
future_direction: Train a smaller Transformer model on the same corpus to determine architectural effects.
Investigate whether increased training time improves syntactic generalization for filler-gap dependencies.
papers.abstract: Humans develop their grammars by making structural generalizations from finite input. We ask how filler-gap dependencies, which share a structural generalization despite diverse surface forms, might arise from the input. We explicitly control the input to a neural language model (NLM) to uncover whether the model posits a shared representation for filler-gap dependencies. We show that while NLMs do have success differentiating grammatical from ungrammatical filler-gap dependencies, they rely on superficial properties of the input, rather than on a shared generalization. Our work highlights the need for specific linguistic inductive biases to model language acquisition.

papers.title: Unveiling Multilinguality in Transformer Models: Exploring Language Specificity in Feed-Forward Networks
papers.research_question: Do neurons in the feed-forward networks of multilingual transformer models exhibit language-specific or language-agnostic behavior across layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that in multilingual transformer models, feed-forward network layers near the input and output are more language-specific, whereas middle layers are more language-agnostic.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that language specificity in FFNs is higher near the input and output layers, and training data imbalance influences detector activations.
papers.key_findings:
Layers closest to the input and output exhibit more language-specific behavior compared to middle layers.
The number of detectors triggered by English prefixes is higher than for Czech, reflecting training data imbalance.
The number of unique detectors varies across layers, with sparsity patterns observed in FFN activations.
Linear classifiers can predict the language of input prefixes from detector activations with higher accuracy in input and output layers.
Czech-specific detectors decrease in middle layers, suggesting semantic processing uses more language-agnostic detectors.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is limited to only the XGLM model.
Study is centred on the Czech-English language pair, and findings may not generalize to other languages.
Lack of qualitative analysis of linguistic cues triggering detector activation.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more language pairs and other multilingual autoregressive language models.
papers.abstract: Recent research suggests that the feed-forward module within Transformers can be viewed as a collection of key-value memories, where the keys learn to capture specific patterns from the input based on the training examples. The values then combine the output from the 'memories' of the keys to generate predictions about the next token. This leads to an incremental process of prediction that gradually converges towards the final token choice near the output layers. This interesting perspective raises questions about how multilingual models might leverage this mechanism. Specifically, for autoregressive models trained on two or more languages, do all neurons (across layers) respond equally to all languages? No! Our hypothesis centers around the notion that during pretraining, certain model parameters learn strong language-specific features, while others learn more language-agnostic (shared across languages) features. To validate this, we conduct experiments utilizing parallel corpora of two languages that the model was initially pretrained on. Our findings reveal that the layers closest to the network's input or output tend to exhibit more language-specific behaviour compared to the layers in the middle.

papers.title: Talking Heads: Understanding Inter-layer Communication in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How is information represented and routed between layers in transformer language models, specifically through low-rank communication channels?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer LMs use low-rank subspaces (communication channels) in the residual stream to pass information between layers; these channels can be identified via SVD of weight matrices and are causally important for model behaviors.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn intricately structured representations through pretraining, and the discovered communication channels provide a mechanistic explanation for some prompt sensitivities, enabling improved model performance and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer LMs use low-rank (1D or 2D) subspaces in the residual stream for inter-layer communication.
These communication channels can be identified by applying SVD to weight matrices (OV and QK) and computing composition scores on the rank-1 components.
The identified channels are causally important for model behaviors, such as inhibition in the IOI task.
The model's sensitivity to item order in a list (Laundry List task) is explained by the limited capacity of these low-rank channels.
Model editing (zeroing or scaling components) based on these channels can significantly improve performance on the Laundry List task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not work for key composition (Appendix B).
Analysis is limited to two small models (GPT-2 small and Pythia 160m).
Difficulty in controlling all variables in the available data (Section 7).
future_direction: Future work in static weight analysis more generally.
More rigorous analysis of interactions between specific heads (e.g., 8.3 and 9.9).
Extending the method to analyze more complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: Although it is known that transformer language models (LMs) pass features from early layers to later layers, it is not well understood how this information is represented and routed by the model. We analyze a mechanism used in two LMs to selectively inhibit items in a context in one task, and find that it underlies a commonly used abstraction across many context-retrieval behaviors. Specifically, we find that models write into low-rank subspaces of the residual stream to represent features which are then read out by later layers, forming low-rank communication channels (Elhage et al., 2021) between layers. A particular 3D subspace in model activations in GPT-2 can be traversed to positionally index items in lists, and we show that this mechanism can explain an otherwise arbitrary-seeming sensitivity of the model to the order of items in the prompt. That is, the model has trouble copying the correct information from context when many items ``crowd" this limited space. By decomposing attention heads with the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), we find that previously described interactions between heads separated by one or more layers can be predicted via analysis of their weight matrices alone. We show that it is possible to manipulate the internal model representations as well as edit model weights based on the mechanism we discover in order to significantly improve performance on our synthetic Laundry List task, which requires recall from a list, often improving task accuracy by over 20%. Our analysis reveals a surprisingly intricate interpretable structure learned from language model pretraining, and helps us understand why sophisticated LMs sometimes fail in simple domains, facilitating future analysis of more complex behaviors.

papers.title: Why Safeguarded Ships Run Aground? Aligned Large Language Models' Safety Mechanisms Tend to Be Anchored in The Template Region
papers.research_question: Why are aligned large language models vulnerable to jailbreak attacks? The paper hypothesizes that their safety mechanisms are overly reliant on the template region (Template-Anchored Safety Alignment).
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies Template-Anchored Safety Alignment (TASA) as a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, where safety mechanisms overly rely on the template region, and shows that detaching safety mechanisms from this region can mitigate jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Template-anchored safety alignment is a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, and future safety alignment techniques should reduce reliance on the template region to improve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Attention shifts from the instruction region to the template region when processing harmful inputs.
The template region has a causal effect on safety decisions, as shown by activation patching.
Intervening in the template region (TEMP PATCH) can jailbreak models with high success rates.
Jailbreak attacks suppress harmfulness features in the template region.
Harmfulness probes from the template region can be transferred to response generation to detect harmful content.
papers.limitation:
The analysis may not generalize to all safety-aligned LLMs, as some may have mitigated TASA through training data or feature suppression.
The proposed detachment method does not eliminate the learned safety shortcuts and is only a proof-of-concept.
future_direction: Develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.
Integrate adversarial defense patterns during training.
Proactively suppress shortcut-prone features during alignment.
papers.abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable, as their initial behavior can be easily jailbroken by even relatively simple attacks. Since infilling a fixed template between the input instruction and initial model output is a common practice for existing LLMs, we hypothesize that this template is a key factor behind their vulnerabilities: LLMs' safety-related decision-making overly relies on the aggregated information from the template region, which largely influences these models' safety behavior. We refer to this issue as template-anchored safety alignment. In this paper, we conduct extensive experiments and verify that template-anchored safety alignment is widespread across various aligned LLMs. Our mechanistic analyses demonstrate how it leads to models' susceptibility when encountering inference-time jailbreak attacks. Furthermore, we show that detaching safety mechanisms from the template region is promising in mitigating vulnerabilities to jailbreak attacks. We encourage future research to develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.

papers.title: How Alignment and Jailbreak Work: Explain LLM Safety through Intermediate Hidden States
papers.research_question: How do alignment and jailbreak work in large language models? The paper investigates the mechanisms of safety alignment and how jailbreak circumvents it by analyzing intermediate hidden states.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs learn ethical concepts during pre-training and can identify malicious inputs in early layers. Safety alignment associates these early concepts with positive/negative emotions in middle layers, which are refined into accept/reject tokens. Jailbreak works by disturbing this association.
papers.conclusion: The work explains how alignment and jailbreak function through intermediate hidden states, enhancing transparency and offering a new perspective for LLM safety development.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs learn ethical concepts during pre-training, not just from alignment.
Weak classifiers can distinguish malicious and normal inputs from early layer hidden states with >95% accuracy.
Alignment associates early ethical concepts with emotion guesses (positive/negative) in middle layers, which are refined into stylistic accept/reject tokens.
Jailbreak does not deceive early ethical classification but disturbs the association between early and middle layers.
Logit Grafting, which grafts positive emotions onto malicious inputs, approximates jailbreak and confirms the disturbance mechanism.
papers.limitation: Used default settings of simple weak classifiers and only examined safety perspective; method might generalize to other capabilities but not tested.
future_direction: Apply the method to interpret other capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) rely on safety alignment to avoid responding to malicious user inputs. Unfortunately, jailbreak can circumvent safety guardrails, resulting in LLMs generating harmful content and raising concerns about LLM safety. Due to language models with intensive parameters often regarded as black boxes, the mechanisms of alignment and jailbreak are challenging to elucidate. In this paper, we employ weak classifiers to explain LLM safety through the intermediate hidden states. We first confirm that LLMs learn ethical concepts during pre-training rather than alignment and can identify malicious and normal inputs in the early layers. Alignment actually associates the early concepts with emotion guesses in the middle layers and then refines them to the specific reject tokens for safe generations. Jailbreak disturbs the transformation of early unethical classification into negative emotions. We conduct experiments on models from 7B to 70B across various model families to prove our conclusion. Overall, our paper indicates the intrinsical mechanism of LLM safety and how jailbreaks circumvent safety guardrails, offering a new perspective on LLM safety and reducing concerns. Our code is available at https://github.com/ydyjya/LLM-IHS-Explanation.

papers.title: How Syntax Specialization Emerges in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does syntactic specialization emerge and evolve over training, and how do model initialization, scale, and training data shape this development?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Syntactic Sensitivity Index (SSI) to measure syntactic specialization in language models, revealing that syntactic sensitivity emerges gradually, concentrates in specific layers, exhibits a critical period, and is consistent across architectures but implemented by different neurons.
papers.conclusion: Provides the first systematic, mechanistic account of how syntactic specialization emerges in transformer language models by introducing SSI and applying it across training trajectories, seeds, and model scales, offering an integrated picture of when, where, and how syntax is represented.
papers.key_findings:
SSI correlates with grammaticality judgment accuracy and outperforms supervised probing methods like SVM and regression.
Syntactic specialization emerges gradually during training, with different syntactic phenomena showing distinct acquisition timelines and layer profiles.
There is a critical period (around 16 million tokens) during which syntactic specialization rapidly emerges and then stabilizes.
While layer-level syntactic representations converge across different random seeds, the specific neurons responsible for syntax sensitivity differ (convergent layers, divergent neurons).
Larger models and more training data enhance syntactic abstraction and specialization, but the effect varies across syntactic phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Relies on sentence embeddings (mean pooling) which may miss token-level nuance or positional dynamics.
BLiMP focuses on binary acceptability, leaving gradient judgments, semantic-pragmatic interactions, and multi-sentence structures underexplored.
Open theoretical questions about minimal inductive bias, architectural interventions, and relation to semantic grounding.
future_direction: Extend SSI to token-level activations or attention maps.
Explore gradient judgments, semantic-pragmatic interactions, and multi-sentence structures beyond binary acceptability.
Investigate the minimal inductive bias or data regime required for syntactic specialization, architectural interventions, and how syntactic development relates to semantic grounding.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been found to develop surprising internal specializations: Individual neurons, attention heads, and circuits become selectively sensitive to syntactic structure, reflecting patterns observed in the human brain. While this specialization is well-documented, how it emerges during training and what influences its development remains largely unknown. In this work, we tap into the black box of specialization by tracking its formation over time. By quantifying internal syntactic consistency across minimal pairs from various syntactic phenomena, we identify a clear developmental trajectory: Syntactic sensitivity emerges gradually, concentrates in specific layers, and exhibits a 'critical period' of rapid internal specialization. This process is consistent across architectures and initialization parameters (e.g., random seeds), and is influenced by model scale and training data. We therefore reveal not only where syntax arises in LLMs but also how some models internalize it during training. To support future research, we will release the code, models, and training checkpoints upon acceptance.

papers.title: Language Embeddings Sometimes Contain Typological Generalizations
papers.research_question: To what extent can neural network models learn generalizations about language structure, and how do we find out what they have learned? Which typological features can be discovered when the system is not told what to look for?
papers.core_contribution: This paper finds that neural models can sometimes learn typological generalizations in their language representations, but less readily than suggested by prior work, and that careful evaluation is essential to avoid false positives. It also releases several resources for 1295 languages.
papers.conclusion: Neural models can discover typological generalizations, but they do so less readily than suggested by previous research, and careful evaluation is necessary to confirm such discoveries.
papers.key_findings:
Some generalizations in learned language representations are surprisingly close to traditional typological features, but most models (including those from previous work) do not appear to have made linguistically meaningful generalizations.
Careful attention to evaluation details, such as controlling for genealogical and areal correlations, is essential to avoid false positives.
The word-level language model (WordLM) captures word order features and some morphological features, while many other models (including MTVec, MTCell, and Ö&T) show little evidence of encoding typological features when evaluated with their method.
Lexical baselines (ASJP and Lexical similarity vectors) do not encode structural features, as expected, and can serve as a baseline for evaluation.
papers.limitation: The study only tries to connect neural language representations with known features from the typological literature, not with potentially novel generalizations.
future_direction: Investigating whether models make typological generalizations that human linguists have not previously made.
papers.abstract: To what extent can neural network models learn generalizations about language structure, and how do we find out what they have learned? We explore these questions by training neural models for a range of natural language processing tasks on a massively multilingual dataset of Bible translations in 1295 languages. The learned language representations are then compared to existing typological databases as well as to a novel set of quantitative syntactic and morphological features obtained through annotation projection. We conclude that some generalizations are surprisingly close to traditional features from linguistic typology, but that most of our models, as well as those of previous work, do not appear to have made linguistically meaningful generalizations. Careful attention to details in the evaluation turns out to be essential to avoid false positives. Furthermore, to encourage continued work in this field, we release several resources covering most or all of the languages in our data: (i) multiple sets of language representations, (ii) multilingual word embeddings, (iii) projected and predicted syntactic and morphological features, (iv) software to provide linguistically sound evaluations of language representations.

papers.title: Unraveling Syntax: How Language Models Learn Context-Free Grammars
papers.research_question: How does language modeling loss decompose with respect to the subgrammar structure of context-free grammars, and do models learn subgrammars in parallel?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language modeling loss decomposes linearly over the subgrammars of a context-free grammar, and that small transformers learn subgrammars in parallel, unlike children. Subgrammar pretraining can improve performance for tiny models and leads to internal representations that better reflect the grammar's substructure.
papers.conclusion: The work initiates the study of language modeling dynamics with respect to CFG substructure, showing loss decomposes into subgrammar-local contributions and that small transformers learn subgrammars in parallel. Subgrammar pretraining acts as an inductive bias, and depth of recursion remains a challenge.
papers.key_findings:
Language modeling loss (KL divergence) recurses linearly over the top-level subgrammars of a CFG.
Under certain assumptions, parametrized models learn subgrammars in parallel.
Empirically, small transformers learn all subgrammars in parallel, unlike children who master simpler substructures first.
Subgrammar pretraining can improve final performance for tiny models, and leads to internal representations that better align with the grammar's substructure.
Models struggle with deep recursion, even when they achieve low loss on training data.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical results do not fully explain when gradient-based training yields parallel improvement across subgrammars.
Experiments use a small set of synthetic PCFGs and scaled-down transformers, not covering the full diversity of CFGs (e.g., ambiguous grammars).
It is unresolved whether failures at deep recursion reflect representational limits or optimization barriers.
future_direction: Studying when and why models learn subgrammars in parallel.
Understanding why subgrammar pretraining yields more aligned representations and the optimal pretraining duration.
Exploring the effect of ambiguous CFGs and comparing other language classes in the Chomsky hierarchy.
papers.abstract: We introduce a new framework for understanding how language models acquire syntax. While large models achieve impressive results, little is known about their learning dynamics. Our approach starts with the observation that most domains of interest, such as natural language syntax, coding languages, arithmetic problems, are captured by probabilistic context-free grammars (PCFGs). We study the learning dynamics of small models trained on synthetic languages generated from PCFGs, enabling precise control over grammar complexity, recursion depth, and subgrammar structure. We prove several general, recursive formulae for the training loss and Kullback-Leibler divergence over the subgrammar structure of a PCFG. Empirically, we find that unlike children, who first master simple substructures before progressing to more complex constructions, transformers reduce loss across all subgrammars in parallel. We further show that subgrammar pretraining can improve the final loss for smaller models, and that pretrained models develop internal representations more aligned with the grammar's substructure. Finally, we demonstrate that models struggle with deeper recursive structures (a limitation even of large language models), revealing fundamental challenges in how neural networks represent hierarchical syntax. Overall, our work initiates the study of the learning dynamics of transformers on PCFGs as a versatile testbed for probing learning in language models, opening a research direction with many open questions.

papers.title: Filler-gaps that neural networks fail to generalize
papers.research_question: Do recurrent neural network (RNN) language models learn abstract syntactic constraints governing filler-gap dependencies, beyond surface heuristics?
papers.core_contribution: RNN language models learn a general representation for the existence of filler-gap dependencies but do not learn the underlying syntactic constraints (subjacency, ECP, L-marking, D-linking).
papers.conclusion: RNNs learn abstract representations shared across constructions for filler-gap existence, but not the deeper syntactic constraints, raising questions about the depth of abstractions learned by RNN language models.
papers.key_findings:
RNNs represent the existence of filler-gap dependencies across different constructions.
RNNs do not encode shared representations for the syntactic constraints subjacency, ECP, L-marking, or D-linking.
Models assign lower probability (higher surprisal) to D-linked sentences than to non-D-linked ones, which is the opposite of human behavior.
papers.limitation:
The priming sets might be too small to observe constraint-specific effects, though the authors argue the effects are large enough.
The syntactic theories of the constraints might be incorrect, but RNNs could still have learned them as plausible abstractions to aid processing.
papers.abstract: It can be difficult to separate abstract linguistic knowledge in recurrent neural networks (RNNs) from surface heuristics. In this work, we probe for highly abstract syntactic constraints that have been claimed to govern the behavior of filler-gap dependencies across different surface constructions. For models to generalize abstract patterns in expected ways to unseen data, they must share representational features in predictable ways. We use cumulative priming to test for representational overlap between disparate filler-gap constructions in English and find evidence that the models learn a general representation for the existence of filler-gap dependencies. However, we find no evidence that the models learn any of the shared underlying grammatical constraints we tested. Our work raises questions about the degree to which RNN language models learn abstract linguistic representations.

papers.title: SABER: Uncovering Vulnerabilities in Safety Alignment via Cross-Layer Residual Connection
papers.research_question: How can safety alignment in Large Language Models be bypassed by exploiting the layer-wise distribution of safety mechanisms and using cross-layer residual connections?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SABER, a white-box jailbreak method that uses a cross-layer residual connection to bypass safety alignment in LLMs by routing information around safety-enforcing middle-to-late layers.
papers.conclusion: SABER is an effective jailbreak method that highlights a critical vulnerability in open-source language models to subtle architectural perturbations, demonstrating that safety alignment can be circumvented via cross-layer residual connections.
papers.key_findings:
Safety mechanisms in LLMs are predominantly embedded in the middle-to-late layers.
SABER achieves up to a 51% improvement in Attack Success Rate over the best-performing baseline on the HarmBench test set.
SABER induces only a marginal shift in perplexity on benign inputs, preserving general language capabilities.
Euclidean norm-based scaling is a critical component for SABER's effectiveness.
SABER creates an alternative pathway that reduces denial responses without significantly increasing hallucinations, balancing attack success and output coherence.
papers.limitation: The outcome when more than one layer is connected is still unexplored.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) with safe-alignment training are powerful instruments with robust language comprehension capabilities. These models typically undergo meticulous alignment procedures involving human feedback to ensure the acceptance of safe inputs while rejecting harmful or unsafe ones. However, despite their massive scale and alignment efforts, LLMs remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, where malicious users manipulate the model to produce harmful outputs that it was explicitly trained to avoid. In this study, we find that the safety mechanisms in LLMs are predominantly embedded in the middle-to-late layers. Building on this insight, we introduce a novel white-box jailbreak method, SABER (Safety Alignment Bypass via Extra Residuals), which connects two intermediate layers $s$ and $e$ such that $s < e$, through a residual connection. Our approach achieves a 51% improvement over the best-performing baseline on the HarmBench test set. Furthermore, SABER induces only a marginal shift in perplexity when evaluated on the HarmBench validation set. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/PalGitts/SABER.

papers.title: Uncovering Safety Risks of Large Language Models through Concept Activation Vector
papers.research_question: How can safety risks of large language models be uncovered by interpreting their safety mechanisms and generating effective attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Safety Concept Activation Vector framework to interpret LLM safety mechanisms and develops an SCAV-guided attack method that generates effective attacks with automatic hyperparameter selection, improving attack success rates and response quality.
papers.conclusion: The paper uncovers severe safety risks in current LLMs and provides insights into their safety mechanisms using the SCAV framework.
papers.key_findings:
SCAV significantly improves attack success rates and response quality compared to baselines.
Generated attacks are transferable to black-box models like GPT-4 and other white-box LLMs.
Aligned LLMs show high vulnerability with average attack success rates up to 99.14%.
Existing unlearn methods may not fully erase harmful knowledge, as attacks still succeed.
Linear separability of embeddings indicates the formation of safety mechanisms in LLMs.
future_direction: Extending SCAV to multimodal models
Developing more robust defense methods against attacks
papers.abstract: Despite careful safety alignment, current large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to various attacks. To further unveil the safety risks of LLMs, we introduce a Safety Concept Activation Vector (SCAV) framework, which effectively guides the attacks by accurately interpreting LLMs' safety mechanisms. We then develop an SCAV-guided attack method that can generate both attack prompts and embedding-level attacks with automatically selected perturbation hyperparameters. Both automatic and human evaluations demonstrate that our attack method significantly improves the attack success rate and response quality while requiring less training data. Additionally, we find that our generated attack prompts may be transferable to GPT-4, and the embedding-level attacks may also be transferred to other white-box LLMs whose parameters are known. Our experiments further uncover the safety risks present in current LLMs. For example, in our evaluation of seven open-source LLMs, we observe an average attack success rate of 99.14%, based on the classic keyword-matching criterion. Finally, we provide insights into the safety mechanism of LLMs. The code is available at https://github.com/SproutNan/AI-Safety_SCAV.

papers.title: Can We Predict Alignment Before Models Finish Thinking? Towards Monitoring Misaligned Reasoning Models
papers.research_question: In this work, we ask whether the long CoTs can be leveraged for predictive safety monitoring: do the reasoning traces provide early signals of final response alignment that could enable timely intervention?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a simple linear probe trained on CoT activations significantly outperforms text-based methods for predicting response alignment, and that alignment signals can be detected early in the CoT, enabling potential real-time monitoring.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that lightweight probes on activations could enable real-time safety monitoring and early intervention during generation for reasoning language models.
papers.key_findings:
A linear probe on CoT activations outperforms all text-based monitoring baselines by a large margin (average absolute increase of 13 in F1 scores).
CoT texts are often unfaithful and misleading for safety prediction, while model latents provide a more reliable predictive signal.
The linear probe can predict response alignment from early CoT segments, showing alignment signals appear before reasoning completes.
A subset of responses called 'performative CoTs', where the reasoning consistently contradicts the final response, accounts for the performance gap between text classifiers and the linear probe.
The linear probe is data-efficient, remaining effective with as few as 50 training samples.
papers.abstract: Reasoning language models improve performance on complex tasks by generating long chains of thought (CoTs), but this process can also increase harmful outputs in adversarial settings. In this work, we ask whether the long CoTs can be leveraged for predictive safety monitoring: do the reasoning traces provide early signals of final response alignment that could enable timely intervention? We evaluate a range of monitoring methods using either CoT text or activations, including highly capable large language models, fine-tuned classifiers, and humans. First, we find that a simple linear probe trained on CoT activations significantly outperforms all text-based baselines in predicting whether a final response is safe or unsafe, with an average absolute increase of 13 in F1 scores over the best-performing alternatives. CoT texts are often unfaithful and misleading, while model latents provide a more reliable predictive signal. Second, the probe can be applied to early CoT segments before the response is generated, showing that alignment signals appear before reasoning completes. Error analysis reveals that the performance gap between text classifiers and the linear probe largely stems from a subset of responses we call performative CoTs, where the reasoning consistently contradicts the final response as the CoT progresses. Our findings generalize across model sizes, families, and safety benchmarks, suggesting that lightweight probes could enable real-time safety monitoring and early intervention during generation.

papers.title: How Post-Training Reshapes LLMs: A Mechanistic View on Knowledge, Truthfulness, Refusal, and Confidence
papers.research_question: How does post-training affect the internal mechanisms of large language models in terms of knowledge storage, truthfulness, refusal, and confidence?
