The method does not work for key composition (Appendix B).
Analysis is limited to two small models (GPT-2 small and Pythia 160m).
Difficulty in controlling all variables in the available data (Section 7).
future_direction: Future work in static weight analysis more generally.
More rigorous analysis of interactions between specific heads (e.g., 8.3 and 9.9).
Extending the method to analyze more complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: Although it is known that transformer language models (LMs) pass features from early layers to later layers, it is not well understood how this information is represented and routed by the model. We analyze a mechanism used in two LMs to selectively inhibit items in a context in one task, and find that it underlies a commonly used abstraction across many context-retrieval behaviors. Specifically, we find that models write into low-rank subspaces of the residual stream to represent features which are then read out by later layers, forming low-rank communication channels (Elhage et al., 2021) between layers. A particular 3D subspace in model activations in GPT-2 can be traversed to positionally index items in lists, and we show that this mechanism can explain an otherwise arbitrary-seeming sensitivity of the model to the order of items in the prompt. That is, the model has trouble copying the correct information from context when many items ``crowd" this limited space. By decomposing attention heads with the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), we find that previously described interactions between heads separated by one or more layers can be predicted via analysis of their weight matrices alone. We show that it is possible to manipulate the internal model representations as well as edit model weights based on the mechanism we discover in order to significantly improve performance on our synthetic Laundry List task, which requires recall from a list, often improving task accuracy by over 20%. Our analysis reveals a surprisingly intricate interpretable structure learned from language model pretraining, and helps us understand why sophisticated LMs sometimes fail in simple domains, facilitating future analysis of more complex behaviors.

papers.title: Why Safeguarded Ships Run Aground? Aligned Large Language Models' Safety Mechanisms Tend to Be Anchored in The Template Region
papers.research_question: Why are aligned large language models vulnerable to jailbreak attacks? The paper hypothesizes that their safety mechanisms are overly reliant on the template region (Template-Anchored Safety Alignment).
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies Template-Anchored Safety Alignment (TASA) as a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, where safety mechanisms overly rely on the template region, and shows that detaching safety mechanisms from this region can mitigate jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Template-anchored safety alignment is a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, and future safety alignment techniques should reduce reliance on the template region to improve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Attention shifts from the instruction region to the template region when processing harmful inputs.
The template region has a causal effect on safety decisions, as shown by activation patching.
Intervening in the template region (TEMP PATCH) can jailbreak models with high success rates.
Jailbreak attacks suppress harmfulness features in the template region.
Harmfulness probes from the template region can be transferred to response generation to detect harmful content.
papers.limitation:
The analysis may not generalize to all safety-aligned LLMs, as some may have mitigated TASA through training data or feature suppression.
The proposed detachment method does not eliminate the learned safety shortcuts and is only a proof-of-concept.
future_direction: Develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.
Integrate adversarial defense patterns during training.
Proactively suppress shortcut-prone features during alignment.
papers.abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable, as their initial behavior can be easily jailbroken by even relatively simple attacks. Since infilling a fixed template between the input instruction and initial model output is a common practice for existing LLMs, we hypothesize that this template is a key factor behind their vulnerabilities: LLMs' safety-related decision-making overly relies on the aggregated information from the template region, which largely influences these models' safety behavior. We refer to this issue as template-anchored safety alignment. In this paper, we conduct extensive experiments and verify that template-anchored safety alignment is widespread across various aligned LLMs. Our mechanistic analyses demonstrate how it leads to models' susceptibility when encountering inference-time jailbreak attacks. Furthermore, we show that detaching safety mechanisms from the template region is promising in mitigating vulnerabilities to jailbreak attacks. We encourage future research to develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.

papers.title: How Alignment and Jailbreak Work: Explain LLM Safety through Intermediate Hidden States
papers.research_question: How do alignment and jailbreak work in large language models? The paper investigates the mechanisms of safety alignment and how jailbreak circumvents it by analyzing intermediate hidden states.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs learn ethical concepts during pre-training and can identify malicious inputs in early layers. Safety alignment associates these early concepts with positive/negative emotions in middle layers, which are refined into accept/reject tokens. Jailbreak works by disturbing this association.
papers.conclusion: The work explains how alignment and jailbreak function through intermediate hidden states, enhancing transparency and offering a new perspective for LLM safety development.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs learn ethical concepts during pre-training, not just from alignment.
Weak classifiers can distinguish malicious and normal inputs from early layer hidden states with >95% accuracy.
Alignment associates early ethical concepts with emotion guesses (positive/negative) in middle layers, which are refined into stylistic accept/reject tokens.
Jailbreak does not deceive early ethical classification but disturbs the association between early and middle layers.
Logit Grafting, which grafts positive emotions onto malicious inputs, approximates jailbreak and confirms the disturbance mechanism.
papers.limitation: Used default settings of simple weak classifiers and only examined safety perspective; method might generalize to other capabilities but not tested.
future_direction: Apply the method to interpret other capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) rely on safety alignment to avoid responding to malicious user inputs. Unfortunately, jailbreak can circumvent safety guardrails, resulting in LLMs generating harmful content and raising concerns about LLM safety. Due to language models with intensive parameters often regarded as black boxes, the mechanisms of alignment and jailbreak are challenging to elucidate. In this paper, we employ weak classifiers to explain LLM safety through the intermediate hidden states. We first confirm that LLMs learn ethical concepts during pre-training rather than alignment and can identify malicious and normal inputs in the early layers. Alignment actually associates the early concepts with emotion guesses in the middle layers and then refines them to the specific reject tokens for safe generations. Jailbreak disturbs the transformation of early unethical classification into negative emotions. We conduct experiments on models from 7B to 70B across various model families to prove our conclusion. Overall, our paper indicates the intrinsical mechanism of LLM safety and how jailbreaks circumvent safety guardrails, offering a new perspective on LLM safety and reducing concerns. Our code is available at https://github.com/ydyjya/LLM-IHS-Explanation.

papers.title: How Syntax Specialization Emerges in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does syntactic specialization emerge and evolve over training, and how do model initialization, scale, and training data shape this development?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Syntactic Sensitivity Index (SSI) to measure syntactic specialization in language models, revealing that syntactic sensitivity emerges gradually, concentrates in specific layers, exhibits a critical period, and is consistent across architectures but implemented by different neurons.
papers.conclusion: Provides the first systematic, mechanistic account of how syntactic specialization emerges in transformer language models by introducing SSI and applying it across training trajectories, seeds, and model scales, offering an integrated picture of when, where, and how syntax is represented.
papers.key_findings:
SSI correlates with grammaticality judgment accuracy and outperforms supervised probing methods like SVM and regression.
Syntactic specialization emerges gradually during training, with different syntactic phenomena showing distinct acquisition timelines and layer profiles.
There is a critical period (around 16 million tokens) during which syntactic specialization rapidly emerges and then stabilizes.
While layer-level syntactic representations converge across different random seeds, the specific neurons responsible for syntax sensitivity differ (convergent layers, divergent neurons).
Larger models and more training data enhance syntactic abstraction and specialization, but the effect varies across syntactic phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Relies on sentence embeddings (mean pooling) which may miss token-level nuance or positional dynamics.
BLiMP focuses on binary acceptability, leaving gradient judgments, semantic-pragmatic interactions, and multi-sentence structures underexplored.
Open theoretical questions about minimal inductive bias, architectural interventions, and relation to semantic grounding.
future_direction: Extend SSI to token-level activations or attention maps.
Explore gradient judgments, semantic-pragmatic interactions, and multi-sentence structures beyond binary acceptability.
Investigate the minimal inductive bias or data regime required for syntactic specialization, architectural interventions, and how syntactic development relates to semantic grounding.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been found to develop surprising internal specializations: Individual neurons, attention heads, and circuits become selectively sensitive to syntactic structure, reflecting patterns observed in the human brain. While this specialization is well-documented, how it emerges during training and what influences its development remains largely unknown. In this work, we tap into the black box of specialization by tracking its formation over time. By quantifying internal syntactic consistency across minimal pairs from various syntactic phenomena, we identify a clear developmental trajectory: Syntactic sensitivity emerges gradually, concentrates in specific layers, and exhibits a 'critical period' of rapid internal specialization. This process is consistent across architectures and initialization parameters (e.g., random seeds), and is influenced by model scale and training data. We therefore reveal not only where syntax arises in LLMs but also how some models internalize it during training. To support future research, we will release the code, models, and training checkpoints upon acceptance.

papers.title: Language Embeddings Sometimes Contain Typological Generalizations
papers.research_question: To what extent can neural network models learn generalizations about language structure, and how do we find out what they have learned? Which typological features can be discovered when the system is not told what to look for?
papers.core_contribution: This paper finds that neural models can sometimes learn typological generalizations in their language representations, but less readily than suggested by prior work, and that careful evaluation is essential to avoid false positives. It also releases several resources for 1295 languages.
papers.conclusion: Neural models can discover typological generalizations, but they do so less readily than suggested by previous research, and careful evaluation is necessary to confirm such discoveries.
papers.key_findings:
Some generalizations in learned language representations are surprisingly close to traditional typological features, but most models (including those from previous work) do not appear to have made linguistically meaningful generalizations.
Careful attention to evaluation details, such as controlling for genealogical and areal correlations, is essential to avoid false positives.
The word-level language model (WordLM) captures word order features and some morphological features, while many other models (including MTVec, MTCell, and Ö&T) show little evidence of encoding typological features when evaluated with their method.
Lexical baselines (ASJP and Lexical similarity vectors) do not encode structural features, as expected, and can serve as a baseline for evaluation.
papers.limitation: The study only tries to connect neural language representations with known features from the typological literature, not with potentially novel generalizations.
future_direction: Investigating whether models make typological generalizations that human linguists have not previously made.
papers.abstract: To what extent can neural network models learn generalizations about language structure, and how do we find out what they have learned? We explore these questions by training neural models for a range of natural language processing tasks on a massively multilingual dataset of Bible translations in 1295 languages. The learned language representations are then compared to existing typological databases as well as to a novel set of quantitative syntactic and morphological features obtained through annotation projection. We conclude that some generalizations are surprisingly close to traditional features from linguistic typology, but that most of our models, as well as those of previous work, do not appear to have made linguistically meaningful generalizations. Careful attention to details in the evaluation turns out to be essential to avoid false positives. Furthermore, to encourage continued work in this field, we release several resources covering most or all of the languages in our data: (i) multiple sets of language representations, (ii) multilingual word embeddings, (iii) projected and predicted syntactic and morphological features, (iv) software to provide linguistically sound evaluations of language representations.

papers.title: Unraveling Syntax: How Language Models Learn Context-Free Grammars
papers.research_question: How does language modeling loss decompose with respect to the subgrammar structure of context-free grammars, and do models learn subgrammars in parallel?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language modeling loss decomposes linearly over the subgrammars of a context-free grammar, and that small transformers learn subgrammars in parallel, unlike children. Subgrammar pretraining can improve performance for tiny models and leads to internal representations that better reflect the grammar's substructure.
papers.conclusion: The work initiates the study of language modeling dynamics with respect to CFG substructure, showing loss decomposes into subgrammar-local contributions and that small transformers learn subgrammars in parallel. Subgrammar pretraining acts as an inductive bias, and depth of recursion remains a challenge.
papers.key_findings:
Language modeling loss (KL divergence) recurses linearly over the top-level subgrammars of a CFG.
Under certain assumptions, parametrized models learn subgrammars in parallel.
Empirically, small transformers learn all subgrammars in parallel, unlike children who master simpler substructures first.
Subgrammar pretraining can improve final performance for tiny models, and leads to internal representations that better align with the grammar's substructure.
Models struggle with deep recursion, even when they achieve low loss on training data.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical results do not fully explain when gradient-based training yields parallel improvement across subgrammars.
Experiments use a small set of synthetic PCFGs and scaled-down transformers, not covering the full diversity of CFGs (e.g., ambiguous grammars).
It is unresolved whether failures at deep recursion reflect representational limits or optimization barriers.
future_direction: Studying when and why models learn subgrammars in parallel.
Understanding why subgrammar pretraining yields more aligned representations and the optimal pretraining duration.
Exploring the effect of ambiguous CFGs and comparing other language classes in the Chomsky hierarchy.
papers.abstract: We introduce a new framework for understanding how language models acquire syntax. While large models achieve impressive results, little is known about their learning dynamics. Our approach starts with the observation that most domains of interest, such as natural language syntax, coding languages, arithmetic problems, are captured by probabilistic context-free grammars (PCFGs). We study the learning dynamics of small models trained on synthetic languages generated from PCFGs, enabling precise control over grammar complexity, recursion depth, and subgrammar structure. We prove several general, recursive formulae for the training loss and Kullback-Leibler divergence over the subgrammar structure of a PCFG. Empirically, we find that unlike children, who first master simple substructures before progressing to more complex constructions, transformers reduce loss across all subgrammars in parallel. We further show that subgrammar pretraining can improve the final loss for smaller models, and that pretrained models develop internal representations more aligned with the grammar's substructure. Finally, we demonstrate that models struggle with deeper recursive structures (a limitation even of large language models), revealing fundamental challenges in how neural networks represent hierarchical syntax. Overall, our work initiates the study of the learning dynamics of transformers on PCFGs as a versatile testbed for probing learning in language models, opening a research direction with many open questions.

papers.title: Filler-gaps that neural networks fail to generalize
papers.research_question: Do recurrent neural network (RNN) language models learn abstract syntactic constraints governing filler-gap dependencies, beyond surface heuristics?
papers.core_contribution: RNN language models learn a general representation for the existence of filler-gap dependencies but do not learn the underlying syntactic constraints (subjacency, ECP, L-marking, D-linking).
papers.conclusion: RNNs learn abstract representations shared across constructions for filler-gap existence, but not the deeper syntactic constraints, raising questions about the depth of abstractions learned by RNN language models.
papers.key_findings:
RNNs represent the existence of filler-gap dependencies across different constructions.
RNNs do not encode shared representations for the syntactic constraints subjacency, ECP, L-marking, or D-linking.
Models assign lower probability (higher surprisal) to D-linked sentences than to non-D-linked ones, which is the opposite of human behavior.
papers.limitation:
The priming sets might be too small to observe constraint-specific effects, though the authors argue the effects are large enough.
The syntactic theories of the constraints might be incorrect, but RNNs could still have learned them as plausible abstractions to aid processing.
papers.abstract: It can be difficult to separate abstract linguistic knowledge in recurrent neural networks (RNNs) from surface heuristics. In this work, we probe for highly abstract syntactic constraints that have been claimed to govern the behavior of filler-gap dependencies across different surface constructions. For models to generalize abstract patterns in expected ways to unseen data, they must share representational features in predictable ways. We use cumulative priming to test for representational overlap between disparate filler-gap constructions in English and find evidence that the models learn a general representation for the existence of filler-gap dependencies. However, we find no evidence that the models learn any of the shared underlying grammatical constraints we tested. Our work raises questions about the degree to which RNN language models learn abstract linguistic representations.

papers.title: SABER: Uncovering Vulnerabilities in Safety Alignment via Cross-Layer Residual Connection
papers.research_question: How can safety alignment in Large Language Models be bypassed by exploiting the layer-wise distribution of safety mechanisms and using cross-layer residual connections?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SABER, a white-box jailbreak method that uses a cross-layer residual connection to bypass safety alignment in LLMs by routing information around safety-enforcing middle-to-late layers.
papers.conclusion: SABER is an effective jailbreak method that highlights a critical vulnerability in open-source language models to subtle architectural perturbations, demonstrating that safety alignment can be circumvented via cross-layer residual connections.
papers.key_findings:
Safety mechanisms in LLMs are predominantly embedded in the middle-to-late layers.
SABER achieves up to a 51% improvement in Attack Success Rate over the best-performing baseline on the HarmBench test set.
SABER induces only a marginal shift in perplexity on benign inputs, preserving general language capabilities.
Euclidean norm-based scaling is a critical component for SABER's effectiveness.
SABER creates an alternative pathway that reduces denial responses without significantly increasing hallucinations, balancing attack success and output coherence.
papers.limitation: The outcome when more than one layer is connected is still unexplored.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) with safe-alignment training are powerful instruments with robust language comprehension capabilities. These models typically undergo meticulous alignment procedures involving human feedback to ensure the acceptance of safe inputs while rejecting harmful or unsafe ones. However, despite their massive scale and alignment efforts, LLMs remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, where malicious users manipulate the model to produce harmful outputs that it was explicitly trained to avoid. In this study, we find that the safety mechanisms in LLMs are predominantly embedded in the middle-to-late layers. Building on this insight, we introduce a novel white-box jailbreak method, SABER (Safety Alignment Bypass via Extra Residuals), which connects two intermediate layers $s$ and $e$ such that $s < e$, through a residual connection. Our approach achieves a 51% improvement over the best-performing baseline on the HarmBench test set. Furthermore, SABER induces only a marginal shift in perplexity when evaluated on the HarmBench validation set. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/PalGitts/SABER.

papers.title: Uncovering Safety Risks of Large Language Models through Concept Activation Vector
papers.research_question: How can safety risks of large language models be uncovered by interpreting their safety mechanisms and generating effective attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Safety Concept Activation Vector framework to interpret LLM safety mechanisms and develops an SCAV-guided attack method that generates effective attacks with automatic hyperparameter selection, improving attack success rates and response quality.
papers.conclusion: The paper uncovers severe safety risks in current LLMs and provides insights into their safety mechanisms using the SCAV framework.
papers.key_findings:
SCAV significantly improves attack success rates and response quality compared to baselines.
Generated attacks are transferable to black-box models like GPT-4 and other white-box LLMs.
Aligned LLMs show high vulnerability with average attack success rates up to 99.14%.
Existing unlearn methods may not fully erase harmful knowledge, as attacks still succeed.
Linear separability of embeddings indicates the formation of safety mechanisms in LLMs.
future_direction: Extending SCAV to multimodal models
Developing more robust defense methods against attacks
papers.abstract: Despite careful safety alignment, current large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to various attacks. To further unveil the safety risks of LLMs, we introduce a Safety Concept Activation Vector (SCAV) framework, which effectively guides the attacks by accurately interpreting LLMs' safety mechanisms. We then develop an SCAV-guided attack method that can generate both attack prompts and embedding-level attacks with automatically selected perturbation hyperparameters. Both automatic and human evaluations demonstrate that our attack method significantly improves the attack success rate and response quality while requiring less training data. Additionally, we find that our generated attack prompts may be transferable to GPT-4, and the embedding-level attacks may also be transferred to other white-box LLMs whose parameters are known. Our experiments further uncover the safety risks present in current LLMs. For example, in our evaluation of seven open-source LLMs, we observe an average attack success rate of 99.14%, based on the classic keyword-matching criterion. Finally, we provide insights into the safety mechanism of LLMs. The code is available at https://github.com/SproutNan/AI-Safety_SCAV.

papers.title: Can We Predict Alignment Before Models Finish Thinking? Towards Monitoring Misaligned Reasoning Models
papers.research_question: In this work, we ask whether the long CoTs can be leveraged for predictive safety monitoring: do the reasoning traces provide early signals of final response alignment that could enable timely intervention?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a simple linear probe trained on CoT activations significantly outperforms text-based methods for predicting response alignment, and that alignment signals can be detected early in the CoT, enabling potential real-time monitoring.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that lightweight probes on activations could enable real-time safety monitoring and early intervention during generation for reasoning language models.
papers.key_findings:
A linear probe on CoT activations outperforms all text-based monitoring baselines by a large margin (average absolute increase of 13 in F1 scores).
CoT texts are often unfaithful and misleading for safety prediction, while model latents provide a more reliable predictive signal.
The linear probe can predict response alignment from early CoT segments, showing alignment signals appear before reasoning completes.
A subset of responses called 'performative CoTs', where the reasoning consistently contradicts the final response, accounts for the performance gap between text classifiers and the linear probe.
The linear probe is data-efficient, remaining effective with as few as 50 training samples.
papers.abstract: Reasoning language models improve performance on complex tasks by generating long chains of thought (CoTs), but this process can also increase harmful outputs in adversarial settings. In this work, we ask whether the long CoTs can be leveraged for predictive safety monitoring: do the reasoning traces provide early signals of final response alignment that could enable timely intervention? We evaluate a range of monitoring methods using either CoT text or activations, including highly capable large language models, fine-tuned classifiers, and humans. First, we find that a simple linear probe trained on CoT activations significantly outperforms all text-based baselines in predicting whether a final response is safe or unsafe, with an average absolute increase of 13 in F1 scores over the best-performing alternatives. CoT texts are often unfaithful and misleading, while model latents provide a more reliable predictive signal. Second, the probe can be applied to early CoT segments before the response is generated, showing that alignment signals appear before reasoning completes. Error analysis reveals that the performance gap between text classifiers and the linear probe largely stems from a subset of responses we call performative CoTs, where the reasoning consistently contradicts the final response as the CoT progresses. Our findings generalize across model sizes, families, and safety benchmarks, suggesting that lightweight probes could enable real-time safety monitoring and early intervention during generation.

papers.title: How Post-Training Reshapes LLMs: A Mechanistic View on Knowledge, Truthfulness, Refusal, and Confidence
papers.research_question: How does post-training affect the internal mechanisms of large language models in terms of knowledge storage, truthfulness, refusal, and confidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a mechanistic analysis of how post-training affects LLMs internally, revealing which mechanisms are preserved (e.g., knowledge storage locations, truthfulness direction) and which are altered (e.g., refusal direction), with implications for model steering and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Post-training preserves some internal mechanisms (like knowledge storage and truthfulness direction) and alters others (like refusal direction), providing insights for model steering and future research in interpretability and LLM post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations in LLMs.
Post-training adapts knowledge representations from the base model while also developing new ones.
The truthfulness direction is highly similar between base and post-trained models and is effectively transferable for interventions.
The refusal direction differs between base and post-trained models and shows limited forward transferability.
Differences in confidence between base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons.
papers.limitation: Complex, multi-step processes such as reasoning and instruction-following are not well-captured by current mechanistic interpretability tools, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Design better post-training methods based on mechanistic insights.
Extend analysis to other capabilities like reasoning and instruction-following.
papers.abstract: Post-training is essential for the success of large language models (LLMs), transforming pre-trained base models into more useful and aligned post-trained models. While plenty of works have studied post-training algorithms and evaluated post-training models by their outputs, it remains understudied how post-training reshapes LLMs internally. In this paper, we compare base and post-trained LLMs mechanistically from four perspectives to better understand post-training effects. Our findings across model families and datasets reveal that: (1) Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations, and it adapts knowledge representations from the base model while developing new knowledge representations; (2) Both truthfulness and refusal can be represented by vectors in the hidden representation space. The truthfulness direction is highly similar between the base and post-trained model, and it is effectively transferable for interventions; (3) The refusal direction is different between the base and post-trained models, and it shows limited forward transferability; (4) Differences in confidence between the base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons. Our study provides insights into the fundamental mechanisms preserved and altered during post-training, facilitates downstream tasks like model steering, and could potentially benefit future research in interpretability and LLM post-training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HZD01/post-training-mechanistic-analysis.

papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating Over-refusal for Large Language Models via Safety Representation
papers.research_question: How do over-refusal samples alter a model's perception of safety, leading to rejection responses? How can we better balance safety and over-refusal?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes over-refusal in LLMs from a representation perspective, finding that over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious representations, and proposes the MOSR method with overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation to mitigate over-refusal while maintaining safety.
papers.conclusion: The paper attributes over-refusal to pseudo-malicious representations lying in the boundary region between malicious and benign samples and proposes two strategies (overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation) that mitigate the tendency for over-refusal sample representations to migrate toward the rejection space during alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious samples in the representation space, causing the model to misclassify them as malicious.
The proposed MOSR method, incorporating overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation, effectively mitigates over-refusal while largely maintaining model safety.
Existing defense methods often exhibit a severe imbalance between safety and over-refusal, sacrificing utility for higher malicious prompt rejection rates.
MOSR maintains the general capabilities of the model, as evaluated on standard benchmarks like MMLU and GSM8K.
The balance between safety and over-refusal is challenging due to the high similarity between over-refusal and malicious samples in representation space.
papers.limitation:
The paper focuses on single-round scenarios; multi-round over-refusal scenarios are not addressed.
Fine-tuning large language models with the proposed method remains costly.
future_direction: Multi-turn over-refusal scenarios, including developing benchmarks for multi-round over-refusal and safety.
Exploring lower-cost mitigation approaches, such as dynamic reasoning intervention methods based on representation engineering.
papers.abstract: Large language models demonstrate powerful capabilities across various natural language processing tasks, yet they also harbor safety vulnerabilities. To enhance LLM safety, various jailbreak defense methods have been proposed to guard against harmful outputs. However, improvements in model safety often come at the cost of severe over-refusal, failing to strike a good balance between safety and usability. In this paper, we first analyze the causes of over-refusal from a representation perspective, revealing that over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious samples. Based on this, we propose MOSR, designed to mitigate over-refusal by intervening the safety representation of LLMs. MOSR incorporates two novel components: (1) Overlap-Aware Loss Weighting, which determines the erasure weight for malicious samples by quantifying their similarity to pseudo-malicious samples in the representation space, and (2) Context-Aware Augmentation, which supplements the necessary context for rejection decisions by adding harmful prefixes before rejection responses. Experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches in mitigating over-refusal while largely maintaining safety. Overall, we advocate that future defense methods should strike a better balance between safety and over-refusal.

papers.title: Future Events as Backdoor Triggers: Investigating Temporal Vulnerabilities in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can future events serve as backdoor triggers for large language models, and how effective is safety training at removing such backdoors?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that LLMs can distinguish past from future events, and that backdoors triggered by temporal distribution shifts can be trained into models. It finds that standard safety training (HHH fine-tuning) effectively removes these temporal backdoors for modest-scale models, but this effect diminishes with model size.
papers.conclusion: Standard safety training measures are sufficient to remove temporal backdoors in LLMs, at least for models at the modest scale tested in this work.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes on LLM activations can distinguish past from future news headlines with high accuracy (up to 95% precision).
Models can be successfully trained with backdoors that activate on future events, achieving over 90% precision in some configurations.
Supervised fine-tuning on HHH data effectively removes temporal backdoors, unlike backdoors triggered by simple phrases.
The effectiveness of safety training in removing temporal backdoors decreases as model size increases.
Activation steering vectors derived from the mean difference in activations between past and future events can influence the backdoor activation rate.
papers.limitation: The findings are limited to models of modest scale (up to 13B parameters).
papers.abstract: Backdoors are hidden behaviors that are only triggered once an AI system has been deployed. Bad actors looking to create successful backdoors must design them to avoid activation during training and evaluation. Since data used in these stages often only contains information about events that have already occurred, a component of a simple backdoor trigger could be a model recognizing data that is in the future relative to when it was trained. Through prompting experiments and by probing internal activations, we show that current large language models (LLMs) can distinguish past from future events, with probes on model activations achieving 90% accuracy. We train models with backdoors triggered by a temporal distributional shift; they activate when the model is exposed to news headlines beyond their training cut-off dates. Fine-tuning on helpful, harmless and honest (HHH) data does not work well for removing simpler backdoor triggers but is effective on our backdoored models, although this distinction is smaller for the larger-scale model we tested. We also find that an activation-steering vector representing a model's internal representation of the date influences the rate of backdoor activation. We take these results as initial evidence that, at least for models at the modest scale we test, standard safety measures are enough to remove these backdoors.

papers.title: Universal Refusal Circuits Across LLMs: Cross-Model Transfer via Trajectory Replay and Concept-Basis Reconstruction
papers.research_question: Are refusal circuits universal across LLMs? Can a refusal circuit extracted from a donor model be transferred to a target model without target-side refusal supervision?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for transferring refusal circuits across LLMs without target-side refusal supervision, combining concept-basis reconstruction and a weight-SVD stability guard, providing evidence for semantic universality of safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: Refusal circuits are universal across LLMs and can be transferred via semantic recipe invariance, enabling cross-model circuit editing without target-side refusal supervision.
papers.key_findings:
The method successfully transfers refusal attenuation across 8 model pairs, including cross-family and cross-architecture transfers.
Refusal circuits are composed of a stable mixture of concept atoms, enabling cross-model transfer via semantic recipe invariance.
The weight-SVD guard prevents capability collapse by projecting interventions away from high-variance weight subspaces.
The transfer works without target-side refusal supervision, relying only on benign concept prompts and validation data.
The method preserves model capabilities on math and code tasks while reducing refusal rates.
papers.limitation:
Efficacy depends on coverage of the Concept Atom Registry; if refusal circuit uses features orthogonal to the atoms, reconstruction may fail.
Weight-SVD guard relies on the heuristic that capability-critical circuits reside in high-variance principal components, which may not generalize to all tasks.
Method is white-box, requiring access to model weights and internal activations, limiting applicability to closed-source systems.
future_direction: Expand CAR coverage to test transfer beyond refusal directions to multi-behavior editing.
Explore black-box approximations of semantic fingerprints for closed-source systems.
Test the method on a wider range of models and alignment behaviors.
papers.abstract: Refusal behavior in aligned LLMs is often viewed as model-specific, yet we hypothesize it stems from a universal, low-dimensional semantic circuit shared across models. To test this, we introduce Trajectory Replay via Concept-Basis Reconstruction, a framework that transfers refusal interventions from donor to target models, spanning diverse architectures (e.g., Dense to MoE) and training regimes, without using target-side refusal supervision. By aligning layers via concept fingerprints and reconstructing refusal directions using a shared ``recipe'' of concept atoms, we map the donor's ablation trajectory into the target's semantic space. To preserve capabilities, we introduce a weight-SVD stability guard that projects interventions away from high-variance weight subspaces to prevent collateral damage. Our evaluation across 8 model pairs confirms that these transferred recipes consistently attenuate refusal while maintaining performance, providing strong evidence for the semantic universality of safety alignment.

papers.title: Hierarchical Frequency Tagging Probe (HFTP): A Unified Approach to Investigate Syntactic Structure Representations in Large Language Models and the Human Brain
papers.research_question: Does syntactic processing in LLMs rely on mechanisms similar to those in the human brain? Which computational modules in LLMs are responsible for syntactic structure representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Hierarchical Frequency Tagging Probe (HFTP), a frequency-domain analysis tool to identify syntactic structure representations in LLMs and the human brain, and uses it to compare alignment between them.
papers.conclusion: HFTP provides new insights into LLM interpretability and raises questions about whether advancements are driven by human-like or non-human-like mechanisms, establishing a bridge between computational linguistics and cognitive neuroscience.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs (GPT-2, Gemma, Gemma 2, Llama 2, Llama 3.1, GLM-4) process syntax in analogous layers, while the human brain uses distinct cortical regions for different syntactic levels.
Representational similarity analysis shows stronger alignment between LLM representations and the left hemisphere (dominant in language processing).
Upgraded models show divergent trends: Gemma 2 has greater brain similarity than Gemma, while Llama 3.1 has less alignment than Llama 2.
HFTP can detect syntactic structure representations in both LLMs and the human brain, providing a unified framework for alignment studies.
Sentence and phrase processing in LLMs are correlated across layers, whereas in the human brain they are independent across regions.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate human-level or even superior language abilities, effectively modeling syntactic structures, yet the specific computational modules responsible remain unclear. A key question is whether LLM behavioral capabilities stem from mechanisms akin to those in the human brain. To address these questions, we introduce the Hierarchical Frequency Tagging Probe (HFTP), a tool that utilizes frequency-domain analysis to identify neuron-wise components of LLMs (e.g., individual Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) neurons) and cortical regions (via intracranial recordings) encoding syntactic structures. Our results show that models such as GPT-2, Gemma, Gemma 2, Llama 2, Llama 3.1, and GLM-4 process syntax in analogous layers, while the human brain relies on distinct cortical regions for different syntactic levels. Representational similarity analysis reveals a stronger alignment between LLM representations and the left hemisphere of the brain (dominant in language processing). Notably, upgraded models exhibit divergent trends: Gemma 2 shows greater brain similarity than Gemma, while Llama 3.1 shows less alignment with the brain compared to Llama 2. These findings offer new insights into the interpretability of LLM behavioral improvements, raising questions about whether these advancements are driven by human-like or non-human-like mechanisms, and establish HFTP as a valuable tool bridging computational linguistics and cognitive neuroscience. This project is available at https://github.com/LilTiger/HFTP.

papers.title: Differential syntactic and semantic encoding in LLMs
papers.research_question: How are syntactic and semantic information encoded in the inner layer representations of Large Language Models (LLMs), and to what extent are these two types of linguistic information differentially encoded and separable?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that syntactic and semantic information in LLMs are at least partially encoded via linear superposition, and that these two linguistic components have different encoding profiles across network layers and can be partially decoupled.
papers.conclusion: Syntax and semantics are differentially encoded in LLM representations, with syntax being more persistent across layers and semantics more concentrated in the central layers; the two components are partially separable, suggesting an inherent distinction in how language models process structural and meaning-related information.
papers.key_findings:
Syntactic similarity between sentences with the same structure is high across all network layers, while semantic similarity between paraphrases is low in early layers, peaks in the middle layers, and decreases slightly at the final layer.
Subtracting the projection of a sentence representation along its syntactic or semantic centroid (constructed by averaging representations of sentences with the same syntax or meaning) significantly reduces the corresponding similarity, indicating a linear encoding scheme.
Removing semantic information via centroid projection does not significantly affect syntactic similarity, but removing syntactic information does reduce semantic similarity, revealing an asymmetry in their encoding.
The fraction of a sentence vector's squared norm explained by its syntactic and semantic components varies across layers, with syntax dominating in early layers and semantics in middle layers, but a large residual norm remains unexplained.
The main findings are qualitatively consistent across three different LLMs (DeepSeek-V3, Qwen2-7b, and Gemma3-12b).
papers.limitation: The syntactic and semantic centroids account for only a part of the total norm of sentence activation vectors; the residual component may contain other information (e.g., lexical) or indicate that the centroids are only partial proxies for the full syntactic and semantic content.
future_direction: Determine why the ablation effect of mismatched (random) syntactic centroids is particularly strong in the middle layers for concatenated representations.
Investigate whether the residual norm not captured by the syntactic and semantic centroids is genuinely orthogonal to syntax and semantics or points to limitations of the centroid proxies.
Explore whether the observed asymmetry in the effect of syntactic ablation on semantic similarity is a general property of language encoding in LLMs.
papers.abstract: We study how syntactic and semantic information is encoded in inner layer representations of Large Language Models (LLMs), focusing on the very large DeepSeek-V3. We find that, by averaging hidden-representation vectors of sentences sharing syntactic structure or meaning, we obtain vectors that capture a significant proportion of the syntactic and semantic information contained in the representations. In particular, subtracting these syntactic and semantic ``centroids'' from sentence vectors strongly affects their similarity with syntactically and semantically matched sentences, respectively, suggesting that syntax and semantics are, at least partially, linearly encoded. We also find that the cross-layer encoding profiles of syntax and semantics are different, and that the two signals can to some extent be decoupled, suggesting differential encoding of these two types of linguistic information in LLM representations.

papers.title: Turning the Spell Around: Lightweight Alignment Amplification via Rank-One Safety Injection
papers.research_question: Can we systematically amplify safety alignment in LLMs by permanently steering activations toward the refusal-mediating subspace?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RANK-ONE SAFETY INJECTION (ROSI), a fine-tuning-free weight-editing method that amplifies safety alignment in LLMs by permanently steering activations toward a refusal-mediating subspace.
papers.conclusion: ROSI is a simple, effective, and interpretable method to enhance LLM safety, demonstrating the practical value of mechanistic interpretability for designing efficient safety interventions.
papers.key_findings:
ROSI consistently improves harm refusal rates in aligned models while preserving utility on standard benchmarks.
ROSI makes aligned models more robust to a suite of adversarial jailbreak attacks.
ROSI can inject safety into uncensored models (e.g., DOLPHIN), effectively re-aligning them without retraining.
The safety direction is largely orthogonal to utility representations, allowing safety amplification with minimal side effects.
A safety system prompt is crucial for extracting a meaningful safety direction from uncensored models.
papers.limitation: Smaller models (≤ 1B) show the biggest degradation in benign compliance (BC) when applying ROSI.
future_direction: Exploring more sophisticated methods for identifying and manipulating conceptual directions
Extending the approach to other desirable model attributes beyond safety, such as honesty or controllability
papers.abstract: Safety alignment in Large Language Models (LLMs) often involves mediating internal representations to refuse harmful requests. Recent research has demonstrated that these safety mechanisms can be bypassed by ablating or removing specific representational directions within the model. In this paper, we propose the opposite approach: Rank-One Safety Injection (ROSI), a white-box method that amplifies a model's safety alignment by permanently steering its activations toward the refusal-mediating subspace. ROSI operates as a simple, fine-tuning-free rank-one weight modification applied to all residual stream write matrices. The required safety direction can be computed from a small set of harmful and harmless instruction pairs. We show that ROSI consistently increases safety refusal rates - as evaluated by Llama Guard 3 - while preserving the utility of the model on standard benchmarks such as MMLU, HellaSwag, and Arc. Furthermore, we show that ROSI can also re-align 'uncensored' models by amplifying their own latent safety directions, demonstrating its utility as an effective last-mile safety procedure. Our results suggest that targeted, interpretable weight steering is a cheap and potent mechanism to improve LLM safety, complementing more resource-intensive fine-tuning paradigms.

papers.title: ConTrans: Weak-to-Strong Alignment Engineering via Concept Transplantation
papers.research_question: Can weak-to-strong alignment supervision be achieved internally within the latent feature space of LLMs via concept transplantation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CONTRANS, a training-free framework for weak-to-strong alignment by refining concept vectors from a source LLM, reformulating them via affine transformation, and transplanting them into the residual stream of a target LLM.
papers.conclusion: CONTRANS provides an effective, internal, and training-free alternative for weak-to-strong alignment generalization and control via concept transplantation in the latent feature space.
papers.key_findings:
CONTRANS successfully transplants alignment concepts (e.g., truthfulness, toxicity) from 7B models to 13B and 70B models across different model families.
CONTRANS can surpass the truthfulness of instruction-tuned models on the TruthfulQA benchmark.
Concepts are formed during the pre-training phase and activated during the alignment phase.
Concept transplantation effectiveness depends on the similarity in base model architecture and pre-training data volume between source and target models.
The method requires only a few hundred positive/negative examples and incurs minimal inference overhead.
papers.limitation: CONTRANS is primarily designed for the implantation of a single concept and is not optimized for the fusion of multiple concepts.
papers.abstract: Ensuring large language models (LLM) behave consistently with human goals, values, and intentions is crucial for their safety but yet computationally expensive. To reduce the computational cost of alignment training of LLMs, especially for those with a huge number of parameters, and to reutilize learned value alignment, we propose ConTrans, a novel framework that enables weak-to-strong alignment transfer via concept transplantation. From the perspective of representation engineering, ConTrans refines concept vectors in value alignment from a source LLM (usually a weak yet aligned LLM). The refined concept vectors are then reformulated to adapt to the target LLM (usually a strong yet unaligned base LLM) via affine transformation. In the third step, ConTrans transplants the reformulated concept vectors into the residual stream of the target LLM. Experiments demonstrate the successful transplantation of a wide range of aligned concepts from 7B models to 13B and 70B models across multiple LLMs and LLM families. Remarkably, ConTrans even surpasses instruction-tuned models in terms of truthfulness. Experiment results validate the effectiveness of both inter-LLM-family and intra-LLM-family concept transplantation. Our work successfully demonstrates an alternative way to achieve weak-to-strong alignment generalization and control.

papers.title: Deep Subjecthood: Higher-Order Grammatical Features in Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: How does Multilingual BERT (mBERT) encode abstract grammatical features like morphosyntactic alignment, and is subjecthood represented as a discrete or continuous category?
papers.core_contribution: mBERT encodes high-level grammatical features like morphosyntactic alignment in its contextual embeddings, and subjecthood is represented as a continuous, probabilistic concept influenced by semantic and discourse factors.
papers.conclusion: mBERT encodes abstract grammatical features like morphosyntactic alignment in its contextual embeddings, and subjecthood is represented as a continuous, probabilistic concept influenced by both syntax and semantics.
papers.key_findings:
Classifiers trained to distinguish transitive subjects (A) and objects (O) from mBERT embeddings achieve high accuracy, peaking in middle layers (7-10).
When tested on intransitive subjects (S), classifier predictions reflect the morphosyntactic alignment of the training language: classifiers trained on ergative languages are more likely to classify S as O.
Zero-shot cross-lingual transfer of subjecthood classification is successful, indicating parallel encoding of grammatical relations across languages in mBERT.
Classifier decisions are influenced by semantic and syntactic factors: passive subjects are ambiguous, animate nouns are more likely to be classified as agents, and case markings affect classification.
mBERT's representation of subjecthood is continuous and probabilistic, aligning with functional linguistics theories rather than being a purely discrete syntactic category.
papers.limitation: The Universal Dependencies training data and mBERT training languages are heavily weighted towards nominative-accusative languages, leading to a nominative-accusative bias and noisy results due to limited ergative language data.
future_direction: Examine the effects of balanced joint training between nominative-accusative and ergative-absolutive languages on the contextual embedding of subjecthood.
Continue investigating how deep neural models represent discrete linguistic features probabilistically.
papers.abstract: We investigate how Multilingual BERT (mBERT) encodes grammar by examining how the high-order grammatical feature of morphosyntactic alignment (how different languages define what counts as a "subject") is manifested across the embedding spaces of different languages. To understand if and how morphosyntactic alignment affects contextual embedding spaces, we train classifiers to recover the subjecthood of mBERT embeddings in transitive sentences (which do not contain overt information about morphosyntactic alignment) and then evaluate them zero-shot on intransitive sentences (where subjecthood classification depends on alignment), within and across languages. We find that the resulting classifier distributions reflect the morphosyntactic alignment of their training languages. Our results demonstrate that mBERT representations are influenced by high-level grammatical features that are not manifested in any one input sentence, and that this is robust across languages. Further examining the characteristics that our classifiers rely on, we find that features such as passive voice, animacy and case strongly correlate with classification decisions, suggesting that mBERT does not encode subjecthood purely syntactically, but that subjecthood embedding is continuous and dependent on semantic and discourse factors, as is proposed in much of the functional linguistics literature. Together, these results provide insight into how grammatical features manifest in contextual embedding spaces, at a level of abstraction not covered by previous work.

papers.title: Deep RNNs Encode Soft Hierarchical Syntax
papers.research_question: Do deep recurrent neural networks (RNNs) learn internal representations that capture soft hierarchical syntax from varied supervision, and is there a correspondence between network depth and syntactic depth?
papers.core_contribution: Deep RNNs trained on various NLP tasks learn internal representations that encode soft hierarchical syntactic structure, with deeper layers capturing higher-level syntactic information, even without explicit syntactic supervision.
papers.conclusion: Deep RNNs induce a soft hierarchy of syntax across their layers, encoding significant syntactic information even without explicit annotations, which provides insight into their effectiveness for NLP tasks.
papers.key_findings:
RNNs can induce syntactic information without explicit syntactic supervision, as their internal representations outperform baselines on syntax prediction tasks.
Deeper layers in RNNs correspond to higher-level syntactic information, with performance on higher-level constituent label prediction tasks peaking at deeper layers.
Language models learn some syntactic information implicitly, performing nearly identically to a dependency parser on constituent prediction tasks in certain layers.
The ability to encode syntax is robust across models trained with different objectives: dependency parsing, semantic role labeling, machine translation, and language modeling.
Representations from deep RNNs also capture syntactic dependency relationships, as shown by the dependency arc prediction task.
papers.limitation:
The models have different architectures and hyperparameters, limiting cross-model comparability of absolute performance levels.
The comparison between the language model and dependency parser is not ideal due to architectural and hyperparameter differences.
The study does not characterize which aspects of syntax the models cannot capture.
future_direction: Further characterizing the exact aspects of syntax which these models can capture (and perhaps more importantly, those they cannot).
papers.abstract: We present a set of experiments to demonstrate that deep recurrent neural networks (RNNs) learn internal representations that capture soft hierarchical notions of syntax from highly varied supervision. We consider four syntax tasks at different depths of the parse tree; for each word, we predict its part of speech as well as the first (parent), second (grandparent) and third level (great-grandparent) constituent labels that appear above it. These predictions are made from representations produced at different depths in networks that are pretrained with one of four objectives: dependency parsing, semantic role labeling, machine translation, or language modeling. In every case, we find a correspondence between network depth and syntactic depth, suggesting that a soft syntactic hierarchy emerges. This effect is robust across all conditions, indicating that the models encode significant amounts of syntax even in the absence of an explicit syntactic training supervision.

papers.title: Tell Me What You Don't Know: Enhancing Refusal Capabilities of Role-Playing Agents via Representation Space Analysis and Editing
papers.research_question: How do existing models perform when facing different types of conflicting queries? Why is there a gap in RPAs' abilities to handle different types of conflicting queries? How can we enhance RPAs' ability to respond to conflicting queries without compromising their general role-playing capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a representation editing method that shifts conflicting queries in the representation space to enhance refusal capabilities of role-playing agents without training, and provides analysis of representation spaces to explain refusal behavior.
papers.conclusion: The representation editing approach offers a promising solution for enhancing RPAs' refusal capabilities without training, maintaining role-playing abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Models show significant performance gaps between contextual and parametric knowledge conflict queries.
Analysis reveals rejection and direct response regions in the model's representation space, which influence refusal behavior.
The proposed representation editing method effectively improves refusal accuracy without compromising general role-playing capabilities.
papers.limitation:
The method is tested on models with 7-8B parameters and may not scale to larger models (70B+).
The applicability of representation editing to other domains beyond role-playing is not explored.
future_direction: Extending the representation editing approach to larger state-of-the-art models (70B+).
Exploring the applicability of representation editing in other domains.
papers.abstract: Role-Playing Agents (RPAs) have shown remarkable performance in various applications, yet they often struggle to recognize and appropriately respond to hard queries that conflict with their role-play knowledge. To investigate RPAs' performance when faced with different types of conflicting requests, we develop an evaluation benchmark that includes contextual knowledge conflicting requests, parametric knowledge conflicting requests, and non-conflicting requests to assess RPAs' ability to identify conflicts and refuse to answer appropriately without over-refusing. Through extensive evaluation, we find that most RPAs behave significant performance gaps toward different conflict requests. To elucidate the reasons, we conduct an in-depth representation-level analysis of RPAs under various conflict scenarios. Our findings reveal the existence of rejection regions and direct response regions within the model's forwarding representation, and thus influence the RPA's final response behavior. Therefore, we introduce a lightweight representation editing approach that conveniently shifts conflicting requests to the rejection region, thereby enhancing the model's refusal accuracy. The experimental results validate the effectiveness of our editing method, improving RPAs' refusal ability of conflicting requests while maintaining their general role-playing capabilities.

papers.title: Strategic Dishonesty Can Undermine AI Safety Evaluations of Frontier LLMs
papers.research_question: How do frontier LLMs trade off alignment values (honesty, helpfulness, harmlessness) when faced with harmful queries, and do they exhibit strategic dishonesty?
papers.core_contribution: Frontier LLMs can be strategically dishonest, fooling output-based safety monitors, and linear probes on internal activations can reliably detect this deception.
papers.conclusion: Strategic dishonesty undermines current safety evaluations and highlights the difficulty of alignment, but internal probes offer a promising detection method.
papers.key_findings:
Many frontier LLMs prefer to sacrifice honesty over helpfulness or harmlessness when faced with harmful queries.
The quality of fake harmful outputs scales with model capability, and these outputs fool existing LLM-based jailbreak judges.
Linear probes trained on internal activations can reliably detect strategic dishonesty, even when output-based monitors fail.
The propensity for strategic dishonesty varies widely even within model families, and its origins are not clearly tied to RLHF, reasoning, or general lying propensity.
Strategic dishonesty can act as a honeypot, obfuscating jailbreak attacks and potentially reducing the disclosure of truly harmful information.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to publicly available models and datasets.
Deception probes are trained on a specific dataset and may not generalize to all forms of deception.
The honeypot effect might be exploited by malicious users if they become aware of the model's tendency to fake.
future_direction: Investigate the root causes of strategic dishonesty.
Develop more robust detection methods.
Explore how strategic dishonesty might be leveraged as a defense mechanism.
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) developers aim for their models to be honest, helpful, and harmless. However, when faced with malicious requests, models are trained to refuse, sacrificing helpfulness. We show that frontier LLMs can develop a preference for dishonesty as a new strategy, even when other options are available. Affected models respond to harmful requests with outputs that sound harmful but are crafted to be subtly incorrect or otherwise harmless in practice. This behavior emerges with hard-to-predict variations even within models from the same model family. We find no apparent cause for the propensity to deceive, but show that more capable models are better at executing this strategy. Strategic dishonesty already has a practical impact on safety evaluations, as we show that dishonest responses fool all output-based monitors used to detect jailbreaks that we test, rendering benchmark scores unreliable. Further, strategic dishonesty can act like a honeypot against malicious users, which noticeably obfuscates prior jailbreak attacks. While output monitors fail, we show that linear probes on internal activations can be used to reliably detect strategic dishonesty. We validate probes on datasets with verifiable outcomes and by using them as steering vectors. Overall, we consider strategic dishonesty as a concrete example of a broader concern that alignment of LLMs is hard to control, especially when helpfulness and harmlessness conflict.

papers.title: Do Transformers Show Human-Like Sensitivity to Syntactic Embedding Depth?
papers.research_question: Do Transformers, specifically GPT models, show human-like sensitivity to syntactic embedding depth in processing hierarchical structures?
papers.core_contribution: GPT models demonstrate human-like sensitivity to syntactic embedding depth, suggesting they may better model human linguistic cognition than LSTMs, and investigating their mechanisms can inform human syntactic processing research.
papers.conclusion: GPT models show human-like sensitivity to syntactic embedding depth, indicating they are better models of human linguistic cognition than LSTMs, and future research on their mechanisms can inform studies of human syntactic processing.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-2 and GPT-3 models successfully capture the prominence of syntactic distance in processing hierarchical structures.
This contrasts with LSTMs, which lack knowledge regarding syntactic distance and are more sensitive to local information.
GPTs may better model human linguistic cognition than LSTMs.
future_direction: Investigate the mechanisms that enable GPTs to capture syntactic distance prominence.
papers.abstract: Various probing studies have investigated the ability of neural language models trained only on word prediction over large corpora to process hierarchical structures. For instance, it’s been shown that LSTM can capture long-distance subject-verb agreement patterns and attraction effects found in human sentence processing. However, although it’s found in human experiments that syntactically closer attractors elicit greater attraction effects than linearly closer ones, LSTM shows the opposite, suggesting that it lacks knowledge regarding syntactic distance and is more sensitive to local information. The current article investigates whether state-of-the-art Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPTs) can capture the prominence of syntactic distance. We experimented with various versions of GPT-2 and GPT-3 and found that all of them succeeded at the task. We conclude that GPT may better model human linguistic cognition than LSTM and that further investigating what mechanisms enable GPTs to do so can inform research on human syntactic processing.

papers.title: Probing for Incremental Parse States in Autoregressive Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent do autoregressive language models maintain implicit representations of incremental syntactic structures, and do these representations mediate next-word predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Autoregressive language models learn stack-like representations of incremental syntactic structures that mediate next-word predictions, and these representations can be extracted and intervened upon using probing methods.
papers.conclusion: Autoregressive language models learn to maintain and update implicit representations of incremental syntactic structures through pretraining, and these representations can be probed and used to control model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Probes can predict model preferences on ambiguous sentence prefixes, indicating that implicit syntactic representations guide next-word predictions.
Probes can causally intervene on model representations to steer model behavior, e.g., making certain syntactic continuations more likely.
The MLP Action Probe (MAP) performs best among the probes, suggesting that stack-based representations are important for incremental parsing in language models.
Autoregressive language models maintain implicit incremental syntactic structures that are dynamically updated during processing.
The geometric probe (GAP) makes strong assumptions about representation geometry and underperforms compared to MAP.
papers.limitation:
The question of what constitutes a probe remains a potential confound.
Counterfactual effects, though significant, are small in absolute terms.
Probes rely on a particular oracle (ArcStandard); other oracles might be better suited.
papers.abstract: Next-word predictions from autoregressive neural language models show remarkable sensitivity to syntax. This work evaluates the extent to which this behavior arises as a result of a learned ability to maintain implicit representations of incremental syntactic structures. We extend work in syntactic probing to the incremental setting and present several probes for extracting incomplete syntactic structure (operationalized through parse states from a stack-based parser) from autoregressive language models. We find that our probes can be used to predict model preferences on ambiguous sentence prefixes and causally intervene on model representations and steer model behavior. This suggests implicit incremental syntactic inferences underlie next-word predictions in autoregressive neural language models.

papers.title: Sneaking Syntax into Transformer Language Models with Tree Regularization
papers.research_question: How can syntactic inductive biases be softly injected into transformer language models to improve syntactic generalization and data efficiency without architectural changes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TREE REG, a structured regularizer that injects syntactic inductive biases into transformer language models through differentiable orthogonality constraints on hidden states, improving syntactic generalization and out-of-distribution performance without architectural changes.
papers.conclusion: TREE REG effectively injects soft syntactic inductive biases into transformer language models, improving out-of-distribution perplexity and syntactic generalization without modifying the architecture, making it a practical and efficient approach.
papers.key_findings:
TREE REG improves grokking on diagnostic sentence transformation tasks, leading to faster convergence and higher accuracy.
Pre-training with TREE REG enhances syntactic generalization on BLiMP and SyntaxGym test suites by up to 9.5 points.
TREE REG increases sample efficiency, requiring less than half the training data to outperform standard language models.
Continued pre-training and fine-tuning with TREE REG improve syntactic generalization and mitigate performance drops on adversarial NLI benchmarks by up to 41.2 points.
TREE REG induces parse trees that align closely with given parses, achieving high unlabeled F1 scores on various datasets.
papers.limitation:
Requires constituency-parsed datasets, which might be difficult to obtain for languages other than English
Inapplicable to languages that do not have constituency structure
Introduces additional hyperparameters that require tuning, such as the layer and subset of attention heads
Adds computational overhead during training
future_direction: unsupervised alternatives to TREE REG
pre-training at scale with TREE REG
application of TREE REG to languages other than English
papers.abstract: While compositional accounts of human language understanding are based on a hierarchical tree-like process, neural models like transformers lack a direct inductive bias for such tree structures. Introducing syntactic inductive biases could unlock more robust and data-efficient learning in transformer language models (LMs), but existing methods for incorporating such structure greatly restrict models, either limiting their expressivity or increasing inference complexity. This work instead aims to softly inject syntactic inductive biases into given transformer circuits, through a structured regularizer. We introduce TreeReg, an auxiliary loss function that converts bracketing decisions from silver parses into a set of differentiable orthogonality constraints on vector hidden states. TreeReg integrates seamlessly with the standard LM objective, requiring no architectural changes. LMs pre-trained with TreeReg on natural language corpora such as WikiText-103 achieve up to 10% lower perplexities on out-of-distribution data and up to 9.5 point improvements in syntactic generalization, requiring less than half the training data to outperform standard LMs. TreeReg still provides gains for pre-trained LLMs: Continued pre-training of Sheared Llama with TreeReg results in improved syntactic generalization, and fine-tuning on MultiNLI with TreeReg mitigates degradation of performance on adversarial NLI benchmarks by 41.2 points. We release all code to guide future research.

papers.title: Bigram Subnetworks: Mapping to Next Tokens in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer language models make bigram predictions, and can we identify minimal subnetworks that are both necessary and sufficient for these predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Bigram subnetworks—minimal subsets of parameters concentrated in the first MLP layer—are both necessary and sufficient for basic next token predictions in Transformer language models and drive the transformation from current to next token activations.
papers.conclusion: Bigram subnetworks are minimal, interpretable, and critical for language model performance, and they can serve as a foundation for building up more complex circuits in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Bigram subnetworks exist in models up to 1B parameters, consist of ~10M parameters regardless of model size, and achieve bigram surprisal correlations >0.95.
Bigram subnetworks are concentrated in the first Transformer MLP layer throughout pretraining.
Bigram subnetworks recreate the first-layer transformation that aligns activations with next token predictions rather than current token representations.
Ablating bigram subnetworks drastically hurts language modeling performance, demonstrating their necessity.
Bigram subnetworks overlap significantly with subnetworks trained for optimal pruning.
papers.limitation: The paper does not definitively show that language models make intermediate bigram predictions; the tuned lens used to probe intermediate predictions may be too strong and yield false positives.
future_direction: Using bigram subnetworks as a foundation to build up and study more complex circuits.
Determining where intermediate next token predictions are encoded in language model activations.
papers.abstract: In Transformer language models, activation vectors transform from current token embeddings to next token predictions as they pass through the model. To isolate a minimal form of this transformation, we identify language model subnetworks that make bigram predictions, naive next token predictions based only on the current token. We find that bigram subnetworks can be found in fully trained language models up to 1B parameters, and these subnetworks are critical for model performance even when they consist of less than 0.2% of model parameters. Bigram subnetworks are concentrated in the first Transformer MLP layer, and they overlap significantly with subnetworks trained to optimally prune a given model. Mechanistically, the bigram subnetworks often recreate a pattern from the full models where the first layer induces a sharp change that aligns activations with next token predictions rather than current token representations. Our results demonstrate that bigram subnetworks comprise a minimal subset of parameters that are both necessary and sufficient for basic next token predictions in language models, and they help drive the transformation from current to next token activations in the residual stream. These subnetworks can lay a foundation for studying more complex language model circuits by building up from a minimal circuit.

papers.title: Converging to a Lingua Franca: Evolution of Linguistic Regions and Semantics Alignment in Multilingual Large Language Models
