papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that refusal directions are universal across safety-aligned languages; a refusal vector extracted from one language can effectively modulate refusal behavior in other languages.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that refusal directions are universal across safety-aligned languages, providing insights for multilingual safety defenses.
papers.key_findings:
English-derived refusal vectors can jailbreak models across multiple languages.
Refusal vectors derived from any safety-aligned language (e.g., German, Chinese, Thai) transfer to other languages.
The universality is due to parallelism of refusal vectors across languages in the embedding space.
Models fail to separate harmful and harmless prompts in non-English languages, leading to vulnerabilities.
Adding refusal vectors can reduce compliance rates, demonstrating controllability.
papers.abstract: Refusal mechanisms in large language models (LLMs) are essential for ensuring safety. Recent research has revealed that refusal behavior can be mediated by a single direction in activation space, enabling targeted interventions to bypass refusals. While this is primarily demonstrated in an English-centric context, appropriate refusal behavior is important for any language, but poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the refusal behavior in LLMs across 14 languages using PolyRefuse, a multilingual safety dataset created by translating malicious and benign English prompts into these languages. We uncover the surprising cross-lingual universality of the refusal direction: a vector extracted from English can bypass refusals in other languages with near-perfect effectiveness, without any additional fine-tuning. Even more remarkably, refusal directions derived from any safety-aligned language transfer seamlessly to others. We attribute this transferability to the parallelism of refusal vectors across languages in the embedding space and identify the underlying mechanism behind cross-lingual jailbreaks. These findings provide actionable insights for building more robust multilingual safety defenses and pave the way for a deeper mechanistic understanding of cross-lingual vulnerabilities in LLMs.

papers.title: Language Modeling Teaches You More Syntax than Translation Does: Lessons\n Learned Through Auxiliary Task Analysis
papers.research_question: How does the choice of pretraining objective (language modeling, translation, skip-thought, autoencoding) affect the learning of syntactic and part-of-speech information in LSTM representations, and how does the amount of training data influence this?
papers.core_contribution: Bidirectional language models (BiLMs) outperform translation, skip-thought, and autoencoding objectives in inducing syntactic information useful for part-of-speech and CCG supertagging, even when trained on less data. Randomly initialized LSTMs perform well on these tasks only when auxiliary classifiers are trained on large amounts of data.
papers.conclusion: Bidirectional language models capture more useful syntactic features for transfer learning than translation encoders, and randomly initialized encoders can perform well on syntactic tasks only when auxiliary classifiers have abundant training data.
papers.key_findings:
Bidirectional language model (BiLM) representations consistently perform best on part-of-speech (POS) and CCG supertagging auxiliary tasks, even when trained on relatively small amounts of data (1 million sentences).
BiLMs trained on 1 million sentences outperform translation and skip-thought models trained on larger datasets (5 million and 63 million sentences, respectively).
Randomly initialized, untrained LSTM encoders perform nearly as well as trained models on syntactic tasks when auxiliary classifiers are trained on all available labeled data, but their performance drops sharply when classifier training data is reduced.
Trained encoders underperform randomly initialized ones on the task of predicting neighboring word identity, confirming they capture syntactic features beyond mere word identity.
Lower LSTM layers encode more local neighboring word information, while upper layers encode more distant context, suggesting depth increases the receptive field.
papers.abstract:
Recent work using auxiliary prediction task classifiers to investigate the
properties of LSTM representations has begun to shed light on why pretrained
representations, like ELMo (Peters et al., 2018) and CoVe (McCann et al.,
2017), are so beneficial for neural language understanding models. We still,
though, do not yet have a clear understanding of how the choice of pretraining
objective affects the type of linguistic information that models learn. With
this in mind, we compare four objectives---language modeling, translation,
skip-thought, and autoencoding---on their ability to induce syntactic and
part-of-speech information. We make a fair comparison between the tasks by
holding constant the quantity and genre of the training data, as well as the
LSTM architecture. We find that representations from language models
consistently perform best on our syntactic auxiliary prediction tasks, even
when trained on relatively small amounts of data. These results suggest that
language modeling may be the best data-rich pretraining task for transfer
learning applications requiring syntactic information. We also find that the
representations from randomly-initialized, frozen LSTMs perform strikingly well
on our syntactic auxiliary tasks, but this effect disappears when the amount of
training data for the auxiliary tasks is reduced.

papers.title: Loop as a Bridge: Can Looped Transformers Truly Link Representation Space and Natural Language Outputs?
papers.research_question: Can Looped Transformers align linguistic verification output with representations? Can LTs enhance their introspective awareness on representations?
papers.core_contribution: Increasing loop iterations in Looped Transformers narrows the gap between self-verification and representation readout, but partly due to degradation of representation quality. Moreover, LTs only show introspective awareness in the final loop, not continuously across loops.
papers.conclusion: Current Looped Transformers do not yet achieve continuous introspection across loops, and the observed gap narrowing is partly driven by a degradation in representation quality.
papers.key_findings:
The accuracy of textual self-verification improves with more loop iterations.
The performance of representation-based linear probes declines with more loop iterations.
The gap between representation readout and self-verification narrows with more loops, but partly because of the decline in representation readout.
LTs are only aware of injected concepts when the injection occurs in the final loop, not in earlier loops.
papers.limitation: The experiments are a preliminary exploration conducted on a single specific implementation of LTs (Ouro), so the observed limitations should not be interpreted as intrinsic flaws of the general LTs paradigm.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit a gap between their internal knowledge and their explicit linguistic outputs. In this report, we empirically investigate whether Looped Transformers (LTs)--architectures that increase computational depth by iterating shared layers--can bridge this gap by utilizing their iterative nature as a form of introspection. Our experiments reveal that while increasing loop iterations narrows the gap, it is partly driven by a degradation of their internal knowledge carried by representations. Moreover, another empirical analysis suggests that current LTs' ability to perceive representations does not improve across loops; it is only present in the final loop. These results suggest that while LTs offer a promising direction for scaling computational depth, they have yet to achieve the introspection required to truly link representation space and natural language.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Understanding of Alignment Algorithms: A Case Study on DPO and Toxicity
papers.research_question: How does the alignment algorithm DPO reduce toxicity in language models, and what are the mechanisms by which it does so?
papers.core_contribution: DPO reduces toxicity not by removing toxic capabilities but by learning an offset in the residual stream to bypass toxic regions, and this alignment can be easily undone.
papers.conclusion: Alignment algorithms like DPO work by bypassing undesirable capabilities rather than removing them, which explains the vulnerability to jailbreaks.
papers.key_findings:
Toxicity is represented by specific value vectors in MLP blocks of GPT2-medium.
DPO does not remove these toxic vectors; instead, it learns a distributed offset in the residual stream to avoid activating them.
The offset is achieved through minimal weight changes across many value vectors in earlier layers.
Alignment can be undone by scaling toxic key vectors, reactivating toxic behavior.
The findings provide a mechanistic explanation for why aligned models can be jailbroken.
future_direction: Designing robust alignment algorithms that eliminate undesirable regions instead of bypassing them.
Updating only specific weights (e.g., toxic vectors) or only bias terms during alignment.
Adding 'suppression heads' or updating late layers to suppress undesirable behavior.
Characterizing 'jailbreak-ability' without relying on test samples.
Studying the role of KL-divergence regularization in distributed vs. localized changes.
papers.abstract: While alignment algorithms are now commonly used to tune pre-trained language models towards a user's preferences, we lack explanations for the underlying mechanisms in which models become ``aligned'', thus making it difficult to explain phenomena like jailbreaks. In this work we study a popular algorithm, direct preference optimization (DPO), and the mechanisms by which it reduces toxicity. Namely, we first study how toxicity is represented and elicited in a pre-trained language model, GPT2-medium. We then apply DPO with a carefully crafted pairwise dataset to reduce toxicity. We examine how the resulting model averts toxic outputs, and find that capabilities learned from pre-training are not removed, but rather bypassed. We use this insight to demonstrate a simple method to un-align the model, reverting it back to its toxic behavior.

papers.title: Why Representation Engineering Works: A Theoretical and Empirical Study in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can Representation Engineering (RepE) be extended to Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and what theoretical principles explain the stability of neural activity across layers in this context?
papers.core_contribution: This work extends Representation Engineering (RepE) to Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and provides a theoretical framework explaining that the stability of neural activity across layers is governed by the principal eigenvector of the attention matrix, while a shrinking spectral gap allows subdominant eigenvectors to differentiate between concepts.
papers.conclusion: By integrating theoretical analysis with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new avenues for improving AI robustness, interpretability, and transparency in multimodal settings.
papers.key_findings:
The principal eigenvector of the self-attention matrix serves as a stable 'backbone' for neural activity propagation across layers.
The spectral gap (difference between the largest and second-largest eigenvalues) shrinks in deeper layers, enabling subdominant eigenvectors to capture subtle distinctions between concepts like honesty and fairness.
Representation Engineering (RepE) is effective in VLMs for extracting and analyzing high-level conceptual representations, such as honesty and fairness, from internal activations.
Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) scans reveal distinct activation patterns across layers for different high-level concepts, demonstrating how representations evolve through the network.
future_direction: Extend RepE to broader multimodal settings, exploring its potential for bias mitigation, honest detection, and countless concept applications.
papers.abstract: Representation Engineering (RepE) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing AI transparency by focusing on high-level representations rather than individual neurons or circuits. It has proven effective in improving interpretability and control, showing that representations can emerge, propagate, and shape final model outputs in large language models (LLMs). However, in Vision-Language Models (VLMs), visual input can override factual linguistic knowledge, leading to hallucinated responses that contradict reality. To address this challenge, we make the first attempt to extend RepE to VLMs, analyzing how multimodal representations are preserved and transformed. Building on our findings and drawing inspiration from successful RepE applications, we develop a theoretical framework that explains the stability of neural activity across layers using the principal eigenvector, uncovering the underlying mechanism of RepE. We empirically validate these instrinsic properties, demonstrating their broad applicability and significance. By bridging theoretical insights with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new directions for improving AI robustness, fairness, and transparency.

papers.title: What Language(s) Does Aya-23 Think In? How Multilinguality Affects Internal Language Representations
papers.research_question: How does balanced multilingual training affect internal language processing in LLMs, specifically in terms of language activation, neuron sharing, and layer-wise distribution of language-specific neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Balanced multilingual training leads to distinct internal language processing, with language-specific neurons concentrated in final layers and activation of typologically related languages during translation, unlike English-centric models.
papers.conclusion: Balanced multilingual training fundamentally alters how decoder-only LLMs process language internally, leading to language-specific neurons concentrated in final layers and activation of multiple languages during translation.
papers.key_findings:
Aya-23 activates typologically related language representations during translation, unlike English-centric models that rely on a single pivot language.
Code-mixed neuron activation patterns vary with mixing rates and are shaped more by the base language than the mixed-in one.
Aya-23’s language-specific neurons for code-mixed inputs concentrate in final layers, diverging from prior findings on decoder-only models.
Neuron overlap analysis shows that script similarity and typological relations impact processing across model types.
French-based code-mixed inputs show higher neuron clustering than Chinese-based inputs across all models, regardless of training data composition.
papers.limitation:
Token overlap between languages in the logit lens experiments may affect analysis of language-specific activation patterns.
Neuron specialization analysis using binary activations results in information loss that may obscure subtle activation patterns.
Code-mixed dataset created via rule-based word-to-word translation produces unnatural sentences that may not represent authentic code-switching.
Analysis is limited to three models and may not generalize to other architectures or sizes.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at multilingual tasks, yet their internal language processing remains poorly understood. We analyze how Aya-23-8B, a decoder-only LLM trained on balanced multilingual data, handles code-mixed, cloze, and translation tasks compared to predominantly monolingual models like Llama 3 and Chinese-LLaMA-2. Using logit lens and neuron specialization analyses, we find: (1) Aya-23 activates typologically related language representations during translation, unlike English-centric models that rely on a single pivot language; (2) code-mixed neuron activation patterns vary with mixing rates and are shaped more by the base language than the mixed-in one; and (3) Aya-23's languagespecific neurons for code-mixed inputs concentrate in final layers, diverging from prior findings on decoder-only models. Neuron overlap analysis further shows that script similarity and typological relations impact processing across model types. These findings reveal how multilingual training shapes LLM internals and inform future cross-lingual transfer research.

papers.title: Intrinsic Self-correction for Enhanced Morality: An Analysis of Internal Mechanisms and the Superficial Hypothesis
papers.research_question: The paper investigates three research questions: (1) In what scenarios does moral self-correction work? (2) What are the internal mechanisms of LLMs influenced by self-correction instructions? (3) Is intrinsic moral self-correction actually superficial?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that intrinsic moral self-correction in LLMs is superficial, as it only provides a shortcut to moral outputs without significantly reducing immorality in internal hidden states.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that intrinsic moral self-correction is superficial, relying on shortcuts rather than fundamentally reducing immorality in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Self-correction works best when the correct answer is already top-ranked.
Morality levels in intermediate hidden states are strong indicators of instruction effectiveness.
Self-correction reduces immorality in attention heads but increases it in feed-forward layers for QA tasks.
The slight difference in hidden states with and without self-correction supports the superficial hypothesis.
Internal hidden states can be used to predict the effectiveness of self-correction instructions.
papers.limitation:
The exact underlying reason for the superficial phenomenon is not uncovered.
Defining superficial self-correction is challenging.
future_direction: Automating methods for optimizing instruction development for self-correction.
Exploring fine-tuning to enhance LLMs' self-correction capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are capable of producing content that perpetuates stereotypes, discrimination, and toxicity. The recently proposed moral self-correction is a computationally efficient method for reducing harmful content in the responses of LLMs. However, the process of how injecting self-correction instructions can modify the behavior of LLMs remains under-explored. In this paper, we explore the effectiveness of moral self-correction by answering three research questions: (1) In what scenarios does moral self-correction work? (2) What are the internal mechanisms of LLMs, e.g., hidden states, that are influenced by moral self-correction instructions? (3) Is intrinsic moral self-correction actually superficial in terms of reduced immorality in hidden states? We argue that self-correction can help LLMs find a shortcut to more morally correct output, rather than truly reducing the immorality stored in hidden states. Through empirical investigation with tasks of language generation and multi-choice question answering, we conclude:(i) LLMs exhibit good performance across both tasks, and self-correction instructions are particularly beneficial when the correct answer is already top-ranked; (ii) The morality levels in intermediate hidden states are strong indicators as to whether one instruction would be more effective than another; (iii) Based on our analysis of intermediate hidden states and task case studies of self-correction behaviors, we are first to propose the hypothesis that intrinsic moral self-correction is in fact superficial.

papers.title: Accurate Word Alignment Induction from Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: Do attention weights in Transformer models capture accurate word alignments, and how can word alignments be better induced from neural machine translation models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that Transformer attention weights can capture accurate word alignments if the correct decoding step and layer are chosen, and introduces two novel methods (SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET) that induce alignments at the step when the target token is the decoder input, significantly improving alignment accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET effectively induce word alignments from Transformer models, with SHIFT-AET achieving state-of-the-art performance without compromising translation quality.
papers.key_findings:
SHIFT-ATT, a pure interpretation method, reduces AER by 7.0-10.2 points over the NAIVE-ATT baseline and 5.5-7.9 points over FAST-ALIGN on three datasets.
SHIFT-AET, which adds and trains an alignment module supervised by SHIFT-ATT alignments, outperforms the statistical aligner GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.
A proposed layer selection criterion, based on agreement between source-to-target and target-to-source model alignments, effectively identifies the best layer for alignment induction.
Both SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET improve performance on the downstream task of dictionary-guided decoding compared to the NAIVE-ATT baseline.
Probing experiments show decoder hidden states at lower layers are more relevant to the input token than the output token, validating the shift in alignment step.
future_direction: Extend the study to more downstream tasks and systems.
papers.abstract: Despite its original goal to jointly learn to align and translate, prior researches suggest that Transformer captures poor word alignments through its attention mechanism. In this paper, we show that attention weights DO capture accurate word alignments and propose two novel word alignment induction methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET. The main idea is to induce alignments at the step when the to-be-aligned target token is the decoder input rather than the decoder output as in previous work. SHIFT-ATT is an interpretation method that induces alignments from the attention weights of Transformer and does not require parameter update or architecture change. SHIFT-AET extracts alignments from an additional alignment module which is tightly integrated into Transformer and trained in isolation with supervision from symmetrized SHIFT-ATT alignments. Experiments on three publicly available datasets demonstrate that both methods perform better than their corresponding neural baselines and SHIFT-AET significantly outperforms GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.

papers.title: MM-RLHF: The Next Step Forward in Multimodal LLM Alignment
papers.research_question: Is alignment with human preferences only capable of enhancing MLLMs in a limited set of tasks? The paper demonstrates that a well-designed alignment pipeline can comprehensively enhance MLLMs across multiple dimensions.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MM-RLHF, a large-scale human-annotated multimodal preference dataset, and proposes a critique-based reward model and dynamic reward scaling method for DPO, leading to significant improvements in MLLM alignment across multiple dimensions.
papers.conclusion: The MM-RLHF dataset and alignment approach holistically improve MLLM performance across diverse dimensions, demonstrating the value of comprehensive alignment strategies.
papers.key_findings:
The MM-RLHF dataset offers superior size, diversity, annotation granularity, and quality over existing resources.
The proposed Critique-Based Reward Model generates critiques before scoring, providing enhanced interpretability and more informative feedback.
Dynamic Reward Scaling adjusts loss weights based on reward margins, optimizing the use of high-quality comparison pairs and improving training efficiency.
Alignment with human preferences using MM-RLHF and the proposed methods comprehensively enhances MLLM performance across visual perception, reasoning, dialogue, and safety.
Fine-tuning LLaVA-OV-7B with MM-RLHF and the alignment algorithm leads to a 19.5% increase in conversational abilities and a 60% improvement in safety.
papers.limitation: The cost of human annotation poses scalability challenges.
future_direction: Leveraging annotation granularity with advanced optimization techniques
Integrating high-resolution data to address limitations in specific benchmarks
Scaling the dataset efficiently using semi-automated strategies
papers.abstract: Despite notable advancements in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), most state-of-the-art models have not undergone thorough alignment with human preferences. This gap exists because current alignment research has primarily achieved progress in specific areas (e.g., hallucination reduction), while the broader question of whether aligning models with human preferences can systematically enhance MLLM capability remains largely unexplored. To this end, we introduce MM-RLHF, a dataset containing $\mathbf{120k}$ fine-grained, human-annotated preference comparison pairs. This dataset represents a substantial advancement over existing resources, offering superior size, diversity, annotation granularity, and quality. Leveraging this dataset, we propose several key innovations to improve both the quality of reward models and the efficiency of alignment algorithms. Notably, we introduce a Critique-Based Reward Model, which generates critiques of model outputs before assigning scores, offering enhanced interpretability and more informative feedback compared to traditional scalar reward mechanisms. Additionally, we propose Dynamic Reward Scaling, a method that adjusts the loss weight of each sample according to the reward signal, thereby optimizing the use of high-quality comparison pairs. Our approach is rigorously evaluated across $\mathbf{10}$ distinct dimensions and $\mathbf{27}$ benchmarks, with results demonstrating significant and consistent improvements in model performance. Specifically, fine-tuning LLaVA-ov-7B with MM-RLHF and our alignment algorithm leads to a $\mathbf{19.5}$% increase in conversational abilities and a $\mathbf{60}$% improvement in safety. We have open-sourced the preference dataset, reward model, training and evaluation code, as well as reward modeling and safety benchmarks. For more details, please visit our project page: https://mm-rlhf.github.io.

papers.title: Mind the Inconspicuous: Revealing the Hidden Weakness in Aligned LLMs' Refusal Boundaries
papers.research_question: How can appending end-of-sequence (eos) tokens bypass the learned refusal boundary in aligned LLMs, and what is the underlying mechanism of 'context segmentation'?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals the 'context segmentation' phenomenon where appending eos tokens shifts prompts towards the refusal boundary in hidden space, and introduces BOOST, a simple method to enhance jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens.
papers.conclusion: The work highlights a critical blind spot in LLM alignment and content filtering, urging the community to address the security implications of control tokens and develop more robust refusal boundaries.
papers.key_findings:
Appending multiple eos tokens causes both harmful and benign prompts to shift toward the learned refusal boundary in the hidden representation space, a phenomenon termed 'context segmentation'.
BOOST significantly increases the attack success rate (ASR) of existing jailbreak techniques across a wide range of open-source LLMs.
Commercial LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Qwen) do not filter eos tokens, making them vulnerable to BOOST-enhanced attacks.
eos tokens have low attention values, minimizing distraction from the harmful content and preserving jailbreak effectiveness.
BOOST can be made more robust to simple filtering through eos token obfuscation and dynamic positioning strategies.
future_direction: Implement input-filtering defenses for control tokens like eos.
Develop more robust and generalizable refusal boundaries to defend against context segmentation attacks.
Investigate the security impact of all control tokens and develop comprehensive defense strategies.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have led to impressive alignment where models learn to distinguish harmful from harmless queries through supervised finetuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). In this paper, we reveal a subtle yet impactful weakness in these aligned models. We find that simply appending multiple end of sequence (eos) tokens can cause a phenomenon we call context segmentation, which effectively shifts both harmful and benign inputs closer to the refusal boundary in the hidden space. Building on this observation, we propose a straightforward method to BOOST jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens. Our systematic evaluation shows that this strategy significantly increases the attack success rate across 8 representative jailbreak techniques and 16 open-source LLMs, ranging from 2B to 72B parameters. Moreover, we develop a novel probing mechanism for commercial APIs and discover that major providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Qwen do not filter eos tokens, making them similarly vulnerable. These findings highlight a hidden yet critical blind spot in existing alignment and content filtering approaches. We call for heightened attention to eos tokens' unintended influence on model behaviors, particularly in production systems. Our work not only calls for an input-filtering based defense, but also points to new defenses that make refusal boundaries more robust and generalizable, as well as fundamental alignment techniques that can defend against context segmentation attacks.

papers.title: Sparse Latents Steer Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders uncover interpretable latents that govern RAG behaviors (context vs. memory prioritization and response generation vs. query rejection) and enable precise control over these behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that sparse autoencoders can uncover interpretable latents that govern RAG behaviors, and that intervening on these latents allows precise control over context-following and refusal decisions without architectural modifications.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders provide a powerful method for understanding and controlling RAG behaviors through the discovery and intervention of sparse, interpretable latents.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can uncover interpretable latents that correlate with two core RAG decisions: context versus memory prioritization and response generation versus query rejection.
Intervening on these latents enables precise control over RAG behavior, with high success rates in steering the model towards desired behaviors.
The identified latents maintain effectiveness across model variants (base and instruction-tuned) and scaled context lengths (1 to 5 documents).
Latents from early layers generalize better to prompt changes, suggesting they encode fundamental decision-making processes, while later layers are more task/token specific.
Mechanistic analysis reveals that latent interventions modify attention patterns of retrieval heads, redistributing focus between documents and refusal tokens.
papers.abstract: Chunlei Xin, Shuheng Zhou, Huijia Zhu, Weiqiang Wang, Xuanang Chen, Xinyan Guan, Yaojie Lu, Hongyu Lin, Xianpei Han, Le Sun. Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Multilingual Chart-based Constituency Parse Extraction from Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we extract constituency parses from pre-trained language models without training, and can this be done effectively across multiple languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a chart-based method and a top-K ensemble technique for extracting constituency parses from pre-trained language models without training, and demonstrates that multilingual PLMs enable effective parsing across multiple languages.
papers.conclusion: The chart-based method and top-K ensemble improve constituency parse extraction from PLMs, and multilingual PLMs enable effective parsing across multiple languages, providing a foundation for unsupervised parsing for under-represented languages and probing multilingual PLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Chart-based methods (CP and CC) outperform the top-down method (TD) in most cases.
The top-K ensemble technique significantly improves parsing performance.
Multilingual PLMs can be used for constituency parse extraction across multiple languages, achieving performance comparable or superior to unsupervised PCFGs.
The method is robust to cross-lingual transfer, with minimal performance loss when using attention heads selected for English on other languages.
There exist universal attention heads that are sensitive to syntactic information across languages.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on a validation set for hyperparameter selection (attention head selection), so it is not entirely unsupervised.
The performance, while competitive, still falls short of standard supervised parsers.
The chart parsing algorithm has O(n^3) time complexity, which is less efficient than top-down parsing.
future_direction: Developing a method that is free from validation set annotations.
Designing an ensemble method that gathers information from heterogeneous PLMs.
Thorough analysis of the effect of parsing strategies across languages.
papers.abstract: As it has been unveiled that pre-trained language models (PLMs) are to some extent capable of recognizing syntactic concepts in natural language, much effort has been made to develop a method for extracting complete (binary) parses from PLMs without training separate parsers. We improve upon this paradigm by proposing a novel chart-based method and an effective top-K ensemble technique. Moreover, we demonstrate that we can broaden the scope of application of the approach into multilingual settings. Specifically, we show that by applying our method on multilingual PLMs, it becomes possible to induce non-trivial parses for sentences from nine languages in an integrated and language-agnostic manner, attaining performance superior or comparable to that of unsupervised PCFGs. We also verify that our approach is robust to cross-lingual transfer. Finally, we provide analyses on the inner workings of our method. For instance, we discover universal attention heads which are consistently sensitive to syntactic information irrespective of the input language.

papers.title: BlueGlass: A Framework for Composite AI Safety
papers.research_question: How can we build a unified framework to integrate and compose diverse AI safety tools for comprehensive safety analysis?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces BlueGlass, a framework for composite AI safety that enables integration of diverse safety tools, and demonstrates its utility with three safety analyses on vision-language models for object detection.
papers.conclusion: The BlueGlass framework facilitates composite AI safety research, and the case studies provide empirical and mechanistic insights into VLM capabilities and limitations, informing safety-aware deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Distributional evaluation reveals performance trade-offs and potential failure modes of VLMs across diverse datasets.
Approximation probes reveal a phase transition in decoder layers of VLMs and vision-only detectors, indicating shared hierarchical feature learning.
Sparse autoencoders identify interpretable concepts and spurious correlations in VLMs, such as a hand unit co-activating with objects like knives and cell phones.
VLMs show decent zero-shot performance but lag behind fine-tuned models on domain-specific tasks.
The need for geometric priors in VLMs for precise object localization is highlighted.
papers.abstract: As AI systems become increasingly capable and ubiquitous, ensuring the safety of these systems is critical. However, existing safety tools often target different aspects of model safety and cannot provide full assurance in isolation, highlighting a need for integrated and composite methodologies. This paper introduces BlueGlass, a framework designed to facilitate composite AI safety workflows by providing a unified infrastructure enabling the integration and composition of diverse safety tools that operate across model internals and outputs. Furthermore, to demonstrate the utility of this framework, we present three safety-oriented analyses on vision-language models for the task of object detection: (1) distributional evaluation, revealing performance trade-offs and potential failure modes across distributions; (2) probe-based analysis of layer dynamics highlighting shared hierarchical learning via phase transition; and (3) sparse autoencoders identifying interpretable concepts. More broadly, this work contributes foundational infrastructure and findings for building more robust and reliable AI systems.

papers.title: Investigating Semantic Subspaces of Transformer Sentence Embeddings through Linear Structural Probing
papers.research_question: What kinds of semantic information are encoded in sentence-level representations of different Transformer-based language models (encoder-only, decoder-only, encoder-decoder) and how does this information vary across layers and model sizes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified methodology (semantic structural probing) for analyzing sentence-level representations across different Transformer architectures and model sizes, finding that model families differ in performance and layer dynamics but results are largely model-size invariant.
papers.conclusion: Sentence representations from pre-trained Transformer models are task-dependent, and different architectures exhibit distinct layer-wise patterns of semantic information, which can be analyzed using the proposed structural probing methodology.
papers.key_findings:
Model families (encoder-only, decoder-only, encoder-decoder) differ substantially in their performance and layer dynamics on semantic tasks, but the results are largely invariant to model size.
No single architecture is best for representation learning; the informativeness of sentence representations depends on the specific task.
Different models exhibit distinct patterns of information processing across layers (e.g., ELECTRA shows degradation in upper layers, causal models like Llama and OPT show cyclic performance patterns).
For Semantic Textual Similarity (STS), RoBERTa provides the best representations, outperforming larger causal models. For Natural Language Inference (NLI), causal models can provide more informative embeddings even at smaller sizes.
The proposed structural probing method provides a lower-bound estimate of the semantic information contained in vanilla pre-trained sentence embeddings.
papers.limitation:
Results depend on a series of design choices (sentence embedding extraction, task reformulation, loss function, etc.).
The notion of semantics as encoded by language models is not well-defined, and STS and NLI are only approximations.
Small validation and test splits for ANLI in the triplet setting lead to noticeable instability in model performance.
future_direction: Applying the proposed methodology to other tasks such as political scaling or emotion-intensity estimation.
Disentangling lexical and semantic effects in the representations to better understand model interpretability.
papers.abstract: The question of what kinds of linguistic information are encoded in different layers of Transformer-based language models is of considerable interest for the NLP community. Existing work, however, has overwhelmingly focused on word-level representations and encoder-only language models with the masked-token training objective. In this paper, we present experiments with semantic structural probing, a method for studying sentence-level representations via finding a subspace of the embedding space that provides suitable task-specific pairwise distances between data-points. We apply our method to language models from different families (encoder-only, decoder-only, encoder-decoder) and of different sizes in the context of two tasks, semantic textual similarity and natural-language inference. We find that model families differ substantially in their performance and layer dynamics, but that the results are largely model-size invariant.

papers.title: Middle-Layer Representation Alignment for Cross-Lingual Transfer in Fine-Tuned LLMs
papers.research_question: How can cross-lingual transfer in fine-tuned LLMs be improved by explicitly aligning internal representations, and which layers are most effective for this alignment?
papers.core_contribution: Aligning middle-layer representations during task-specific fine-tuning improves cross-lingual transfer, especially to lower-resource languages, and this improvement generalizes to languages unseen during alignment.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a simple yet effective approach for enhancing cross-lingual transfer in LLMs through middle-layer representation alignment during fine-tuning, offering practical recommendations such as aligning a few weakly-performing languages and using minimal parallel data.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of LLMs exhibit the strongest potential for cross-lingual semantic alignment, with a positive correlation between base model alignment and downstream transfer performance.
Explicitly aligning middle-layer representations during fine-tuning improves cross-lingual transfer across tasks (slot filling, machine translation) while generally preserving supervised task performance.
The benefits of alignment extend to languages not included in the alignment training data, suggesting a general enhancement of cross-lingual capabilities.
Alignment is robust to the choice of alignment languages and domains, and separately trained alignment modules can be merged with task-specific modules post-hoc.
Task-specific fine-tuning alone preserves but does not enhance the inherent cross-lingual semantic alignment present in the base LLM.
papers.limitation:
Smaller gains on languages with non-Latin scripts, likely due to suboptimal tokenization impacting the quality of mean-pooled representations.
Doubles the computational cost during training compared to standard fine-tuning due to alternating optimization between task and alignment objectives.
Can lead to a trade-off between improved transfer and supervised performance in specific scenarios, such as structured text generation or with models having weak initial cross-lingual alignment.
papers.abstract: While large language models demonstrate remarkable capabilities at task-specific applications through fine-tuning, extending these benefits across diverse languages is essential for broad accessibility.However, effective crosslingual transfer is hindered by LLM performance gaps across languages and the scarcity of fine-tuning data in many languages.Through analysis of LLM internal representations from over 1,000+ language pairs, we discover that middle layers exhibit the strongest potential for cross-lingual alignment.Building on this finding, we propose a middle-layer alignment objective integrated into task-specific training.Our experiments on slot filling, machine translation, and structured text generation show consistent improvements in cross-lingual transfer, especially to lower-resource languages.The method is robust to the choice of alignment languages and generalizes to languages unseen during alignment.Furthermore, we show that separately trained alignment modules can be merged with existing task-specific modules, improving cross-lingual capabilities without full re-training.Our code is publicly available 1 .0 4 8 12 16 20 24 28 32 Layer ID 0 50 100 Avg.retrieval accuracy (%) Llama 3 0 4 8 12 16 20 24 28 Layer ID Qwen 2.5 Overall Low-res.(a) Cross-lingual semantic alignment (measured by average retrieval accuracy over 35 languages and 1190 language directions) varies by layer, with the middle layer showing the highest score.Lower-resource languages are poorly aligned.

papers.title: The Semantic Hub Hypothesis: Language Models Share Semantic Representations Across Languages and Modalities
papers.research_question: To what extent do language models learn and use a shared semantic representation space across different languages and modalities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the semantic hub hypothesis, which posits that language models learn a shared representation space across languages and modalities, and provides evidence through representation similarity and intervention experiments.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models learn a shared semantic representation space (the semantic hub) that is anchored by the dominant language and is causally involved in processing across languages and modalities.
papers.key_findings:
Model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in intermediate layers.
The shared representation space is scaffolded by the model's dominant language (e.g., English) and can be interpreted via the logit lens.
This phenomenon extends to other data types: arithmetic expressions, code, images, and audio.
Interventions in the shared space using the dominant language affect model outputs in other data types, indicating causal usage.
The shared space is not just a byproduct but actively used during processing.
papers.limitation:
Chameleon-7B cannot answer more sophisticated reasoning questions about images, such as asking for a country flag or spatial relationships, even without interventions.
The logit lens analysis for audio is a lower bound because many words in labels (e.g., prepositions) are unlikely to be represented in the audio hidden states.
future_direction: Future work aimed at better controlling models using insights from the semantic hub hypothesis.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can process inputs across diverse languages and modalities. We hypothesize that models acquire this capability through learning a shared representation space across heterogeneous data types (e.g., different languages and modalities), which places semantically similar inputs near one another, even if they are from different modalities/languages. We term this the semantic hub hypothesis, following the hub-and-spoke model from neuroscience (Patterson et al., 2007) which posits that semantic knowledge in the human brain is organized through a transmodal semantic "hub" which integrates information from various modality-specific "spokes" regions. We first show that model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in the intermediate layers, and that this space can be interpreted using the model's dominant pretraining language via the logit lens. This tendency extends to other data types, including arithmetic expressions, code, and visual/audio inputs. Interventions in the shared representation space in one data type also predictably affect model outputs in other data types, suggesting that this shared representations space is not simply a vestigial byproduct of large-scale training on broad data, but something that is actively utilized by the model during input processing.

papers.title: Probing BERT on Syntactic Representation Paradigms: Dependency vs Constituency Trees
papers.research_question: Whether different Syntactic Representation Paradigms (dependency vs constituency) have an impact on the performance of Neural Language Models (specifically BERT) when probing for syntactic information.
papers.core_contribution: The paper creates a new multilingual resource of aligned dependency and constituency treebanks and finds that BERT's performance on probing tasks is minimally but consistently affected by the syntactic representation paradigm, with the best-fitting paradigm varying across languages and tasks.
papers.conclusion: The choice of syntactic representation paradigm (dependency vs constituency) has a small but consistent impact on the probing results, suggesting that the model is slightly affected by the way syntactic information is represented, with the best-fitting paradigm varying between languages and probing tasks.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's performance on probing tasks shows small but consistent differences between dependency and constituency tree representations.
The preference for one syntactic representation paradigm over the other varies across languages and is influenced by sentence length.
The impact of the syntactic representation paradigm is more pronounced for specific linguistic phenomena and for very short or very long sentences.
The study provides evidence that the choice of linguistic formalism can affect probing results, even for syntactic tasks.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to 10 languages, which may not be representative of all linguistic typologies.
The treebanks used are not perfectly parallel, and conversion processes may introduce noise or inconsistencies.
The probing tasks are limited to a set of structural properties and do not cover all syntactic phenomena.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to a larger set of languages and syntactic phenomena.
Investigate the impact of syntactic representation paradigms on other neural language models.
Explore the use of more sophisticated probing models and control tasks.
papers.abstract: Abstract On the quest for interpreting deep Neural Language Models (NLMs), linguistically annotated probing sets are essential tools for investigating models' linguistic abilities. Such a line of research is currently dominated by dependency-based syntactic annotation formalisms, and particularly by Universal Dependencies treebanks. In this work, we test whether different Syntactic Representation Paradigms (SRP) have an impact on the performance of NLMs. To this aim, we set up a multilingual study where we compare the scores obtained by BERT on a set of probing tasks performed on 10 treebanks annotated according to two paradigms, i.e. the dependency and the constituency one, which diverges on fundamental annotation principles. Results suggest that BERT performance is minimally but consistently affected by SRPs and that such impact mostly concerns specific linguistic phenomena.

papers.title: How to Make LLMs Forget: On Reversing In-Context Knowledge Edits
papers.research_question: How can in-context knowledge edits (IKE) in LLMs be detected and reversed to mitigate potential malicious use?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the novel task of reversing in-context knowledge edits (IKE) and demonstrates that specially tuned continuous reversal tokens can recover the original, unedited model outputs with over 80% accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Detecting and reversing IKE-edits is feasible; continuous reversal tokens offer a promising method for mitigating malicious edits and improving LLM security and transparency.
papers.key_findings:
IKE-edits can be detected with high accuracy (F1 > 80%) using only the top-10 output probabilities of the next token, even in a black-box setting.
Continuous reversal tokens can reverse over 80% of IKE-edits across multiple LLMs (GPT2-XL, GPT-J, LLAMA3.1 8B), with minimal impact on unedited prompts.
Discrete reversal tokens are less effective and more variable in performance compared to continuous tokens.
The <BOS> (beginning of sentence) token is found to be an effective discrete reversal token in GPT models, helping the model ignore prior editing context.
Analysis shows IKE causes the model to become certain about its edited output earlier in the layers, and adding reversal tokens (like <BOS>) restores the normal refinement process until the final layer.
papers.limitation: Reversal tokens, especially discrete ones, can affect the outputs of normal, unedited prompts (side-effects).
future_direction: Developing more robust methods to minimize side-effects on unedited prompts.
Exploring generalization to other datasets and models.
papers.abstract: In-context knowledge editing (IKE) enables efficient modification of large language model (LLM) outputs without parameter changes and at zero-cost. However, it can be misused to manipulate responses opaquely, e.g., insert misinformation or offensive content. Such malicious interventions could be incorporated into high-level wrapped APIs where the final input prompt is not shown to end-users. To address this issue, we investigate the detection and reversal of IKE-edits. First, we demonstrate that IKE-edits can be detected with high accuracy (F1 > 80\%) using only the top-10 output probabilities of the next token, even in a black-box setting, e.g. proprietary LLMs with limited output information. Further, we introduce the novel task of reversing IKE-edits using specially tuned reversal tokens. We explore using both continuous and discrete reversal tokens, achieving over 80\% accuracy in recovering original, unedited outputs across multiple LLMs. Our continuous reversal tokens prove particularly effective, with minimal impact on unedited prompts. Through analysis of output distributions, attention patterns, and token rankings, we provide insights into IKE's effects on LLMs and how reversal tokens mitigate them. This work represents a significant step towards enhancing LLM resilience against potential misuse of in-context editing, improving their transparency and trustworthiness.

papers.title: Interpretable Safety Alignment via SAE-Constructed Low-Rank Subspace Adaptation
papers.research_question: Why does Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) consistently underperform full fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on safety benchmarks for large language models, and how can this gap be addressed?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SAILS, a method that uses Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to disentangle representations, constructs an interpretable safety subspace from SAE decoder directions, and initializes LoRA adapters with this subspace to achieve parameter-efficient safety alignment with interpretability.
papers.conclusion: SAILS bridges the gap between parameter-efficient fine-tuning and compute-intensive RLHF by leveraging Sparse Autoencoders to construct interpretable safety subspaces for LoRA initialization, achieving both effective and transparent safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
SAILS achieves up to 99.6% safety rate on Gemma-2-9B, exceeding full fine-tuning by 7.4 points and matching RLHF-based models, while updating only 0.19% of parameters.
Theoretical analysis proves SAE-based subspace identification achieves arbitrarily small recovery error under monosemanticity assumptions, while direct identification suffers an irreducible error floor.
Identifies semantic entanglement (polysemanticity) as a key factor limiting LoRA's effectiveness for safety alignment.
SAILS provides built-in interpretability through grounding in SAE features, enabling causal validation of safety-relevant directions.
Empirical results show SAILS outperforms standard LoRA, DoRA, and full fine-tuning across in-distribution safety, out-of-distribution generalization, and adversarial robustness.
papers.limitation:
Dependence on pre-trained Sparse Autoencoders, whose training demands substantial computational resources.
Reliance on auto-generated feature explanations (e.g., from Neuronpedia) can create an 'illusion of interpretability' with high recall but poor precision.
The safety subspace undergoes perturbation during training, limiting strict interpretability of final adapted directions.
future_direction: Develop methods for tracking subspace dynamics throughout training.
Extend SAILS to other alignment objectives beyond safety.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment -- training large language models (LLMs) to refuse harmful requests while remaining helpful -- is critical for responsible deployment. Prior work established that safety behaviors are governed by low-rank structures, suggesting parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) should be well-suited for alignment. However, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) consistently underperforms full fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on safety benchmarks. We attribute this gap to semantic entanglement: safety-relevant directions are intertwined with unrelated concepts due to polysemanticity, impeding implicit subspace identification. To address this, we propose SAILS (Safety Alignment via Interpretable Low-rank Subspace), which leverages Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to disentangle representations into monosemantic features, constructs an interpretable safety subspace from SAE decoder directions, and uses it to initialize LoRA adapters. Theoretically, we prove that SAE-based identification achieves arbitrarily small recovery error under monosemanticity assumptions, while direct identification suffers an irreducible error floor. Empirically, SAILS achieves up to 99.6% safety rate on Gemma-2-9B -- exceeding full fine-tuning by 7.4 points and matching RLHF-based models -- while updating only 0.19% of parameters and providing interpretability.

papers.title: Understanding Syntax in Large Language Models: Successes and Limitations
papers.research_question: How accurately can LLMs handle published examples of complex syntactic phenomena, as described in linguistic theories?
papers.core_contribution: This study evaluates the syntactic competence of LLMs, finding that while they handle simple constructions well, they struggle with complex hierarchical dependencies, highlighting the need for integrating explicit syntactic principles.
papers.conclusion: LLMs demonstrate competence in simple syntax but struggle with complex structures, indicating a gap between surface fluency and deep syntactic competence, necessitating hybrid approaches for improvement.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit high success rates for simple relative clauses and basic wh-movement, but performance declines with increased complexity.
Center-embedding poses significant challenges, with success rates dropping to around 50% for deeply embedded structures.
Errors include truncation of sentences, unresolved syntactic dependencies, and semantic incoherence in complex cases.
LLMs rely on surface-level pattern recognition rather than deep generative syntactic principles.
The limitations suggest that current LLMs lack robust internal representations of hierarchical syntax.
papers.limitation:
The analysis relied exclusively on examples from English linguistic literature, not capturing syntactic diversity across languages.
The evaluation focused only on relative clauses, wh-movement, and center-embedding, without exploring broader syntactic constructs.
The study was limited to publicly available LLMs like GPT-4 and BERT, without considering effects of model size, architecture, or training data.
The evaluation did not delve into underlying representations or mechanisms of the models.
future_direction: Integrating explicit syntactic theory into neural architectures, such as the Minimalist Program or dependency grammar.
Conducting cross-linguistic comparisons to evaluate LLMs' syntactic competence across different languages.
Designing more linguistically focused benchmarks based on theoretical constructs like syntactic islands or scope ambiguity.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to process complex syntactic phenomena, including relative clauses, wh-movement, and center- embedding. By analyzing examples derived from linguistic literature, the study highlights both the strengths and limitations of LLMs in handling syntax. The results reveal that while LLMs exhibit competence in simpler syntactic constructions, they struggle with deeper hierarchical dependencies and abstract syntactic constraints. The study underscores the need for integrating explicit syntactic principles into LLM architectures to bridge the gap between surface-level fluency and generative linguistic competence.

papers.title: OR-Bench: An Over-Refusal Benchmark for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we systematically measure over-refusal in large language models, and what is the trade-off between safety and over-refusal?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces OR-Bench, the first large-scale over-refusal benchmark, and uses it to evaluate 32 LLMs, revealing a strong correlation between safety and over-refusal.
papers.conclusion: OR-Bench provides a large-scale benchmark for evaluating over-refusal, facilitating future research on the trade-off between safety and helpfulness in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
There is a strong correlation between safety and over-refusal (Spearman rank correlation 0.89).
Claude models demonstrate the highest safety but also the most over-refusal.
Mistral models accept most prompts (low over-refusal).
GPT-3.5-turbo exhibits decreasing over-refusal in later versions, but with reduced safety.
Model size does not necessarily correlate with better safety-sensitivity balance.
papers.limitation:
The use of LLM as the moderator may result in the dataset including toxic or debatable prompts.
There may be bias favoring the LLMs used as judges.
future_direction: Future safety alignment algorithms should consider both toxic and over-refusal prompts to achieve improved safety alignment.
Further exploration of fine-tuning LLMs as judges for moderation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) require careful safety alignment to prevent malicious outputs. While significant research focuses on mitigating harmful content generation, the enhanced safety often come with the side effect of over-refusal, where LLMs may reject innocuous prompts and become less helpful. Although the issue of over-refusal has been empirically observed, a systematic measurement is challenging due to the difficulty of crafting prompts that can elicit the over-refusal behaviors of LLMs. This study proposes a novel method for automatically generating large-scale over-refusal datasets. Leveraging this technique, we introduce OR-Bench, the first large-scale over-refusal benchmark. OR-Bench comprises 80,000 over-refusal prompts across 10 common rejection categories, a subset of around 1,000 hard prompts that are challenging even for state-of-the-art LLMs, and an additional 600 toxic prompts to prevent indiscriminate responses. We then conduct a comprehensive study to measure the over-refusal of 32 popular LLMs across 8 model families. Our datasets are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/bench-llms and our codebase is open-sourced at https://github.com/justincui03/or-bench. We hope this benchmark can help the community develop better safety aligned models.

papers.title: Analysis and Visualization of Linguistic Structures in Large Language Models: Neural Representations of Verb-Particle Constructions in BERT
papers.research_question: Do the internal representations of BERT capture lexical semantics and phrase-level structure for verb-particle combinations? Which layers capture these phenomena, and can the activations be explained by usage-based theories?
papers.core_contribution: The study finds that BERT's middle layers most effectively capture syntactic structures of verb-particle constructions, with significant variability in representational accuracy across different verb categories, challenging assumptions of uniform neural network processing.
papers.conclusion: The research underscores the capabilities of neural language models in processing linguistic sequences and provides a foundation for future investigations aimed at advancing their linguistic representational power.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's middle layers are most effective in capturing syntactic structures of verb-particle constructions.
There is significant variability in representational accuracy across different verb categories (e.g., 'agree', 'come', 'give').
The model captures the lexical unity of phrasal verbs (e.g., 'give up') and the compositionality of prepositional verbs (e.g., 'agree on').
Early and intermediate layers show strong clustering of constructions, while late layers show weak clustering, indicating less semantic unity.
The findings suggest a complex interplay between network architecture and linguistic representation.
future_direction: Further research into optimizing neural architectures for enhanced linguistic precision.
A multidisciplinary approach combining insights from computational linguistics, cognitive science, and neuroscience to develop models that better reflect human language understanding.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the internal representations of verb-particle combinations within transformer-based large language models (LLMs), specifically examining how these models capture lexical and syntactic nuances at different neural network layers. Employing the BERT architecture, we analyse the representational efficacy of its layers for various verb-particle constructions such as 'agree on', 'come back', and 'give up'. Our methodology includes a detailed dataset preparation from the British National Corpus, followed by extensive model training and output analysis through techniques like multi-dimensional scaling (MDS) and generalized discrimination value (GDV) calculations. Results show that BERT's middle layers most effectively capture syntactic structures, with significant variability in representational accuracy across different verb categories. These findings challenge the conventional uniformity assumed in neural network processing of linguistic elements and suggest a complex interplay between network architecture and linguistic representation. Our research contributes to a better understanding of how deep learning models comprehend and process language, offering insights into the potential and limitations of current neural approaches to linguistic analysis. This study not only advances our knowledge in computational linguistics but also prompts further research into optimizing neural architectures for enhanced linguistic precision.

papers.title: AISA: Awakening Intrinsic Safety Awareness in Large Language Models against Jailbreak Attacks
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreak attacks in large language models by awakening their intrinsic safety awareness without fine-tuning or external modules?
papers.core_contribution: AISA is a lightweight defense framework that extracts intrinsic safety signals from attention head activations via linear probing and uses them to steer generation through logits adjustment, achieving robust jailbreak defense without model tuning.
papers.conclusion: AISA provides an effective, lightweight defense against jailbreak attacks by leveraging intrinsic safety awareness in LLMs, offering a resource-efficient alternative to safety alignment tuning.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs possess intrinsic safety awareness even without safety-specific fine-tuning, as evidenced by refusal behavior in uncensored models.
Attention head outputs, particularly at the final structural token before generation, provide the strongest discriminative signal for prompt intent.
AISA's data-driven head selection and logits steering outperform existing defense baselines in safety and utility preservation across diverse jailbreak datasets.
The safety awareness signal is architecture-dependent and persists across alignment variants, indicating a common pretrained basis.
AISA enables unaligned models to match or exceed the safety performance of aligned counterparts while avoiding over-refusal.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak prompts that elicit harmful or policy-violating outputs, while many existing defenses rely on expensive fine-tuning, intrusive prompt rewriting, or external guardrails that add latency and can degrade helpfulness. We present AISA, a lightweight, single-pass defense that activates safety behaviors already latent inside the model rather than treating safety as an add-on. AISA first localizes intrinsic safety awareness via spatiotemporal analysis and shows that intent-discriminative signals are broadly encoded, with especially strong separability appearing in the scaled dot-product outputs of specific attention heads near the final structural tokens before generation. Using a compact set of automatically selected heads, AISA extracts an interpretable prompt-risk score with minimal overhead, achieving detector-level performance competitive with strong proprietary baselines on small (7B) models. AISA then performs logits-level steering: it modulates the decoding distribution in proportion to the inferred risk, ranging from normal generation for benign prompts to calibrated refusal for high-risk requests -- without changing model parameters, adding auxiliary modules, or requiring multi-pass inference. Extensive experiments spanning 13 datasets, 12 LLMs, and 14 baselines demonstrate that AISA improves robustness and transfer while preserving utility and reducing false refusals, enabling safer deployment even for weakly aligned or intentionally risky model variants.

papers.title: Morph Call: Probing Morphosyntactic Content of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: What morphosyntactic knowledge do multilingual transformer models encode, and how does fine-tuning for POS-tagging affect this knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Morph Call, a suite of 46 probing tasks for four languages, and uses multiple introspection methods to analyze morphosyntactic knowledge in multilingual transformers, finding that fine-tuning for POS-tagging can both improve and decrease probing performance and change knowledge distribution.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents Morph Call, a probing suite for morphosyntactic content, and finds that knowledge distribution depends on language morphology (with English differing from more morphologically rich languages) and that fine-tuning for POS-tagging can affect the models in multiple ways.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual transformers learn morphosyntactic content in a similar manner across languages, with properties distributed across middle-to-higher layers.
Masked token tasks are more challenging and show unstable performance across layers, with properties best inferred at middle-to-higher layers.
Models are sensitive to syntactic and inflectional perturbations, with syntactic perturbations better solved than inflectional ones.
Distilled models (D-BERT, MiniLM) mimic their teachers' behavior on some tasks but may show uncertain behavior on others.
Fine-tuning for POS-tagging affects model knowledge in various ways: it can improve or decrease probing performance, change the localization of information, and alter the number of neurons required for a property.
future_direction: Analyze the correlation between the number of neurons and probe performance after fine-tuning.
Explore fine-tuning for morphosyntactic analysis over UniMorph.
Test the hypothesis on a more diverse set of morphologically contrasting languages.
papers.abstract: The outstanding performance of transformerbased language models on a great variety of NLP and NLU tasks has stimulated interest in exploring their inner workings. Recent research has focused primarily on higherlevel and complex linguistic phenomena such as syntax, semantics, world knowledge, and common sense. The majority of the studies are anglocentric, and little remains known regarding other languages, precisely their morphosyntactic properties. To this end, our work presents Morph Call, a suite of 46 probing tasks for four Indo-European languages of different morphology: English, French, German and Russian. We propose a new type of probing task based on the detection of guided sentence perturbations. We use a combination of neuron-, layer-and representation-level introspection techniques to analyze the morphosyntactic content of four multilingual transformers, including their less explored distilled versions. Besides, we examine how fine-tuning for POS-tagging affects the model knowledge. The results show that fine-tuning can improve and decrease the probing performance and change how morphosyntactic knowledge is distributed across the model. The code and data are publicly available, and we hope to fill the gaps in the less studied aspect of transformers.

papers.title: Compositional generalization in a deep seq2seq model by separating syntax and semantics
papers.research_question: Does separating syntactic and semantic processing in a neural machine translation model improve compositional generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel seq2seq model, Syntactic Attention, which separates syntactic and semantic processing streams. This architectural constraint substantially improves compositional generalization on the SCAN dataset without hand-engineered features or additional supervision.
papers.conclusion: Separating syntactic and semantic information processing in neural networks encourages systematic, compositional generalization, drawing a conceptual link to hypothesized brain mechanisms and suggesting a useful heuristic for AI.
papers.key_findings:
The Syntactic Attention model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the SCAN dataset's add-jump split, with a median accuracy of 91.0%, a significant improvement over prior models.
The model's performance is highly variable across random initializations on the add-jump split, indicating sensitivity to how the novel verb 'jump' is encoded.
Ablation experiments show that allowing sequential information into the semantic stream ('sequential semantics') degrades compositional generalization, supporting the separation hypothesis.
The model generalizes well from very few examples of a novel verb, achieving near-perfect accuracy with just two training examples containing 'jump'.
The model fails on some SCAN template splits (e.g., 'Primitive opposite right'), indicating limitations in generalizing based on symmetry when training data is skewed.
papers.limitation:
The model's performance on the add-jump split is highly variable and skewed across different random initializations, with some runs failing catastrophically.
The separation between syntax and semantics in the brain is likely not as strict as implemented in the model, suggesting the principle may be more of a useful heuristic than a biological fact.
future_direction: Future research should investigate the factors causing performance variability on tasks like the add-jump split and whether other priors or regularization techniques can overcome it.
The principle of separating syntax and semantics may be a useful heuristic in other natural language processing tasks and other systematic or compositional generalization tasks.
papers.abstract: Standard methods in deep learning for natural language processing fail to capture the compositional structure of human language that allows for systematic generalization outside of the training distribution. However, human learners readily generalize in this way, e.g. by applying known grammatical rules to novel words. Inspired by work in neuroscience suggesting separate brain systems for syntactic and semantic processing, we implement a modification to standard approaches in neural machine translation, imposing an analogous separation. The novel model, which we call Syntactic Attention, substantially outperforms standard methods in deep learning on the SCAN dataset, a compositional generalization task, without any hand-engineered features or additional supervision. Our work suggests that separating syntactic from semantic learning may be a useful heuristic for capturing compositional structure.

papers.title: Should Neural Network Architecture Reflect Linguistic Structure?
papers.research_question: Should neural network architecture reflect linguistic structure for better language modeling and representation of sentence meanings?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces recurrent neural network grammars (RNNGs) that incorporate hierarchical syntactic structure, showing they outperform sequential and tree-structured RNNs in language generation and downstream semantic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Neural network architectures that reflect linguistic structure, such as RNNGs, are more effective for language modeling and representation.
papers.key_findings:
RNNGs achieve better language generation results compared to models that do not exploit linguistic structure.
Unsupervised learning of syntactic structures using reinforcement learning improves performance on downstream semantic tasks over sequential and tree-structured RNNs.
papers.abstract: I explore the hypothesis that conventional neural network models (e.g., recurrent neural networks) are incorrectly biased for making linguistically sensible generalizations when learning, and that a better class of models is based on architectures that reflect hierarchical structures for which considerable behavioral evidence exists. I focus on the problem of modeling and representing the meanings of sentences. On the generation front, I introduce recurrent neural network grammars (RNNGs), a joint, generative model of phrase-structure trees and sentences. RNNGs operate via a recursive syntactic process reminiscent of probabilistic context-free grammar generation, but decisions are parameterized using RNNs that condition on the entire (top-down, left-to-right) syntactic derivation history, thus relaxing context-free independence assumptions, while retaining a bias toward explaining decisions via "syntactically local" conditioning contexts. Experiments show that RNNGs obtain better results in generating language than models that don't exploit linguistic structure. On the representation front, I explore unsupervised learning of syntactic structures based on distant semantic supervision using a reinforcement-learning algorithm. The learner seeks a syntactic structure that provides a compositional architecture that produces a good representation for a downstream semantic task. Although the inferred structures are quite different from traditional syntactic analyses, the performance on the downstream tasks surpasses that of systems that use sequential RNNs and tree-structured RNNs based on treebank dependencies.

papers.title: On the Emergence and Test-Time Use of Structural Information in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models learn abstract structures and utilize the learnt structural information at test-time?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the emergence of structural information during learning correlates with complex reasoning tasks, and that the ability to perform test-time compositional generation remains limited.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can learn structural information during fine-tuning, but their ability to flexibly re-compose out-of-distribution to produce new knowledge is limited. MLP sublayers are more important for syntactic transformations and the separation between concepts emerges during training and is linearly encoded.
papers.key_findings:
The emergence of learning structural information correlates with complex reasoning tasks.
The ability to perform test-time compositional generation remains limited.
Models capture distinct internal representations for different syntactic transformations, and these representations become more separable during training.
MLP blocks contribute more to syntactic transformation success than attention mechanisms.
The probability of predicting the correct token for a transformation increases sharply in the final third of the network.
